BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF 0ALIFOBNIA :At the last Communication of this M.·. W.'. Grand L<tdge you conferred upon
me the highest honor within your gift, and signified in the strongest manner possible your fraternal confidence and esteem, by placing in my hands the Grand
Master's gavel for the year now about expiring. For this most emphatic token of
your high respect my heart responds with sincerest gratitude.
The year of my exaltation now draws to a close, and the report of my stewardship is here presented. I congratulate you, and the fraternity of this juriscliction,
that the past year has not been marked by any serious discord among the craft.
The correspondence of my office has been extensive, but, by rare goi>d fortune, few
perplexing questions have arisen; the exercise of executive power has rarely been
invoked; and in no case has it been deemed necessary to have recourse to the high
prerogative powers of.the office in any but matters of an agreeable nature.
The vear has been one the peace, tranquillity, prosperity, and happiness of
which have been marked and emphasized, rather than interrupted, by only infrequent sounds of discord. No present or Past Grand officer has been summoned
hence; no great pestilence, epidemic, or other wide-spread calamity has visito<I our
territory. Floods and fires have raged in other lauds, but have touched us lightly.
Mother earth has yielded an abundant harvest and gladdened our hearts with her
millions of shining gold and nutritious grain. In ple.oe of the fierce and relentless
storms which have swept over and devastated other States, we have been fanned by
gentle breezes laden with fragrance and life-giying vigor. To God, "from whom
all blessings fiow," let us reverently bend the knee and render grateful adoration
and praise .
While the correspondence of my office has embraced somo hundreds of letters,
very many of these were of a nature to require no special notice in this report.
Many contained inquiries, the answers to which consisted of mere citations to sections of the Constitution, or to resolutions or edicts of this Grand Lodge; and
with such matters I deem it unnecessary to encumber the proceedings of this august
body, but shall confine this report to such questions as seemed to bo new, or of such
importance as to merit your consideration.
In my judgment eru;h subordinate Lodge should be permitted to manage its own
affairs, so far as may be consistent with the good of the craft; but when a Lodge,

having a limited membership and no considerabl~ accumulation of funds, reduc~d
its monthly dues to twen"ty-five cents, I felt constrained to withhold my consent to
the amendment to its by-laws providing for the reduction. Doubtless the paymen.t
of dues frequently becomes an onerous burden upon many a good Ma.son, and possibly the dues in some Lodges are now maintained at too high a figure; but certainly every Lodge should have a secure and reliable income sufficient to meet the
ordinary expenses, and keep something in the treasury for emergencies and works
of charity.

Bro. RucXfill, of La G'range Lodge, No. 99, proposed thisqueation: "Is an actual
residence within the State for six months necessary in order to entitleapartytopetition for the degrees; and will a temporary absence from the State, covering a part
of the last six months before petitioning, debar him?" '.l.'bis was answered in the
negative ; my decision being, that so long as the petitioner is in good faith and
intention a resident of the State, a temporary absence, with the continuous intention of returning to his California domicile, does not· disqualify him.
A somewhat singular case arose in Janesville Lodge, No. 232, and my advice was
called for in the premises. In conferring the third degree upon a candidate, and
just as he was being instructed in the guard and sign, he was seized with sudden
illness and had to be removed from the Lodge room and carried to bis home, where
he continued for some time to be so sick that bis life was in great peril. The Lodge
thereupon desfred to know the status of the afflicted brother, his rights and privileges, and the duties of the craft and Lodge toward him. My decision was that,
since the brother had taken the
which ma.de him a
>II<
>II< >II< ,
he was entitled. for all p~rposes of charity ancl relief, to be so considered and treated,
and in case of his death was entitled to Masonic burial; and that, when his health was
sufficiently restored, it was the duty of the Lodge to begin where its proceedings
were interrupted and impart to him that to which he was already entitled. But it
being feared that, even if he survived his severe illness, he might not sufficiently
recover all hiR faculties to conform to the ritual in the remaining portions of the
degree, the Lodge desired to know what then would be bis statue; and to this I
answered-" He is a Master Mason, and entitled to be so considered for certain'. purposes; but, not having been fully in.structed, he is not a member of the Lodge, and
cannot sit in a Master· Mason's Lodge."
In the matter of charges against the Worshipful Master of Colusa Lodge, No,
142, this Grand Lodge, at its last Annual Comrrnnication, reversed the decision of
the Grand Master, refusing to appoint a Commission, and l}ence it devolved upon
me to make the appointment; but, before the necessary information could be had
and a suitable Co~miesion selected, the annual election was held and another
brother was chosen as Worshipful Master of the Lodge; wherefore, I concluded
that since Colusa Lodge was no longer disqualified to try the charges, it would be.
best to send the matter back there for adjustment, and it was so ordered.
In answer to inquiries from several Secretaries of Lodges, I ,have uniformly
instructed that nQ action of the Lodge· is necessary to authorize the Secretary to
issue a _cert.ificate of membership as a basis for an application for a Grand Lodge
Diploma; that every memqer of a Lodge is en titled to have such certificate so long
as he is in good standing and his dues are paid ; and the Secretary has full authority to issue the certiftca te, attested by the Lodge seal.
A question arose as to which Ludge should pay the expenses of a trial, where one
Lodge preferred charges against a non-affiliate residing within the jurisdiction of
another Lodge. Not being aware of any written law upon the subject, present and
past Grand officers were consulted by me, and the conclusion was arrived at that the
established custom or uslge has been for the Lodge making the charge to defray
the expenses of the trial. While this was my decision, it does not entirely satisfy .
my judgment, and it" is respectfully submitted to the Grand Lodge, that the ques. tion may be settled for the future. There is something meriting consideration in

e11pecia.lly for the benefit of the complaining Lodge.
S?veral Lodges have ma.de inquiries as to the proper course to pursue where a
candidate ha.a been initiated, and, after waiting for several years without apparent
cau~e, has presented himself for advancement. My reply to all has been, that after
taking proper care to ascertain whether or not, in the meantime, any valid objection
to advancement has a.risen, the candidate, if worthy and well qualified, should be
advanced, and that where he was originally elected to the three degrees, an additional ballot was not necessary or proper.
Touching the rights of contributing non-affiliates, the following decision was
ma.de: 1st. A non-affiliated Mason has the right to tender a contribution equal to
the monthly dues to any Lodge in the jurisdiction of which he resides and the
Lodge has the right either to accept or reject the same. 2d. When a no~-affiliated
Mason contributes or tenders to some Lodge an amount equivalent to the monthly
dues, he. thereby merely preserves his standing in tbP, Craft, and is entitled to all
th~ charities and fratemal courtesies due a Mason at large. He does not, by contrib~tiug to any Lodge, become in any sense a member thereof, and has not, neceesa'.ily, any greater claim upon such Lodge than any other non-affiliate in good standmg. Where a non-affiliate resides within the exclusive territorial jurisdiction ofone
:Lodge and contributes thereto, it is clearly the duty of that Lodge to see that he
is not " made a b_u rden to others." Thie duty, however, arises from the fa-0t of hia
~siding wit~n the ~uri~diction of the .~ge, and not as a reciprocal duty result~ng f:om his. contr1but10n-the contribution merely having the effect of preaervmg hl8 standing. But when the contributing non-affiliate lives within 0 city under
the ".°ncurrent ju~d~ction of several Lodges, the fact that one of such Loqgee has
rec.eived his contribution does not increase the measure of duty of that Lod'.ge, nor
reheve any other Lodge, of concurrent jurisdiction, of its obligations. In case of
the death o~ a br~the~· under such .circumstances, he should be buried by the
BoS:d of Rehef, while, if he has contributed for any considerable length of time e:i:clusively to ~ne Lod.ge, a v~ry str.ong moral obligation would rest upon such Lodge
to extend relief to him or his family out of its own treasury.

The Lodges in the Twenty-ninth District, as reported by Bro. McGunlE, transact
all their business in conformity to the Constitutioti and regulations.
A good report comes from Bro. HINES, of the Thirtieth District; "He is a good
man &nd bringeth good tidings." He reports that all the Lodges in his district
work well up to the ritual; that their records and accounts are well kept, and their
financial condition sound. He suggests the consolidation of Santa Barbara, Lodge,
No. 192, and Magnolia, No. 242, both located in Santa Barbara, and occupying the
same Lodge room ; which would make one strong and vigorous Lodge, in place of
two feeble ones. This suggestion is a good one, and if the process of consolidation
should be resorted to in many other localities much good would result.
While the condition of the several Lodges in the Thirty-first District, as reported
by Bro. HINDS, is not all that could be desired, still the outlook is encouraging. He
very justly complains of the too prevalent practice of remitting dues in some of the
Lodges. In one Lodge of eighty-four members, the books show the enormous sum
of $867 of delinquent dues; and in another, members able to pay were relieved of
their arrearages, when the Lodge had not in its treasury enough to pay the dues to
this Grand Lodge.
Bro. ClRTIS, of the Thirty-second District, reporU! fue seed planted by this
Grand Lodge in Arizona soil as flourishing and promising much in the future.
These are the only reports which came to hand in time to receive special mention
in this report. Qt.hers have been received more i·ecently, and are, together with
those already referred to, submitted herewith for your consideration. Much valuable information is contained in some of them, but I feel compelled to limit this
portion of my address to a bare reference to some of their general fea~ures.

I herewith present a circular reoently received from the so-oalled Grand Lodge of
Ontario, but, inasmuch as this matter was pretty effectually disposed of at our Annual Communication in the year 1876, (see printed proceedings at pages 860 au'd 492)
I deem it inexpedient to re-open the question, and therefore submit the same, without comment, for your consideration.
A question of conventional jurisdiction has arisen between Greenville Lodge, No.
249, and Sincerity Lodge, No.132. It is represented that when Greenville Lodgewae
&bout to organize, the petitioning or charter members applied to Sincerity Lodge.,that being the nearest chartered Lodge-for a recommendation that a dispensation
luue; which recommendation was cheerfully given, but with an express agreement
upon a line of jurisdiction about one mile nearer the new Lodge than a central line
between the two. A misunderstanding has arisen, and my opinion as to the validity
of such an arrangement of jurisdiotional lines was invoked by Sincerity Lodge.
Not deeming it essential that the question should be hastily settled, and being in
much doubt, I respectfully refer the question to this Grand Body, and recommend
that the proper committee hear the representatives of the two Lodges, and report
their decision of the question.
With this report l present a circular letter just received from Bro. WILLIAM p.
~NEB, Grand Seoretary of the Grand Lodge of Michigan, appealing to the fraternity of the United States for contributions for the relief of sufferers from the fire
that recently raged over the northeastern part of that State and laid waste a large
section of a flourishing country. The snft'ering is represent.ed to be great and tl1e
need of contributions urgent. Such &n appeal never went unheeded in this land of
generous deedY, and I therefoi:e deem it unneceSBary to do more than bring this cry
of distrees to your knowledge, and leave your own heartll to suggest the response.
. To this Grand Lodge will be submitted the report of a Special Committee appomted at the last Annual Communication to prepare and submit a plan for the establishment of a permanent institution for the relief, care, and maintenance of our
orphan children. The committee is composed of able and thoughtful men, and it
may well be assumed that whatever plan shall be recommended by such committee
will be good. It is not my purpose however to forestall the judgment of any member
of this body in favor of any particular scheme, and you are earnestly entreated to
give this momentous question your most profound consideration. No more important matter will come before you, and now is the time to think and act. Weare about
to lay the foundations of a structure that may, if we act unwisely, dwindle, decay,
and tumble down; or which may grow and increase, and accumulate power for good,
and become so permanent and firmly established that thousands of grateful heart.&
will praise the generous scheme after you and I have been forgotten. Benevolence
to mankind is man's noblest work; and man never approaches nearer the attributes
of Divinity, than when engaged in scheme~ of pure and unselfish charity. We have
it now within our power by the exercise of prudence and good judgment to !naugu·
rate a plan of systematic and substantial charity that will reflect. credit not alone
upon us, but also upon the age in which we live. Let a free and full discussion be
had, and the~ let us adopt the plan proposed by the committee, or such other plan
as maypromlSe better results; and if possible let it be put Into immediate operation.
Above all things let ns avoid the too common error of attempting to conduct an extensive enterprise upon other than sound business princivles. Whatever plan of or·
ganization may be determined upon, this Grand Lodge should, in my judgment,
manage, control, and assume responsibility for it, and not one dollar's indebtedness
whould ever be incurred without the dollar being first provided to meet the debt.
No costly buildings should be erected at present, nor should any unreasonable or
utopian thing be attempted. If we manage wisely, as we must, the necess\ry means
can be readily furnished by the Lodges alone, and if we succeed in laying well the

A painful theme now comes in place. On the second day of last July, while the
nation of which we are proud to be humble citizens, Wiii! decorating its halls, its
streets, and its homes in holiday attire for the joyous celebration of the Nate.I Day
of the proudest enactment of our country's history, a single vile a.ct turned all our
joy to woe and plunged a happy people into the depths of anxious grief. A great
and good man who ha.d been chosen to the highest political place attainable by
man• one with whom a nation was satisfied, and of whom a. nation was proud;
one
whose noble and generous impulses the conflicting sectionalism and distrust hitherto disturbing our land were rapidly yielding; one whose great heart
and honesty of purpose were rapidly uniting the severed chains of mutual confidence and unity, and rekindling the SII\ouldering fires of patriotism throughout
the States · one whose every. thought anii a.ct reflected the light imparted to him
in a Maso~io Lodge-was struck down by an act of unprovoked, nnmitigated,
and fiendish llllSassination. I cannot dwell upon the dreadful thought nor recount to you bow that brave and magnan1mous man, in spite of his ghastly
and mortal wound, kept grim-visaged death at bay week after week, with a sublime
and heroic resolution to cling to life and perform his unfinished mission, until e.11 of
him that was mortal had so wasted away as to be unable longer to contain bis great
soul.
When the solemn clang of the weeping bells tolled out the mournful intelligence
of his death the nations of the earth put on the habiliments of woe, and the twentysixth day or' September, in the yee.r of our Lord 1881, when bis body was consigned
to earth, :was entered upon the calendar as the gloomiest day of time. This
Grand Lodge was specially convened, and joined the sorrowing throng which, all
over the land, celebrated the last sad rites to the nation's dead, and our departed
brother.

It is a matter of much regret to the undersigned that his lack of health did not permit
him to prepare, in time for publication with the proceedings of last year, the enlarged
and corrected catslogue of the books In the library of the Grand Lodge which,
In his report of that year, he had proposed. But in March last the catalogue was
completed and published in a separate pamphlet of fifty-two pages, octavo, and oop·
ies thereof were sent to all the varions Masonic Grand Bodies in the world to which
we are known, and to the'mauy Masonic publishers, collectors, and bibliomaniacs
with whom the writer bas so long held correspondence. It comprised the following:5 volumes, folio, oontainiug 1,220 pages;
39 volumes, 4to., containing 11 ,484 pages;
1032 volumes, 8vo., containing 657 ,490 pages;
l?.7 volumes, 12mo., containing 37,1'6 pages;
16 volumes, 16 mo., containing 2,896 pages;
37 volumes, 24.mo., containing 18, 982 pages;
15 volumes, 32mo., cuntaining 3,126 pages;
being in all one thousand two hundred and seventy-one volumes, and aggregating
six hundred and thirty-two thousand three hundred and forty-four pages ; thus
showing an average of nearly five hundred pages per volume. There are also, in
addition to the six hundred and fifty-three bound volumes of the transactions of
Grand Bodies included in the foregoing, a large number of copies of proceedings on
hand,.which, if a comparatively few missing years can be procured, would, when

held under the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of :France, sGtting forth, in effect,
that the Grand Lodges of New York and California were in error in supposing that
the Lodges of Constantinople were all under the jurisdiction of the Graud Lodge of
England, inasmuch as, in fa.ct, they were· in obedience to several different Grand

France, with the request that ft be forwarded to the two Grand Lodges above named.
Iu accordance with that request, Bro. TBEVJtNoT, Chief of the Secretariat General of
the Grand Orient of France, has forwarded the letter, with a personal note to the
undersigned, dated on the ninth day of July 1111t, stating that he does not write to
our Grand Lodge, officially, in consequence of the severance of Masonic relations
between our two Grand Bodies, b11t giving his a•surance that the statements in the
enclosed letter are just and correct, aud suggesting that they receive such attention
as may be deemed proper by our Grand Lodge.
Early In the present year 11 printed circular, purporting to be from FBEDF.RIOK
CA.BRER, Master of "Star of the EaBt Lodge, No. 880.' 1 at Zante, Greece, was
received by the undersigned. It set forth that the brethren there had "been for
some time endeavoring to build 11 Masonic Lodge, hut had been unsuocesRful ;" and
that, "Masonry In Greece being in Its Infancy, this Lodge cannot recAlve any a'd
from the country; the brethren therefore ht.ve decided to appeal to the Sister Lodges,
etc.'' The circular wa~ accompanied by "sixty tickets for a distribution of prlzeP,"
1vith the Ptatement that" the Siar qf the East Lodge earnestly requestA the brethren
to dispose of them." It was also stated that the money received " may be remitted
as soon as possible to the Union Bank of London;" that "the prizes will be of the
he•t description and forwarded Immediately after the drawing, which wiU take place
on Friday, Ma~ 27th, 1881, In the Lodge Room, at Za.nte ;'' and that" the building·of
a Lodge in Zante is highly necessary, and also it will give an Immense Impulse to
Freemasonry throughout Greece.'' Illness, 11nd a consequent accumulation or correspondence, prewented a response to the foregoing until the Pixth day of Aprll laet,
when, after conference with tile Grand Master, Mr. CARRER was Informed, In effect,
that the proposed sale of lottery tickets did not appear to be the proper method in
which to ask for Masonic aPBistance; that they had not therefore been oft'ered for
sale to our Lodges; and that the tickets, in the original package, were then respectfully returned. At a later period, perhaps before that letter bad reached its destina·
tion, another printed circular was received from Mr. CABBEll, datecl at Zsnte on the
twenty-seventh day of May, 1881, sta\ing, In elfect, that many LodgeM had neglected
to make returns in regard to the tickets sent to them; that consequently "an adjournment of the drawing bad become Indispensable;" that the time therefor had again
" been daflnitely fixed for the 13th October, 1881 ;" and that, the account wltli the
bank before named having bern oloeed, 1111 remittances were to be made to bis name,
etc. To this it was responded, on the eleventh dtly of July last, that the tickets had
been returned at the date ubove given, for the reasons therein set forth. It Is only
necessary to add that no Information has been given in rage.rd to the Grand Body
which bears this "old Lodge," No. 880, on Its register.

The story of the little Masomc orp

Grarul Lodge of California.

35

New Orleans during the .Yellow fever epidemic and who was kindly forwarded by
the Relief Lodge of that city to his aged grandmother, residing in Oakland, near this
city, is too well known to require recitation ; and, at pages 149, 202, 205, and ~il7 of
our Proceedings for 1879, will be found the history of the manner in whioh our Grand
Lodge in some sort adopted the little waif. The sum of six hundred dollars was then
appropriated for his care and maintenance, and, In addition thereto, the sam of sixty·
eight dollars was contributed for the same purpose by members of the Grand Lodgo.
It was understood at the time that these amounts should be expended under the direction of the Grand Master ; and it will be seen in the Address of that officer, at page
422 of the Proceediogs of 1880, that twenty-five dollars per month was thus directed
to be paid. Up to the end of our late fiscal year, Joly SI, 1881, the sum of six hundred nod six doilars had thus been expended, and since then, for the months of
August and September, fifty dollars more have been added to the expenditure ; leaving now to the credit of that charitable and creditable appropriation only the sum of
twelve dollars. The underoigned begs to indulge the hope that a further appropriation will be made at the present Communication.
It will not be improper to present the following l ittle addition to the history of
the t case. About a year ago the child was not well and his grandmother desired to
take him to the East for a time on a visit to ~ome of her friends. Bot she was unable
to incnr the necessary expense, and asked if snlllcient influence could be used to
procure free passage for him . upon an emigrant train. The facts were madQ known
to A. N. TOWNE, Esq., General.S uperintendent of t,he Central Pacific Railroad, who not
only generously offered flrst·class tickets for them both to Ogden, but gave the under·
signed letters to J. T. CLARK, Esq., General Superintendent of the Union Pacific, and
D. W. HrToHoocx, Esq., General Manager of the Chicago, Dnrlington, and Quincy
Railroad ; upon tho receipt of wbiob, with the same liberality and with kindly
promptitude, similar free passes were transmitted for their use to Omaha and Chicago. It is with mnch pleasure that the writer thus publicly acknowledges, on
behalf of the Grand Master and himself, the kindness of the gen Ile men whose names
are above given.
Sundry letters in regard to the little boy, the replies to which will be found in the
l etter books, are herewith submitted.

To the M.'. W.'. (}ranu Lodge of Galifomia :I herewith present my Annual Report of the condition of the Lodges in thl~
jurisdiction, as ascertained from personal observation and from the reports '.of tue
Inspectors of the various districts which have beeo ijUbmitted to me.
I have visited during the year, In company with the Graud Master, di~tricts Nos.
15, 17, 28, aod 26. The Lodges comprised In these districts are but a email proportion of the aggregate nnmber of our jnrisdiction, but our system of Inspection is now
so perfectly organized as to render personal vleit-1 by the Grand Lecturer unneces·
sary, except wlien specially invited, or In some po•sible case of emergency.
In the 15th, 17th, and 26th dlstrlots, upon the occasion of my vlait1, I personally
exemplified the work; while In the other district vl9ited, (the 23d,) the officers of
the various Lodges conferred the tbirtl degree with hn aocur11oy of detail and dignifte<l impressiveness which elicited our heRrty commendation. On tlleee occa·
sions, in addition to instruction In the secret work of the Order, I endeavored
tl imprelll! upon the miude of the brethren the lmpornnce of paying more ol\refui att ~ntion to public ceremonial observances-more e•peclally those connected
with the borial of the dead. The performance of these ceremonle~, conducted, as
they are, In the presence of the bereaved relatives and friends of the deceased and of
the pnhlic generally, &bould be characterized by all the eolemnity, dignity, and !mpres·
slvenese with which it is possible to· invest them. There ls no privilege appertain·
log to the Order of which Masone in general are so tenacious as the right of Masonic
burial; and,so earnestly le this regarded that many, long before the approach of the
dread messenger, reque't some brother,in case he should be the survivor, to see that
this last token of respect to hie memory be paid; and, In n1aoy instances, they select the

40

Procedings of the

brother who is desired to olllciate upon the solemn occasion. In view, therefore, of
the value set upon this privilege by the great majority of Masons, in deference to the
feelings of the relatives and friends of the deceased, and with a proper regard for the
reputation of our Order before the public, no acceesory which will lend dignity and
solemnity to tb.e ceremony should be negleoted. I have often been pained at seeing
the loose and careless manner in which these ceremonies aro sometimes performed.
The solemn act of depositinir in the grave of a deceased brotlier the sprig of acacia
-that emblem so significant to M~sons of the soul's lmmortality-.is often almost
turned into a farce by the careless, hasty, and undignified manner in which it ls per·
formed. Instead of marching around lo solemn procession and reverently deposit·
ing the evergreen when near the head of the grave, It too often occurs that a pr?·
miscuous rush is made, each brother apparently trying to be the fir~t to throw in his
sprig thus converting a beautiful observance into an unseemly scramble.
In' this connection I trust that the Gra;'d Lodge will excuse me for making. two
suggestion•. Tbe apron, which is placed upon the coffin of the deceased brother and
afterwards dApo•ited in bis grave, should be of real lamb-skin, so that, when banded
at the proper time to the Maetar, he may not be obliged t:> exhibit one of cotton or
linen-too often none of the cleanest-and thus make a mockery of that beautiful
language or our ritual, oo well known to every Mason. And, as to the sprig of
acacia, when the Master takes it in his bane a·t the proper period in the ritual, let
all the brethren do the same, and, after the Master bas recited that port;on of the
service already prescrlbed,.let him say-placing the evergreen upon his left breast-:" We cberi~h his memory here,"-then, raising It upwardt.-" We commend bis
spirit to God,"-and then, dropping the sprig Into tb.e grave,-" And bis body
to the earth." The brethren should follow the Master In these movements except
tbat, when he drops the evergreen Into the grave, they should simply .let their hand
fall by their aide. Theo Jet the Marshal form the brethren in procession and march
Rlowly, one by one, past the head of the grave, and, when there arrived, let each, in
depositing bis evergreen, first press it to his left brellll!t, then point it upward, and
lastly deposit It in the grave. The adoption of these suggestions would, in my opln·
ion, add much to the .solemnity and impressiveness of 'tlie occasion.

Grand T.odge. Their condition is generally prosperous and satisfactory, but there
are ln•hnces where it would be better for the Fraternity, and for the Lodges them·
selves, it' they would surrender their charters or consolidate with some other Lodge.

to the Grand Lecturer-but every yee.r shows e. jumble of reports to the one or the
other which no Inspector, who can read his commission, should be guilty of.

It has $1,600 in its treasury. "San Benito Lodge has done no work for two or

I had cherished the hope that, after the report of the committee 11t the last Annual
Communication upon that portion of the Grand Master's Address relative to In·
epectors, I should have been able to ma.k.e a full report upon every district in the
jurisdiction; but in this I have been somewhat disappointed. A few of the older

48

Proceedings qf the

[Oct. 11,

Inspectors, who have hitherto seldom or never failed in the performance or their
duty, have this year proved derelict. The resolution adopted at the la.st Annual
Communication, found on page 571 of the printed proceedings, reads as follows :"Resol1JPd, That no Inspector, who has failed to make the report required by
law, should be re-appointed to such position unless satisfactory explanation be given
for such failure."
It is to be hoped that those Inspectors who have this year failed to make reports, among whom a.re some zealous and hitherto faithful brethren, will be able
to present some satisfactory excuse for their delinquency. The office of Inspector is
an honor11ble and responsible one. He is, in one sense, the deputy of the Grand·
Master, to him is confided the care and supervision of the Lodges in h.is particular
district, and be is in a measure responsible for their good conduct. Lodges in
which such a state of affairs exists as is, in some instances, noticed in this report,
should at once be reported to the Grand Master, that he may take prompt measures
to remedy the evil. Some Inspectors hesitate about visiting a Lodge for the reason
that they have not been invited; but, while exercising a sound discretion in this
matter, they sbould ' bear in mind that the law gives them full power, and that it is
their duty to visit any Lodge in the district " tohe'Mller they may deem it necessary
for the faithful performance of their duties."
The Grand Lodge depends upon the Inspect~rs for a knowledge of the condition
of the various Lodges in their respective districts, and through them much valuable
information may be communicatad which otherwise would, perhaps, never be known
to the Craft. If an Inspector finds, after his appointment, that he cannot perform
the duties of his otHce, he should immediately apprise the Grand Ma~ter of the fact,
in order that another may be appointed to the place. If Inspectors accept their
appointments and arc then allowed quietly to neglect or ignore the responsibilities
devolving upon them, the system may as well be aba ndonerl, aS'its whole intent and
efficacy will be thereby destroyed.
The InspectorA who have failed to m11ke t'reir report> as reqnired by. law, are
Bros. JAMES VANCE, of the second district, JOHN 0. PARTRIDGE, of the fifth district,
ELIAS MoCLURE, of the tenth district, THOMAS c. POOKMAN, of the seveotaenth district,
and BENJAMIN BRUNDAGE, of the twenty-eighth district, being five out of the tliirty·
three, and leaving the condition of thirty·eigbt Lodges unreported npon.
I would once more earnestly call the atte11tion of Inspectors to the Importance of
sending in their reports early in September, in order to allow the Grand Lecturer
time to prepare his report with some degree of care and deliberation. Several of the
reports this year came to hand only a few days since, causing much trouble and
nnnecessary labor in order to place them consecutively herein.
In conclusion I am pleased to say that, from my own observation and from the
reports of the Inspectors of the several districts, I am satisfied that the condition of
the Order, generally, in this jurisdiction, has manifestly improved during the yea~
The Lodges have exhibited an increased desire to conform to the .Prescribed ritual,
and the cloud of depression which has for some time darkened 9ur Masonic horizon
is now breaking away beneath the sunshine of returning prosperity.
Since this report was prepared I have been pained to learn of the death of Bro.
JoHN ·caANEY PARTRIDGE, Inspector of the fifth district. This sad news fully and
sorrowfully accounts for the non-1·eceipt of a report therefrom. Bro. PARTRIDGE
was a true and zealons Mason, and in his death the Grand Lodge has . lost a faithful
officer, the community a good citizen, and his family a devoted·husband and affec·
tlonate father. Let us hope that their and our 1088 may prove bis eternal gain.
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOHN WERNER SHAEF~'ER,
Grand Lecturer.

interests of the Grand Lodge, and of Masonry tbrou11hout the jurisdiction, have been
faithfully conserved; and that the gavel of authority entrusted to him has been employed in proper compliance with the spirit of our noble Fraternity.

Our jurisdiction, from the noble patriarch who first honored the position of chief
Executive of this Grand Lodge, and who, by the blessing of a benign Providence,
yet honors us with his presence, down to him who now, with such marked ability,
fills that position, has been peculiarly fortunate in the selection of those npon whom
to bestow this higheet mark of appreciation and honor. May the same wise discrimination characterize this Grand Body in all its future selections.
The rentiment expressed by the Grand Maater in reference to the " injudicious frequency" with which encomiums upO!l the excellence of our tenets are pronounced,
meets with our hearty concurrence. By our actions, the proper and peculiar fruit of
noble principles, should we be known to the world of "profanes." Whilst we cannot
cultivate too great a regard in our own hearts and minds for the exalted teachings
of our Fraternity, nor too great an appreciation and love of the sublime virtues-Faith, Hope, Obarity-which form the very substratum of our institution, we should
be equally vigilant to see that the material of our Lodges should be ashlars aa susceptible of belug made as nearly perfect '!8 it is possible for frail humanity to be; and
that that material should be of "good men and true," in all particulars. To this
porlion of the Gr~d Master's Address, your committee, and, we doubt not this vaat
concourse of Masters in Masonry, reepond with a hearty " So mote it be."

ALABAMA.
The sixtieth Annual Communication of tbe Grand Lodge or Alabama was com·
menced in tbe city of Montgomery on the sixth day of December, 1880,-the M.·. W.'.
HESRY CLAY TOMPKINS, Grand Master, presiding, and the R,•, W,•. DANIEL SAYRE
being Grand Secretary. Two hundred and one Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master occupies twelve pages of the proceedings, and
is a well written, business-like document. He con11ratul11tes the Fraternity upon the
favorable auspices under which the Grand Lodge now met. Two years ago the fearful pestilence had laid many a worthy brother low in death, and gloom and sorrow
visited almost every hearthstone. It w11s now with the greatest pleasure that he
. could nunounce to them that, so far as he had been informed, "uo brother who had
beeu prominent in this jurisdiction had died." The relations with brethren in other
jurisdictions had been most amicable and pleasant.
The Grand Master publishes twenty-five of his decisions, of two or three of which

Grand Lodge of OaJ,ifornia.

we make note. One was that " the use of ln~nltlng and abusive language in writing
or speaking of a brother, is 11 Masonic offense; so also is sending to him a ch111leoge
to ft11ht a duel with deadly weapons." Another was, that "Masonry does not un1lertake in any way to interfere with the religious views entertained by 11 member of
the Fraternity, however erroneous they may be regarded by 11 large majority of the
Craft. But if 11 Mason should habitually, either iu public or private, advocate and
teach a doctrine which upholds and endorses a relation which Is in direct violation
of the laws of the land, and the moral sentiment of our civilization-suoh l\S polyg·
amy-he would be guilty of 11 Masonic offense." The Grand Master in another part
or his Address, goes into quite a long argument in defense of this decision, from
which we Infer that practical Mot monism had invade() the precincts ot some
Lodges and carried captive some of the silly members. We heartily endorse this
decision. Masonic death is never too severe 11 penalty to inftiot upon such disturbers of the moral and Masonic peace of a community. Masonry wants oo such
n11Stioess and pollution within the Courts of her Temple.
Another decision was, that "the dues of a brother suspended for non-payment of
dues cannot be paid after his death so as to entitle him to a Masonic burial.'' This
Is, we believe, the third jurisdiction where an attempt Iiae been made to bring a
dead brother to M_11sooic life. BeUer, we think, t? adopt onr California rnle, where,
if no other offense has been committed by a brother thau the mere uon·paymeut of
dues, his Lodge may, in its discretion, accord to his remains a Masonic burial.
One item of business transacted by the Grand Lodite was the remitting the dues
or and granting a new oharter to "Loaohapoka" Lodge, it having lost Its hall by
fire. A meritorious act indeed, but we should hardly think that tire would burn a
hall belonging to a Lodge with such a name as that. Will Bro. BEERS of the" M.A.
S.'' tell us what the word means?
A silver service was presente~ to Past Grand Master HENRY Cr..4Y ARH!!TIJONG,

namesakes were suocessively Grand Masters of this large jurisdiction.

ARKANSAS.
The forty-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was commenced in the city of Little Rock on the twenty·third day of November, 1880,-the
M.'. w... GEORGE THORNBURGH, Grand Master, presiding, and the R ... w... LUKE E.
BARBER being Grand Secretary. One hnndred and sixty·eight Lodges were represented.
The Address of Grand Master THORNBURGH occupies thirty pages of the proceedings. It is an excellent document, written in the plainest of English, just as Bro.
THORNBURGH or any other man of common sense would talk to hie fellows in a subordinate Lodge. It Is refreshing, after being obliged to read so mtlch of sophomoric
highfalutin as one is compelled to do who passes io review the addresses of Grand Masters, and especially of Grand.Orators, to sit down to ench a plain dinner of " beef and
cabbage," as we have before us. There is not a teaspoonful of whipped syllabub
from beginning to ena, but plain, substantial farmer's fare, yet toothsome nevertheless. He commences with glowing comments upon the wonderful prosperity that
Arkansas has experienced as a State. He says :The State of our adoption, more dear, if possible, than the one which gave us
birth, has been unusually pro., perous. Mother Earth, ever indulgent aud zealous,
has yielded Ler accustomed bounty from the field, the harvest, and the cotton plantation. The mines. too, have begun to give up their treasures, and the dollars of our
daddies may soon be coined in our· midst.
"Daddies" is good, and fully as expressive as" progenitors."
Here is another homely gem :- " In every quarter flows the pure and sparkling
water with healing upon its wings, until now, with our far-famed Hot Springs, Eureka, Searcy, and a hundred others, nearly all the diseases to which flesh is heir, from
cancer to love siokn6ss, may be cured with 'Adam's ale-God's own be verage for
man." Happy, happy Arkansas! We are almost tempted to "pull up stakes" and
emigrate to its Elysian fields forthwith, not that we are affiicted with either cancer
or love sickness.
One other extract from the opening of this Address, and we pass on to matter;
more Masonic, if not more interesting : The doctor and the lawyer alone are left to mourn the prosperity of the times.
To the one it is distressingly healthy; to the other, the peace and quiet are monoto~L

The future to us, as a State, is full of promise and hope . New discoveries of
hidden wealth are revealed; our agricultural and ti'mber wealth is becoming known ;
our climate is noted for its even temperature ; the • Arkansaw toothpick ' lives only
in imagination; and rumanism has fled before the advance of Cburoh, School and
Lodge.
Tbou•ands of people are coming every year to tLis favored State, where th e

The Grand Master had " traveled from the Missouri border to the Louisiana line;

Brethren, the effects of intemperance have caused my heart to bleed within the
last year more than ever before. I have, with a sad heart, followed to a premature
grave one who was the playmate of my childhood, the companion of my yonth, and

We cannot bring within the scope of onr wildest fancy the unnumbered hosts

all the purposes of his creation, and bursting asunder every tie that binds him to God
or man, is sad indeed.
And how, I ask, can any Meson engage in 1the traffic of the accursed stuff that
inundates with ruin wherever it flows-a. business from which flow, as legitimate
results, more misery, sorrow, grief, vice, and poverty than from all other causes
combined?

In our report last year we took decided ground against the position occupied by
Connecticut, in her unfortnuate difticuliy with New York as to what is now well known
as the " Webotuck matter." We are still of the safite opinion, though we regret the
non-intercourse edict issued by the Grand Lodge of New York, and think it was t oo
harsh a measure. Desiring to give both sides a full hearing, we now copy what
Grand Master BABLow says on the subject:I regret to again call your attention to our unfortunate relation with the Grand
Lodge of New York. The Chairman of the Oommihee on Jurisprudence, to whom
the subject was referred at our last Annual Communication, you will remember, was
given permission to complete his report, and present the same to the Grand Master,
after the close of the session. It wes accordingly presented, and after careful exam·
ination I gave It my approval and directed that it be published in the printed proceedings. On the 28th. of March, I received a communication from M.'. W.'. CHARLES
RooMri:, then Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of New York, notifying me that he
had suspended ofticlal intercourse with our Grand Lodge, and had notified the re·
spective Representatives of the suspension of their duties.
The matter was brougbt before the Grand Lodge of New York at its Annual Communication In Jnne last, and a resolution was passed forbidding all Intercourse with
brethren of onr'own Grand Lodge. That the subject ma.y receive your careful attention, permit me, in as few words as possible, to present a statement of t he matter at
issue. · In August, 1872, a petition was received by M.'. W.·. Brother LUKE A. LocxwooD, then Grand Master, from a constitutional number of brethren residing in the
town of ::>baron, in this State, to.form a Lodge at 1hat place, the petition being in due
form , and accompanied by 11. recommendation from the nearest Lodge. The dispensation was granted and the Lodge opened. At the next Communication of the Grand
Lodge, the dispensation was returned, and the Charter of Hamilton Lodge , No. 64,
formerly located in that vicinity, which had surrendered the same a few years before,
was gi ven the petitioners, among whom were seven or more of Its former members,
and they were constituted Into a regular Lodge, under the name and number above
mentioned. It was subsequently ascertained that two of the petitioners were mem bera
of Webotuck Lodge, No. 480, unJer the jurisdictio n of t he Grand Lodge of New York • .
In consequence of this we are charged b y that Grand Lodge with Invading their jurisdiction and terminating membership in their Lodges without their knowledge or
consent. This we deny, and emphatically disclaim any intention of Interfering with,
or infringing upon its jurisdiction. By the regulations of both Connecticut a nd New
York at that time, a Mason signing a petition fo\· a new Lodge became a member of
that new Lodge when lawfully constituted, and under the provisions of that re~ula­
tion the brethren residing withlh our territorial jurisdiction, and signing the petition
for said Lodge, were made its lawful members. If their membership was not law·
fully terminated in their former Lodll'e, then they are members of both Lodges until
said regulations are oom11Jied with-since which time, to prevent the r ecurrence of
such complaint, Conn ecticut, (and I think New York also), has adopted a regulation
requiring a.I,! petitioners for a new L odge to present their certificates that they are
free of t he books of t he Lodge, before Much new L odge can . be lawfully con•tituted.
By this severe, and as we believe, unjust edict, 70,000 M·asons in New York and
15 ,000 in Connetlcut, among wbom have evM existed the most friendly and fraternal
relations, are time plac~d at a perpetual distance, and the great work of our a ncient
Fraternity sadly impeded. By it, brethren hailing from the Grand Lodge. of Conneo·
iout &nd residing in that jurisdiction, are prevented from enjoylug their Masonic
privile11:es. By it, for a mere difference of opinion on a question of Masonic law, and
without a pretence of even discourtesy towards our sister Grand Lodge, we are
placed under the same ban , by the Grand Lodge of New York, as the Grand Orient
of France, whkh has struck out the most vital landmark of Freemasonry, and as the
Grand Lodge of Hamburg, which has defi antly planted and still mainta ins Lodges
in the State of New York. In view of all this, let us not indulge in harsh words or
severe criticisms, but rather let us cherish the kindliest fraternal regard for onr
brethren of New York, and faithfully perform our :Ma80nic obligations towards them.
Let us manifest to the world that the cords of affection and duty, which bind Muons
of Connecticut to the ancient F raternity, are too strong to be broken by the angry,
unprovoked blow of even a brother, and Jijt us labor t o hasten the t ime when the
true spirit of our Order shall so fill all hearts that lnter dictory edicts sh11ll no more be
resorted to as a remedy for unimportant cases of grievances between sister jurisdictions. Let us continne t o hope and believe that a r eturning sense of justice, and the
hallowed remembrance of our former friendship, may lead our sister Gr.and Lodge to
quickly and cheerfully rescind said edict and accept our extended hand In friendship
and brotherly love.

In our jlfrisdiction the Master and both Wardens represent the Lodge in the Grand
Lodge, and in the absence of the other two, any one of them can cast the three votes
of the Lodge. If all he present, each has one vote; if only one be absent, the senior
officer casts two votes and the junior, one. This we believe to be just and right, and
we wonder that the same rule is not adopted In all Grand f,odges.

In another case the engineer was hoisted by his own petard. A member of a

Io another case a Master of a Lodge was suspended for " being haughty and arbi·

Bro. ROBBINS approves of the act of Grand Master BROWNE in setting aside the
proceedings of a certain trial, although our Jnrisprudence Committee and Grand
Lodge disapproved. He says :We agree that only the Grand Lodge can disturb the judgment of the Lodge
in such cases, provided such judgment is lawfully expressed; but we do not agree
that such Immunity extends to a judgment expressed in defiance of law. The
Grand Master may not review a case on its merits, because the landmark makes
the Lodge the rightful jury, Pnd the Grand Lodge the only court of appeal; but
he has ample authority to enter any Lodge and require its conformity to Masonic
law, the law relating to trials no Jess than any otber. Hence, ii' it shall appear
that judgment has been rendered against a brother who has not properly been
placed on trial, or in total disregard of the forms upon whose observance the law
holds the right of the Lodge to render any judgment at all to be contingent, it is the
right and duty of the Grand Master to set the proceedings aside.

INDIANA.
For financial reasons, and specially with a view of reducing the heavy debt pressing upon the Grand Lodge, no Oommunication of the Grand Lodge of Indiana was
held this year. But we have received the annual reports of the Grund Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, and Board of Trustees, made to the Grand Master in May, 1881.
From the Reports of the Grand Treasurer and Secretary ii appears that some
$26,500 oftloating debt and interest had been paid during the year. This disposed of'
the floating debt, leaving the funded debt at $74,000. The Trustees hoped to reduce
this about $25,000 during the ensuing year, and woald even do better than that if
certain Lodges would pay up their delinquent dues, amounting in the aggregate to
nearly four thous~n~ dollars.

INDIAN TERRITORY.
The sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Indian Territory wns
commenced in the town of Atoka, Choctaw Nation, on the second day of November,
1880,-the M.". W.·. P. J. BYRNE, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.". lV.·. W. A.
McBRIDE being Grand Secretary. Nine Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master in his Address pays a just tribute to a Masonic brother, WILLIAM PENN ADDIS, of the Cherokee Nation. "Amongst bis people," we read, "he
was a chief, and in their counrils was deemed the sagest. In his death Masonry has
lost an honorable member, and the cause of humanity an able advocate," The
Grand Master was happy to report that mo~t of the Lodges were enjoying a good
degree of prosperity. But truth compelled him to report '' that the harmony of some
of the Lo?ges had been much disturbed by the unbridled use of the tongue.
Slanderous TeporLs and gossips have been circulated, frequently without foundation
in fact, and sometimes these have been actuated by selfish and unworthy motives."
From ail which we infer that our red brethren have imitated some of the vices as
well as many of the virtues of their white friends. Both classes, however, would do
well to follow the advioe of our ''Big Indian," whose bead is pre-eminently level:
"To such as are tempted to in.dulge in this evil I say place a sentinel at your
months, to prevent the utterance of an unkind or ungenerous word against your
brother or your neighbor, and let your ear be deaf b the voice of slander and of
malice." We also regret to learn that some of our red brethren, like many of
whiter complexion, indulge in the Intemperate use of ardent spirits, and thus bring
a reproach upon the Craft.
The Report of the Grand Lecturer reminds us of an incident attending a royal
progress in one of the European States. A deputation of citizens waited upon his
Majesty to present seventeen reas ons why there had been no salute to the royal retinue. "First," said the spokesman, "we have no cannon." "You can omit the
other sixteen," was the reply of his llfajesty. So the Grand Lecturer apologizes for
not having paid any ofllcial visits to the Lodges on the ground that " no work had
ever been adopted in the jurisdiction." The Grand Lodge took the hint, and, after
witneylng an exemplification of the work as practiced in the neighboring jurisdictions of Kansas and Arkansas, adopted the former 11s its own. So now the Grand
Lecturer can "tire off his cannon."
Bro. JOSEPHS. MURROW, Chairman of the Committee on Oorrespondence, tells us
that he had made evel'y preparntion to write out a full report of the proceedings of
other Grand Lodges, when he was informed by the Grand Secretary that there
would be no funds to publiAh it if it were written, and so he was compelled to limit
himself to the reasons for not reporting. We regret this, as Bro. Muasow's reports have always well repaid us for the reading. He gives us now only two
pages and says "The ghost of poverty will not down, and so we stop."
The Grand Orator, W.'. Bro. H. ~'. RuoKNEB , delivered an able and well digested
oration on "Freemasonry and the Bibhi1" which the brethren did well to order published in the proceedings. It was and ever will be " a word in season.''

A committee from the Grand Lodge of Tennessee, consisting of Past Grand
Masters JOHN FRIZZELL and JOHN 8. DASHIELL, was introduced to the Grand Lodge,
and presented a communication relative to the so-called TOLIVER case, out of which
considerable difficulty has grown between the Grand Lodges of Kentucky and
Tennessee. It appears that ToLIVEn, confessedly a great scamp, was a member of
one of the border Lodges in Kentucky, bot actually resided over the Tennessee
line. The r.odge In whose jurisdiction he resided tried him for a gross offense
against Masonry and good morals, and expelled him. To this action the Grand
Master and Grand Lodge of Kentucky objected, and insisted that a Mason could
only be tried in the Lodge to which he belonged. Ignoring therefore the action of
the Tennessee Lodge, the Kentucky one also tried the offender and expelled
him. The two Grand Masters had a long and somewhat sharp correspondence on
the snbject, and each Grand Lodge endorsed its own chief officer. To prevent more
serious results, which might naturally have grown out of this matter, this commit·
tee from Tennessee was appointed to visit and arrange the matter with the Urand
Lodge of Kentucky. A committee of Past Grand Masters was appointed to confer
with them, and the result was the presentation of the "following resolutions :Resolved. 1. That we affirm that under our Constitution and Laws there is a
connection existing between a Lod~e and its members which no other jurisdiction
hBB the power to annul without its consent, and we claim and maintain for our
·
subordinate Lodge exclusive jurisdiction over our own members.
2. But, in a sririt ot' Masonic amity, and for the purpose of uniformity of
proceeding and o conformity .to other jurisdictions as far as nossible, that we
recommend an amendment to the Constitution of this Grand Lodge.-[Jn substance
allowing such proceeding in the future as bad been taken by the Tennessee Lodge lo
this case.]
The first resolution was adopted and the second was referred to the next meet·
Ing of the Grand Lodge. And so the matter remains at present.

The Grand Master delivered an interesting Address, well written, and full of good

that, though e. falling off had occnrred in their numbers from a prompt execution of the

it" would be proper or advisable to confer the degrees of Masonry on a party understanding and spea.king the "French language only?" The a.dvice was to permit the
party to apply to the nearest French Lodge. He thought it a grave mistake to confer the degrees upon pa.rties of e. different tongue from that used by the Lodge, and
yet he learned that it was frequently done.
The Grand Master regretted to lea.rn that there was still, on the part of some
Lodges, opposition to the per capita assessment for the benefit of the Grand Lodge.
He thought that all such feelings should cease, In view of the patent fact·that during

wherea.s, without this ta.x, it would ha.ve been increa.sed nearly three thousand dollars.
They have In Louisiana. a peremptory edict that no Lodge rooms shall be she.red
with other bodies. Yet one application bad been made to the Grand Master which
he felt compelled to comply with by the requisite dispensation. The Lodge at Goodrich'R Landing stated that unle•s they permitted the Knights of Pythias to meet in
their room, the owner bad notified them that they must vacate, and that no other suit·
able building could be obtained in the place for Lodge purposes. Here is another
illnstration of the militia officer sitting so straight upon his horse as to lean back·
ward . There must be exceptions, and we can see no sense or propriety in making
·such an ironclad edict as that of Louisiana and some other jurisdictions.

MARYLAND.
Tbe Grand Lodge of Maryland commenced its ninety-fourth Annnal Communication in the city of Baltimore on the sixteenth day of November, 1880,-the M.-. W.-.
JOHN M. CARTER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.'. JACOB H. MEDAIBY
being Grand Secretary. Sixty-five Lodges were represented.
Tbe Grand Master's Address was of very reasonable length, and confined almost
wholly to the local affairs of the jurisdiction. Again was he.compelled, as had been bis
predecessor, to complain of the remissness of most of the Grand Inspectors in neglect.
ing to make 1rny report to him. He could not, therefore, give any general informa·
tion as to the 01·aft, as he had been unable to make personal visitations to tile Lodges.
The Grand Lodge passed a resolution to the effect that such neglect in the future
would not be passed over. This looks like another bunch of grass hurled at the
colpri~. Better, as did the old spelling-book man, try the e1J!c_acy of solid stones.
Tbe Grand Lodge has not yet recovered from the depressing effeci of insuffi cient
resources, bot still the Grand Master could report a gratifying improvement. The
Grand Treasurer had made advances to meet interest accruing on the first of November,
to such an extent that it would require at least one-half of the comiQg receipt! to
reimbnrse him. The debt of the Grand Lodge was still$151,000, besides a stoc.kdebt
of $L47,5.10. The sinking fund, originated under Past Grand Master LATROBE, was
doing well.
One of the Baltimore city L<)dges had had its charter arrested for passing a resolution to remove from the Masonic Temple, with a view of saving rent. The Grand ·
Master devotes considerable space to a defense of this act, which the Grand Lodge
approved, but voted to restore the charter In case the otfensive resolution was re·
scinded. It appears that a regulation of the Grand Lodge requires all city Lodges
to meet in the Temple, that its revenues derived from rents, etc., may not be im·
paired.
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence by Bro. F. J. S. GOROAS la very
brief, occupying but four pages. It is not a review of the proceedings of the Grand
Lodges, but comments upon the difficulties exhting between certain Grand Bodies.
We have quoted elsewhere our brother's account of the settlement of the diffi·
culties between the Grand Lodges of Quebec and Scotland. We copy one item of
news to us, though it may not be to others. It is the first that we had heard about a
"Court of Arbitration," and we apprehend that it will be the last, for no such scheme
will ever be adopted by American Grand Lodges. Bro. GORGAS says:During the Triennial Convocation of the General Grand Royal Arch Chapter of
the United States, at Detroit, in August last, at the suggestion of the Grand Master
of Michigan, a meeting was beld of tbe Representat.ives of the various Grand Lodges
who were at that time in the city of Detroit. Some twenty-five American Gl'and
Lodges were represented at this conference, and responses were read from
twenty Grand Masters, among their number that of the M.'. W:. Grand Master of
Maryland. Tile object of this meeting was to consider the propriety of organizing a
" Court of Arbitra tion " of the American Grand Lodges, for the pnrpose of deciding
questions of jurisdiction and Masonic law which might arise between them. Ry the
unanimous consent of all pre,ent, the chairman of the meeting,],{.-. W.-. Grand Ma~ter
MoGaATH, of Michigan, was authorized to issue a circular letter inviting the co-oper·
ation of all the Am•rican Grand Lodges in perfecti11g such an organization. It was
clearly understood that the proposed "Uourt of Arbitration" should have no jui·is·
diction except by request of Grand Bodies in controversy, and that the decisions
rendered should be accepted as final on the part of those interested.

To-day we saw the column pass· the next the prairie where they stopped was

One of the decisions of the Grand Master was that ;ca reversal of the decisions of
the Lodge made by the Grand Lodge shall have the effectonlytorestore the accused
to the iieneral rights and privlleges of Masonry, and not to membership within the
body from which he was suspended or expelled, without its unanimous consent."
This decieion was in conformity to the law, as it prevails in Minnesota, and the Grand
Master argues in favor of it.s justice and propriety. Our own law is the opposite of
this, and is based upon the common sense and equitable rule that when the Grand
Lodge has reversed the entire action of the subordinate Lodge, and .thus, in effect,
pronounced the alleged culprit innocent of the charges made, it should do full just~ce
to the accused party and place him in the same situation he would have occupied
had his Lodge acquitted him on the trial. We submit that this rule is in consonance
with the eternal law of justioe, Masonic and otherwise, rather than the harsher one
that prevails in :Minnesota. We see that a proposition, similar to our own law, was
offered and laid over until the next Communication.
•.
The Grand Master comes down with heavy condemnation on those officers of
Lodges who use "artificial helps" in the conferring of degrees. "The nefarious
practice" be says, " bas grown too common to be longH ignored or to escape condemnation." 'I'.hc effect, he thinks, Is very bad upon ~be mind . of the young Mason,
who had been taught that the secrets of :Maso0:ry could only be transmitted by the
hearing of the ear. We can appreciate this reasoning, for we well remember the
impression made upon our own mind when, many years ago, in our Masonic youth,
we once saw the Master of our Lodge poring over an illustrated "expoEe of
Masonry," so called, which was publicly for sale upon the co1yiter of a book·store.
Grand Mast ~r WELLS hopes that the bretij'en in Minnesota will "weed off this unnatural fungus," and we trust that in· other jurisdictions they will "go and do likewise."
One thing referred to by·the Grand Master Is" something new" in our Masonic
experience. Certain brethren, members of Red Wing Lodge, had issued a circular addressed to the Masonic fraternity of tbe United States, stating" that tlcey had
been excommunicated from their church because of their refusal to renounce Masonry; that they had organized a new church, and now ~olicited aid as Masons.' in their
org~nization and in the erection of a new church ed1!1ce." After full consideration
of the matter, the Grand Master came to the conclusion that "the appeal was from
brethren in distress, and, as such, entitled to our heartiest ~ympathies and support."
He thus argues in favor of his conclusion: "Masonry does not step aside to accept
assault, nor to antagonize assailants, but it ought ever to assist a falling brother,
whether he is stricken by s~ct or section. It is the conservator of good, its m1ss1on
to make men wiser, better, and consequently happier." He invoked a favorable
conslderntion of the petition of these persecuted brethren. The committee to whom
this subject was referred, and the Grand Lodge, endorsed this recommendation. It

The Grand Master had made but one official decision during the year, referring

The decision was that "a Lodge could not legally. hold its regular communication
on the Sabbath.'' The application for such permission stated that all the members
of the Lodge were farmers, and that it was very inconvenient for them to attend
meetings on week days. The Grand Master gave good reasons for hie refusal. Referrin11 to the Fourth Commandment, be says:Thie command was written upon a tablet of stone, by the band of the Almighty
himself, amidst the thunderings of Sinai, and since then it has been obeyed and
reverenced by the good e.nd purn of every age. and clime. In this land of o_n~s, the

enforces a due observance of that day, and God (orbid that it may ever be said that
:Masons in violation of Divine and human laws, should ever find it necessary to hold
any me~tings on the l:labbath-!nneral occasions alone excepte~. · ~am of the opinion
that it would be improper and illegal to hold a regular oommu01cabon on the Sabbath.
It would be better for the honor and good name of :Masonry that the Lodge shil'nld
cease to exist.
All honor to the Grand Master for this excellent decision.

The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, (to whom all such matters had been
committed by the Grand Master,) enbmitted a detailed report of thei.r r,ulings upon
• some twenty questions sent to them. One question and answer were as follows:Q. A, who has Jost an eye when quite young, now petitions for the degrees in
Masonry; can be be initiated? An11u:er. Yee; he has lost none of the essential
limbs and i•>ints. The privation of the sense of sight is in any event only partial, and
the weight of evidence from the medical faculty goes to prove that one eye being
lost the other has added streugtb.
Score one more for the one-eyed.
In another case a Lodge had initiated a man who was club-footed. The Master
having ascertained snob to be the fact, refu•ed to advance hie. He bad applied for
the F. C. degree, could it be conferred? The committee replied in the negative, and
censured the Lo.dge for even receiving the petition of one thus deformed and incapa·
ble of complying with the requirements of Freemasonry.

MONTANA.
The sixteenth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Montana was held lo
the city of Bozeman on the sixteenth day of September, 1880-the R.·. lJ'.·, GEORGE
W. MONROE, Deputy Grand Master, presiding In the necessary absence of the Grand
Kaster, and the R.·. W.·. CORNll:LIUS HEDGES being Grand Secretary. Sixteen
Lodges were represented.
The Address of Granrl Master KNOWLES was transmitted and read by the Grand
Secretary. · It Is an elaborate and well written document. The growth of the Ma·
~oolc Fraternity during the Masonic year he thinks is tlie best indication of the prosperity of the Territory. He had granted dispensations for the formation of two new
Lodges. Having been consnlted as to the propriety of the incorporation of Lodges,
he had advised the same·, -and argued strongly in favor of his position. It may work
well in a sparsely settled Territory like Montana, but we think ii a dangerous, or at
least a questionable, experiment, and in time they may find themselves compelled to
follow the example of California and dislncorporate. The Grand Mast.er thinks it
time to adopt some measure or policy to guard age.Inst Me.sonic tramps and impo1tors,
11ud suggests that, in all suspicions cases, the Lodge named as that to which the
applicant claims to belong be communicated with, and if he be an impostor that his
name and description be communicated to all the Lodges In the juriediotion. This is
probably tbe most effective mode to a.dopt. A few dimes, or even dollars, spent in
telegraphing, will, in most cases, be a profitable Investment.
In alluding to the fierce and unrelenting opposition of the Roman Cathollo Church
(&nd, we rosy add, of some other small lights,) to Freemasonry, the Grand Master
has a few well-expressed and pointed sentences upon the folly thereof, stating what
are the true teachings of Masonry, viz.: those of the Great Light, and particularly
·
those of the tea commandments of the moral law. He then adds:If the teaching of these make Masonry a religions body, then every organized civil
1ociety is a religion, for they are the root of much of governmental legislation. If it
IA said, the Church teaches these things and therefore there is no need of our Order,
we answer: Thie is the logic of that noted Mohammedan who, when asked to re1train the torch he was about tn apply to the Alexandrian Library, replied : "If
there is anything hostile to the Koran It ought to be destroyed, and IF there Is noth·
Ing here but what Is taught in the Kpran, then there Is no need of Its existence;" and
with this he kindled the extinguishing flames, destroyed much of the learning of
the ancients, and left a memory to be execrated by the enlightened of sncoeeding
ages. There is room enough for all to labor who have the purpose of elevating and
civilizing man, the suppi11ntiog of this hate In his bosom with love, selfishness with
charity, and Inst by a broad and helping fraternity, Such fields are not overcrowded. I can assure the gl'eat mother Church that there is no reaaon for any hostility
between ber and the great parent fraternal association, Masonry• . It was never intended to assume a hostile attitude to any church or creed. Its members may join
any church, or embrace any creed, so they hold fast to the belief In the One, True
God, the immortality of the rnul, and the morality of the Bible. There Is noth·
Ing gained by being misunderstood on this point. We have no desire to Incur unnec111ary enmity. We seek not the crown of the martyr, and especially throngh a misunderstanding. We believe we have a right to hear and follow the teachings of our
Fraternity, e.nd we will not yield at the behests of any.
We have quoted these sentences because they exactly express our own senti·
ments, and becanse we believe they are trne and timely.

NEW JERSEY.
The ninety-fourth Annual Communication of the .Grand Lodge of New Jersey was

The Grand Master, in his Address, says : "The past year has been in most
respects a repetition of many that have gone before. No serious question has arisen
to disturb the harmony of the Craft.'' Death, however, bad invaded the ranks of
the Grand Lodge. The M.-. W.·. DANiEL B. BRUEN, a Past Grand Master, esteemed by
all who knew him as a man and a .Mason, had been called away at the ripe old age
of eighty-five. He was an active .Mason during all the anti-Masonic troubles. The
Grand Master says of him :When we remember what it cost to be a Mason at that time; tha~ a . member of
the Craft forfeited the good opinion of a vast majo!ity of. the commumty m win ch he
lived ; that be suffered in bis good name and in bis busrness ; that with very many
the name Mason was one of r~proach and contempt, we can understand the bravery
and fa\tbfalness of our venerable and venerated brother, who, when almost all were
faithless. dared to brave contumely and reproach for the sake o~ w~at ~e believed
to be right, and, for principle 's sake, to stand at the head of an mst1tutioo then so
thoroughly unpopular. What an examp le to us of f11lthfulness to our vows and
loyalty to our ancient Craft. . .May his memory and example long be green among us.
Tb~ Grand Master further states that more th11n seven hundred Masons attended
the funeral of this aged brother. ".Many other brethren," we are also told , "have
been called away during the past year whose forms we sadly miss as we look around
this large assembly."
One of the decisions of the Grand .Master was that "a person blind in one eye,
when the organ is in other respects substantially perfect., may he made a Mason."
The Committee on "Jurisprudence and Charity" reported against this decision,
"for the reason that a person blind in one eye cannot literally comply with the requirements of the ritual." Why he cannot is a mystery to us. The Grand Lodge
sustained the decision of the Grand Master. Score another for the one-eyed applicants.
In referring to the case of the somewhat notorious CALVIN O. BURT, the Grand
Master thought "it a cause of regret that the Grand Lodge of New Jersey had been
unable to emphatically record its opinion of this man," thus more than hinting that
it. would not be a credential that BuRT would be anxious to show in his peregrin ·
ations wilb his so-called " Rite of Memphis.''

The point at issue between the two Grand Lodges is, briefly: "Can the Grand

quette and say that we will not yield this point! Does the dignity of this Grand

I am as strenuous as llny one to maintain our rights and occupy the position to

arbitration.

The first mutterings were heard in 1826. Fanned by the efforts of the opponents
or Masonry, and also used as an element of J!Olitical warfare, it re11ched such proportions that In some sections of this land-for it was not confined entirely to New York

The Masonic Fraternity has outgrown the spirit of animosity which at times has .
prevailed against It, because its principles and noble purposes are better understood,
and the Grand Lodge is recognized to-day Rs a bod_y worthy of respect and consideration, and has a place among the permanent and esteemed organizations of the present time.
In striking contrast with this Interesting and well written address is the oration
which follo\veJ, by the R ... W.·. FRANK R. LAWRENCE. We doubt whether any Sophomore could outdo this production in froth and;, highfalutin" phraseology. We give

A brother of our order and member of our Lodge is frequently in the habit of
boasting that be is an infidel, ridicnling the Bible. etc., in mixed companies. A few
days ago be boasted, in the presence of several Masons and others, that he was an
infidel of the ·l:los. INGBRBOLL stripe. The oonrae of the brother is e:i-citing considerable comment here among tho•e who are unfriendly to Masonry, and is likely to do us
Injury with th·ose who are disposed to be f1iendly, and to bring the order into disrepute. What do you advise us to do in the matter?
The Grand Master replied :I know of no Masonic regulation which requires belief in the Bible as the revealed
Word of God, or that prescribes any p11rtfcul11r form of religious belief. No atheist can
be made a Mason; but Masonry, as I understand it, go.es no further than to require a
belief in Deity. Morality, Industry, prudence, temperance, brotherly love and char·
lty are enjoined in practice. The Bible.ls laid upon the Masonic altars, and without
it a Lodge canno~ in this country, be opened. On it we obligate a candidate. It Is
declared the Great Light in Masonr.v; In the Installation ceremonies it Is declared
that it will gaide us unto all truth. Yet notwithstanding, Mohammedans and Pagans
have been made Masons wlthoat requJring a renunciation of any opinions, though it
Is well known that they do not believe the Bible to contain the revealed Will of God,
• • • • • However strongly we may disapprove or the act of a brothe1· boasting
of infidelity, and particularly when this is done 10 such manner as to annoy a brother
whose religious f'aith is dru.wn in question or criticised, yet complacent, dignified
silence wilf be a more eftective answer to his foolish boast than anything you might
say, however wise.

The Grand Master in the opening of his Address ruturos a.cknowledgments to an
Overruling Power" f~r the prosperity enjoyed since the last Annual meeting; for
the cheering prospect of a bountiful harvest; for the peace and health which had prevailed throughout the land ; and for the evidence on every hand that assured us of
continued prosperity.'' At no time in the history of the State bad Masonry stood higher
than at the present. Everywhere throughout the Fraternity were heard denuncia·
a.tions of the vices of gambling and drunkenness. Unsound materials were being re·
jected in all the Lodges. " No other than sound timber can be UAed lo our buildings,"
remarks the Grand Master, "and that which is used as sound is now discarded tho
moment its defects are known and found incurable." There had been nothing
to disturb the harmony of the Lodges. For the first time in its history not a single
grievance was brought to the notice of the Grand Lodge. Dispensations had been
granted for three new Lodges.
. One of the Grand Master's decisions was " that the retail traffic in intoxicating
liquors is demoralizing in its tendency, and is a Masonic offense within the meaning
of Section l of the Penal Oode adopted by this Grand Lodge, and a brother engaging
in such occupation is liable to discipline.'' The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence,
in affirming all the decisions of the Grand Master, call partlcnlar attention to this in
these emphatic words :Your committee would especially recommend to the careful consideration of the
m embers of the subordinate Lodges In this jurisdiction the principle enunciated In
this decision; and the several Masters are hereby enjoined to enforce It;
We oongratulate the Grand Lodge of Oregon for having taken this high and truly
Masonic ground. The closing words of the Grand :Master are so good that we copy
tbe m :Draw nearer to the poor, the rich, and the dying. Promote every good interest,
and remove every temptation from the erring. Visit the orphan and do good to all.
If we may use a figure, place a _brick in every material edifice. and have kind words
and charity for every one. This, brethren, should be our work, and thus may we
erect a Masonic Temple everywhere which the re.Ogas of time cannot destroy.
The Grand Orator, w.·. Bro. M. C. GEORGE, delivered an oration, well written,
and containing many excellent thoughts. We would like to copy a few paragraphs,
but find it hard to break the imity of the whole. It occupies twelve pages of the
proceedings. The United Grand Lodge of Colon and the Isli\nd of Cuba was fraternally recognized.

brother always writes so .well that no one will ever complain ~the length of his
reports. Bro. CHADWICK, in his notice of California for 1879, l~o liberal in quantity
and eulogistic in quality, that we fear he will deem our notice of Oregon but meagre
fare In both quantity and quality. Grand Master BROWNE'S Farewell Address is

tice of too many Masons to use the ·Lodge and Masonry as mere debt collectors, Bro.
