The decease of Past Grand Master JOSEPH R. CHANDLER, at the ripe age of eightyeight years, was announced. We copy these items from the minutes adopted by ihe
Grand Lodge :Hie adherence to Masonry continued steadfast during the anti·masonic period,
though hie prominence marked him out as an object of personal attack. He met
his asea!lants coolly, and triumphantly vindicated !ind sustained that Institution of
which he was one of the brightest ornaments. He was an earnest, devoted, thorough
man in all the work he w1s called to perform in the various positions of honor and
trust he filled. His Masonic record is a lesson and example. Though in hie later
years his association with Free-Masonry .was subordinated to other duties and
reiaHooe, from causes that are not here to be other than stated, (he became a Roman
Catholic some f.wenty-three years ago,) yet in all the•e years he never lost for a moment his interest in, or affection for, the Fraternity. This is a fact which is well
known to the Fraternity, and its stat~ment does honor to the teachings of our faith,
and proveR how thoroughly it improved the mind and he•rt of our departed brother.
The authority or power to create Masonic ties exists only in Freemasonry itself.
What it binds no other human authority can loo•en. Sovereign, it acknowledges
no human superior, obeys no mandate of a subordinate, and rejects all pretensions
of a divided snpremacy or a coequal dominion. As Freemasons, we neither recog·
nize nor admit the existence of any human authority that can dissolve the tie• that
we make eternal Rt our altars. Therefor~. as our departed brother held the Ga.vel
and wore the Jewel of the highest Ma.sonic authority in our jurisdictio11, it becomes
us to assert our claims in his Masonic services and relations to our Craft, to deplore
his death, since a light has gone out in o;iur Masonic firmament.

In recognition of the fact that, although achieved on South Carolina soil,

and therefore requested tbe Grand Ma•ter to extend an invitation to all tbe Grand
Masters of the original thirteen States and of Tennessee to be present and take part
in the ceremonies.

should sever its connections with those who di~eve these troths."
The following resolution wa.s adopted by the Grand Lodge:Resolved, That this Grand Lodge at once institute the proper measures to find

In concluding his very able Address, after announcing that, hereafter, Colorado
was to be his home, the Grand Master thus briefiy reviews the history of Masonry in
Utah, and gives good advice to the brethren:Twenty-one years ago, under e. charter from the Grand Lodge of Missouri,
Roo/ty Mountain Lodge was organized at Camp Floyd, in this Territory. It was
composed of officers and soldiers of the United States army stationed at that place.
Two years afterwards, this division of the army was ordered to New Mexico and the
charter of the young r,odge was surrendered. Five years elapsed before another effort was made to erect a Masonic altar in Utah. On the fifth day of l''ebruary, 1866,
Mount Moriah. Lodge was opened under a dispensation from the jurisdiction of Neve.de., and the oorner-stone of Masonry in Utah was permanently laid. Amid institutions alien from the spirit of Republioan Freedom, surrounded bye. people who
viewed with distrust or hostility every movement not under the direction of their
leaders; isolated from the States of the American Union by vast deserts and mountains impabse.ble during the storms of winter, our brethren dedicated their Temple
to the worship of the Supreme Being e.od to the service of humanity. Several years
later the completion of the continental railway marked a new ere. in the history of
Utah. From that time until now, the arts, sciences and aggressive intellect of American civilization have been at work to develop the material resources of this Territory,
and aid Its intellectual progreMs. Masonry was encouraged and strengthened within
these borders by the same influences. It was enriched by accessions from other
jurisdictions In America and Enrope. The withdrawals from the Me.sonic ranks,
occasioned by brethren departlug from the country, have been almost equal to the
additions which they have received. Thus, numerically, Utah Masonry has made
very limited progress in the last ten years, nor can you expect any decided increase
in its roll of members until the condition of affairs in the Territory has radically
cha.nged. Do not, however, feel discouraged by this fact. Remember that yon constitute the ''forlorn !lope" of Am_erican Masonry, and tha.t the glory of victory,
divided among a few, leaves to each a prouder distinction. Remember what you
have done, and press forward to the goal. Within thA le.st decade you have succored
and sheltered hundreds of br~thren who have wandered to this Territory, and who,
but for your timely assistance, might have perished in a land of strangers. In you the·
sick and aftlicted, the oppressed and defenceless, the widow and orphan,'have found
friends and protectors. When the pestlleuce desolated the cities of the Bonth, and
·all human power seemed unavailing to arrest it.a destroying course, none were readier
than the brethren In this jurisdiction to respond to the appeals of the divinest charity.
Let the memory of such actions strengthen you through all the trials which you may
be destined to endure, and excite yon to grander exertions. Be true to the noble
'\principles of our Institution, and yon cannot, then, be false to any duty which arises
from the manifold relations of societr. Let the emblematic lights illumine your
hearts with the holiness of truth, justice, charity and faith. .A.hove all, banish dissensions from your ranks 11nd cherish fraternal love in yonr hearts. Thus united
and harmonious, our brotherhood in Utah may look forward to a future as glorious
as their past has been eventful.

The true object and design of the Committee on Correspondence Is to obtain e.n
111nual statement or history of the progress, condition, and prospects of .Masonry in

the dltferent Grand Lodges of oar own country, and throughout the world. Freeme.·

1onry le the same in every clime ; its intents e.re'everywbere identical ; and the sympathy of Masons is universal. G!owin~ lights a.rise from every altar throughout the
length and breadth of our land. Ours is no meretricious form. The fre.temity works
for the suffering of the race. Dastardly cowards and stealthy eavesdroppers are too
weak to enter the Masonic sanctuary; but the feeble cry of tbe suffering orphan, the
wall of the heart-stricken widow, or the groans of a languishing or nnfortonat.e
brother roll back, as with magic h,aods, the portals of the Lodge, and the .Mason ~oes
forth to heal the affiicted, to comfort the distressed, and console the weak. This is
the spirit which lives in undying freshness, and lingers in the path of life to guide the
wanderer e.nd cheer the pilgrim. It serves to remove the asperities and defects of
our nature, and . like the ivy mantled rock, imparts beaut.y and grace where rough·
llHB and deformity prevailed. Let us rejoice then at the prosperity of our institution,
and send forth the silent breathings of thankful hearts, which ebkll rise up e.s peace
ollerings, richly perfumed with the blood of the early slain. Let us seek peace and
union, friendship and mutual confidence, tbe.t we may aid each other In the grand
drama of life.

We were surprised to learn from this Addre3S that postponement of ballots for

The Address of the Gran~ Master is of reasonable length, well written, and en·

feeling terms the deaths of Past Urand Masters SIDNll:Y S. BAXTER and LEw1s B.

years; "rhe ~rand Master had been diligent in the visitation ~f subordinate Lodges,
nepectlng tlieir work, and encouraging the brethren. From personal observation
he felt safe In saying that " moral effect and practical utility kept pace with their
increasing strength, and so long as such was the case, our loved institution would be
safe and its exalted ends and purposes be carried out.'' He bad granted dispensations for five new Lodges, and had refused many other applications. He reports
seven of his official decisions, the first two of which were:.! brother who has lost the thumb and Index finger of his right hand Is ineligible
tQ receive the degrees. A brother Is ineligible to receive the second and third de·
grees because ef a stilfened knee, notwithstanding the .first degree had been conferred
on him subsequently to receiving the injury which had caused it.
The first is nodoubtedly correct. The second, In our humble opinion, is stretching the physical Landmark further than is necessary. The Grand Master arrested the
charter of one Lodge for conferring the first and second degrees upon a person who
had lost his right arm. The, action of the Grand Ma8ter was approved, but, upon ap·
plication, the charter wns restored. Several Lodges having applied to the Lep;isla·
lature for Acts of Incorporation, the Grand Master takes occasion to express himself
strongly against such action. In conclusion, he thus frees his mind as to a prevail•
ing practice among many Masons: ."I refer," says he, " to the practice
wearing
conspicuous Mu.sonic emblems. This practice, I am pained to say, seems gaining in
favor and popularity every day, and, while ii has nothing intrinsically wrong, it is to
me a sad indication that we are departing from the primitive purity and simplicity of
oar Order."
The venerable Grand Lecturer, the W.'. Bro. JAM EB EvANS, submitted an interestmg
report of his wori.. He claims that "there Is not a Grand Lodge on the globe more
tenaciouA of the letter and spirit of the ritualistic work of Freemasonry than the
Grand Lodge of Virginia. Its earliest elforts were to secure it as it was originally
consummated by the 01·aft, and I have oo doubt that that desirable end was
accomplished." He publishes a letter from Bro. Ros MoRRls, of Kentucky, who,
a quarter of a century before, spent a whole night with him listening to a rehearsai ~'f
the work, and who said he had no donbt that he was then hearing the work introduced
sixty years before from Virginia into Kentucky. In a homogeneone State llke Virginia, and with a Grand Lectnrer like Bro. EVA.NB, who bas grown gray in the service,
it is a comparatively easy matter to preserve the "stately Doric'' undefiled. But in
such a cosmopolitan jurisdiction u.s onr own, the "Composite" order almost necessarily takes its place, and It is very probable that our California work may d11fer
somewhat from that which is thus said to. have been preserved In Virginia unchanged
during fourscore years.

In a Lodge up in Sitka, (wbich is in this jurisdiction,) during a ballot, the Senior

"Bro. VAN DEN WYNGAlllRT, who has lately returned from an extended tour in

from Germany visiting Ame rican Lodges. In spite of existing mutne.l represent&·
tion , and with the legitimate possession of regular certificates, visiting brethren were
subjected to an examintttion with which those coming from Germany were entirely

We are aware that visiting brethren sometimes find difficulties in gaining admis·
sion to our Lodges. Particularly is this the case w ith brethren coming from Germany, who principally rely on their Grand Lodge certificates for admission. While
we respect certificates from Grand Lodges recognized by us, yet we require some
evidence outside of that, that the visitor Is a Ma.son. An experienced examining
committee will, no doabt, make due allowance for the different systems practiced in
Germany, and certainly will not demand that a· brother from that, or any other foreign country, should be familiar with onr catechism. American Lodges practice
easentle.lly the English rite , and no difficulty is experienced in the examination of
brethren coming from Scotland, Ireland, Englttnd, etc., althongh the Grand Lodge s
of tbose countries do not use precisely the same catechism which we do. We require of such visitors a knowledge of tbe essentials of the secret parts of Freemasonry. A general understanding on the snbject by all Grand Lodges would probably obviate the difficulty complained of.

Bro. VON MENSCH was born in the city of Dresden on the. 24th of January, 1798.
After receiving a thorough education, he followed his inclination and entered npon a
mercantile career. J'lis untiring application, great ability, and nio~t scrupulons mteg·
rity gained for him the full confidence of all with whom be came m contact, In the
course of busines~ he visited the greatest part of Europe, and his subsequent connection with one of the largest manufacturing este.bli•hments of France afforded him the
opportunity of traveling extensively in the West Indies and the United States. Be
established himself in the city of New York i11 1824, where he successfully carried o.n
the b11siness of importing manufactured goods from Germany and France. In 1826,
the King of Saxony appointed him Consul for the United States, and, recognizing his
merits, subsequently bestowed on him. several hono1ary titles. In 1831 , Bro. VON
MENSCH retnmed to Europe and became associated with a mercantile house in Hamburg, where be resided for nine ye are. The King of Greece appointed him Consol .in
1887, and rewarded the energy and ability with which he promoted tbe commercial
interoonrse between Greece and the Hanse-towos of Hamburg, Bremen, and Lnbeck,
by investing him with an Order of Knighthood. Ill h ealth, the result of being shipwrecked, compelled him to retire from active mercantile life, and in 1840 he took up
his residence in his native ·city. His active mind, however, did not permit him to
remain altoiether without occupation. He found employment for his able pen In
writing on mercantile snbjects, etc. One of' bis works on Co.usular Business was

In private life Bro. VON MENSCH we..• sine.ere and ardent possessing a confiding

ranks of.our bro~herhood secured for him the esteem and confidence of all who knew

Master, and Bro. WIEPRECHT, Grand Ore.t1Jr. Both brethren were particularly impressive, as this was the last meeting of the Grand'Lodge in the building which had been
occupied for Me.sonic purposes for one hundred years, but which was now required
for public improvements.
Io the address delivered by the Grand Orator he traces the origin of lhe Grand
Lodge back to a Lodge instituted in l 760. It increased in members, granted charters
to a number of Lodges in various p11rts of Prussia, assumed the name of Mother
Lodge in 1783, and proclaimed itself a Grand Lodge, June 11. 1798. For the period
beginning with June 11, 1798, the Grand Lodge has had ten Grand Masters; one of
these presided for eighteen, and another for twenty-two years.
The Grand Lodge has under its jurisdiction fifty-eight Lodges, with 5, 743 members.

GRAND LODGE OF HUNGABY.
The Orient, official organ of this Grand Lodge, for June, August, October, November and Decemb•r, 1880, and February and March, 1881, id received. The
Grand Lodge is in communication, throngh representatives, with a large number of
Grand Lodges.
J
From a statistical report of the Grand Lodge of June, 1880, it appears that there
are twenty-five Lodges affiliated with it; of this number three are . inactive, and
of these the Lodge "Petoly" has dissolved since the report was issued. Number of
members affiliated with the Lodges, 1104. The report states that the number of
Lodge members has remained nearly statiouary during the year, but expresses itself
hope~lly of the future.
GRAND LODGE OF SWEDEN.
The following edict has been promulgated by the Grand Lodge :" The Grand Council of Sweden has noted with regret that the Grand Orient of
France has amended its constitution, permitting its daughter Lodges to initiate persons ignoring the belief in the G. A. 0 . T. U. and immortality of the soul. Without
this belief Freemasonry Is an impossibility. It is therefore resolved to discontinue
all Intercourse with the Grand Orient of France unti!,;urther orders; its daughter
Lodges can no longer be considered just and lawful.
••The Grand Council being convinced, however, that many members of these
Lodges sincerely dissapprove the said act of the Grand Orient of France, takes the
same in due consideration, and therefore grants permi•sion to its daughter Lodges to
admit such brethren of French Lodges as ·were initiated previous to the change in
the constitution of the Grand Orient and who have protested against that change."
GRAND LODGE OF GREECE.
The W.-. Bro. WoRPITZKI, representative 'of the Grand Lodge of Greece near the
Grand Lodge" Royal York zur Freundschaft," &t Berlm, reports as follows" '.l.' he Grand Lodge of Greece was established in 1870; it works the 8cottish rite.
Great caution shonld be exercised in the chartering of Lodges in that country, and
the material carefully selected. The superstition of the people should be taken in
consideration. In 1868 the Lodge at Patras was demolished and burnt by the peo·
pie. J .odges are now established at the Pirreos, Syra, and Chalcis in Eubrea. The
effort made to unite all the Lodges of Greece with the Grand Lodge at Athens bas
been successful; the English and also the French Lodge at Corfu, and the English
Lodge at Zante, have joined the Grand Lodge of Greece. 'l'he French Lodge at
Lamia is dissolved ."
The statement of Bro. WoRPITZKI is no doubt correct so far as the Grand Lodge
he represents is concerned. The body he refers to is probably the Supreme Council
of Greece. But there was a Grand Lodge establish• in that country in 1867, which
adopted a constitntion at it~ session of May 18, orthat year, PBlNCK DEMETRIUS
Ruono KANAKIS, who was initiated in St. Andrew's Lodge, at Edinburgh, Scotland,
being its first Grand Master.

The report speaks of various charitable labors undertaken by several of the

'
The Grand Orient is in possession of favorable reports from its Lodges at the
Cape of Good Hope and the East and West Indies. Several Lodges are reported to
be In the course of formation in the East Indies. Charters were granted to two new
Lodges. one at the Cape, and the other in the East Indies. In 1880 the Grand Orient
had eighty Lodges under its jurisdiction. Of these. forty·nine were located in Holland, seven in the East Indie~, (of these the one in Batavia was constituted in 1769,)
two in the West Indies, and twenty·two in Sooth Africa (of which six are at Cape Colony, three in Orange Free State, and one in Transvaal). Number of members in
Holland and the Colonies, 4,417. The Lodge L ' Unum Roya),e, at the Hague, constituted in 1757, has the largest number of members, 184.; and the Lodge La Belle Alliance, at the Cape, the smallest, six.

H. DRUHll!OND, of Maine, we take the following additional statement of the work a.nd
condition of the Oraft in 1880. Number of Grand Lodges, 54; raised therein, 19,
685; admissions, 17,528; dimissions, 17,102; suspended for non-payment of dues
23,210; deaths, 7.US; rejections, 3,615.
And here ends another year's work, made pleasant, however, by quiet walks
tnrough the green fields and by the still waters of our own and other jurisdictions,

them and our readers the richest blessings of the G. A. 0. T. U., we bid them farewell.

To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of Califo~ni,a :Your committee, to whom was referred the eloquent and touching appeal of the
Grand Master lo behalf of the sufferers by the late fires in the State of Mlchlgan, have
bad the same under consideration and report that the object for which aid is sought
is one of pure charity, appealing directly to the Masonic heart; and that it is not
only the right bat the duty of this Grand Lodge to contribute to the assistance of
that stricken people in proportion to the magnitude of the calamity nnd to our ability
to afford relief without Impairing our power to render assistance in other unforeseen
emergenoles which may arise In the future. They therefore recommend the adoption
of the following resolution:Resol-ced, That the sum of "'one thousand dollars be placed at the disposal of our
Grand Master, who is requested to telegraph the same, forthwith, to the Grand
Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Michigan, for the relief of the suffereIS by the
recent fires in that State.
All which is respectfully submitted by
GEORGE C. PERKINS,
JONATHAN D. HINES,

Your committ~e, to whom was referred the appeal of P ATBICK MCARDLE, a Fel·
low Craft, from the action of Guadalupe Lodge, No. 237, in expelling him from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry on the twenty.fifth day of April, 1881, have ex·
amined the trial-record and find that the commission which tried the accused
aoqnlred no jurisdiction in his case, for the rea8on that the summons served
upon him required him to appear before the commission on the twenty-fifth day of
April, 1881, was issued on the twenty-eighth day of March, 1881, and was served by
mail on the twenty-ninth day of March, 1881, at Ban Luis Obispo, _which was the
residence of the accused at the time; that Ban Luis Obispo is within the State of
California, but without the jurisdiction of Guadalupe Lodge; and that the summons
should therefore have been Issued at least thirty days before the day of trial, as required by Section 3, Art. JV, Part VI, of our Constitution. It was the right of the
accused to have these formalities complied with, and he did not.waive them by an
appearance. Your committee therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its ado6t1on :Re1olved, That the action of Guadalupe Lodge, No. 237, in expelling P ATRIOK
McARDLE from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be reversed and set aside,
and that the case be remanded to said Lodge for further proceedings.

Your committee, to whom was referred the reports of the Masonic Boards of Relief of San Francisco, Sacramento, and Los Angeles, accompanied by their petitions
for such aid as the Grand Lodge in its wisdom may see proper to bestow, have carefully examined and considered those documents, and report that the good works of
charity shown in those admirable papers ought to be a source of just pride to the
whole fraternity of the State.
The report of the San Francisco Board of Relief presents, as usual, a clear exhibit
of all its receipts and disbursements for the year ending September let, 1881, showing In d3tail the amount of money received; when and from what source; the several
payments made; and to whom and on what account-being, in short, a complete at1d
intelligent detail of all its transactions during the year. Its receipts, from all sources,
were $12,507 58; of which sum $3,923 70 was contributed directly by the Lodges of
this city, and $2,500 was received.from the.Grand Lodge. The expenditures of the
Board for all purposes were $8,338 97; the balance on hand last year was $1,499 24;
the balance now on hand is $4,168 61. A careful examination of this valuable
exhibit will afford, to Masons at least, some useful and gratifying information.
The reports of the Boards of Relief of Sacramento and Los Angeles are excellent,
and fully show all their operations for the year ending October let, 1881.
That of Sacramento shows the total receipts for the year to he $690 50. Of this
sum $300 was received from the Grand Lodge, and $223 49 from Sacramento Lodges.
Its total disbursements were $5T2 16, leaving now. on hand a balance of $118 68.
Tbe balance on hand last year was $167 35.
The report of the Los Angeles Board shows that the total receipts were ~286 84.
Of this sum $100 was received from the Grand Lodge, and $60 from the Lodges of
Los Angeles city. The expenditures equaled the receipts and leave no balance on
hand.
The great good which these Boards of Relief are doing fully justitles the former
action of this Grand Lodge in making appropriations for tbeir benefit, and it seems but
right and proper that it should again extend its helping hand to enable the brethren
of those cities to afford necessary assi•tance to distressed Masons of other jurisdic·
tlons, who fin4 their way In large numbers to those centers of business and travel.
Io conseqnence of the large balance in the hands of the Ban Francisco Board,
($4,168 61), It is thought that they may well get along for this year with a smaller
appropriation than was made to them la.st year, and your committee therefore olfer
the follpwlng resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the sum of $2,050 be appropriated from the General Fund, to be dis.
tributed as follows: to the Marnnio Board of Relief of San Francisco, fifteen hundre.d

The following report, which was presented from the Committee
on Grievances at the last Annual Communication and was laid over
for consideration at the present one, was taken up for action:To the M. •. W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the petition for restoration of CHARLES
HOWARD GORDON, who was expelled by Wood.bridge Lodge, No.131, OD the 16th day
of January, 1875, and the protest of the said Lodge against such restoration, have
had the same under consideration and report as follows:Every member of every one of your Committees on Grievances, for a long series
of years, with the exception of a single brother, have satisfied themselves that your
petitioner had committed no offense against our laws for which he could have been
justly expelled; e.nd it is but proper, on the part of this Grand Lodge, that it
should pay some respect to the opinion of those to whom it entrusts, year by year,
the duty of examining into such ml\tters, who are certainly entirely unbiased, and
whose only aim is to do strict justice withou.t fear or favor.
Long years of strife and litigation have so prejudiced the minds of the members
of Woodm·id.ge Lodge, a.nd of some other Lodges in its vicinity, against the petitioner,
that it would seem to be impossible for them to confine themselves to temperate language when talking about him; and yet no one of those who have appeared age.inst
him before your various committees, have ever, when brought down to absolute facts,
been able to state a single transaction in which he has been guilty of any dishonest
or unmasonic conduct. Now, if this man has never been guilty of anything that
would warrant his expulsion; if his punishment was the result of angry feeling and
personal enmity; if his continued exclusion is desired, not because he was guilty but
because he is disliked by his neighbors; if all these things are so-and your commit·
tee regret to say that they can view the subject in no other light-should this Grand
Lodge make itself a party to an act of injustice. Your committee think not, and
they unanimously offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Resolved, 'fhat CHARLES HOWARD GoBDON be and is hereby restored to all his
rights and privileges as a Mason.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS,
SAMUEL G. HILBORN,
JoHN C. P.&RTBIDGE,

To the M." W.-. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of CHARLES MYRON BURLESON,
who was expelled by Oakland Lodge, No.188, on the first day of November, 1879,
have carefully considered all the proceedings and evidence in the case, and are
unanimously of the opinion that no moral turpitude, no fraudulent intent, no Masonic
crime or ~isdemeanor, has been proven in the evidence produced on his trial. It is
apparent that he acted imprudently in allowing the funds of the Oakland Masonic
Temple Association to become a part of the effects of the firm of which he was a member; but his subsequent conduct, in liquidating his obligation to that Association,
proves conclusively to the minds of your committee his complete and unquestionable honesty or purpose. They therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption :Resolved, That the action of OaWand Lodge, No. 188, in expelling CHARLES
MYRON BURLESON, be and the same is hereby annulled, and that said CHARLES
MYRON BURLESON be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

SAMUEL G. HILBORN, }

many of the Grand Bodies in the world a.s is shown by t)le Grand Secretary's Report.

In pursuance of the last resolution, the Grand Master appointed, as such commit·
tee, Bros. N. GREENE OtraTIB, GEORGE 0. PERKINS, and WILLIAMH. HILL. That committee have given to this imporlant subject such careful consideration as was in their
power, and now submit the following:It will be seen that the instructions were positive that some plan should be proposed for the cstablishment of a Ho111E, and the committee have complied therewith,
in the proposed act of incorporation which will be found at the close of this report.
But they do not feel that they are precluded from suggestions of prudence and forethought in the inception of what may prove to' be either one of the most precious
jewels of the Fraternity on the Pacific coast, or a lamentable failure, bringing a blush .
of shame to the faces of all who take part therein. Whenever heavy expenditures
will ·almost necessarily be inevitable, they would adhere to the advice of the old proverb, which bids us to "make haste slowly."
In searching for some precedent to guide their way, the commjttee instinctively
turned to what is deservedly the boast of our Kentucky brethren, the "Masonic
Widows' and Orphans' Home and Infirmary," near Louisville. In reply to their
request, Bro. BASSETT, the Grand Secretary of that jurisdiction, was kind enough to
furnish the tenth .Annual Report of that institution, and it has mainly furnished the
items which they subjoin as a recommendation ·to this Grand Lodge. They do not
wonder that our brethren in Kentucky feel proud of their institution. It well deserves the following eloquent tribute which is found in the report thereupon:Kentucky Masonry can have no more ftttin~ m_onument to con_imemorate her
deeds of charity than the one reared by the contribut1ons of her sons ID the southern
suburbs of her chief city. · She needs no jewels with which to adorn herfl0lf more
rare, beautiful, and precious than. the happy group of more than one h.undred
widowed and orphaned ones._gathermjt around the f;lome s altars every mornlllg and
evening, and sending up their grateful songs of praise and prayer to Jehovah. Our
only reward is a consciousness of duty performed. We have had many, very many
times, th~ prayers of the widow and of the orphan, and we know that our Heavenly
Father approves this work.
The committee wish most heartily that they could point to such an institution
in California, and could take the visiting brethren from all parts of tho world to see
such a building as that of which they have an engraved picture in the pamphlet
before them. But even it and its history give them many a word of caution against
haste and extravagance. They cannot shut their eyes to the fact that it cost, unfurnished, $166,895 29; nor to the further fact that ifoame very near bankrupting the
Grand Lodge of Kenlucky, and caused many a heartburning and feeling of discord
among the brethren because of the onerous taxation of the Lodges ere it was completed and paid for. Thanks to the perseverance and indomitable energy and pride
of the brethren in that ancient commonwealth, and to the opon handed liberality
of others, especially of the ladies, the fearful debt incurred has at length been cancelled and the institution is free from future danger. If such an undertaking was
so heavy a burden to the five hundred and ten Lodges and fifteen thousand Masons
of Kentucky, your committee cannot reconcile it with their sense of duty to recom·
mend a like expenditure by the two hundred and thirteen Lodges and twelve thousand Masons of California. Like the infant, we should creep before we walk, and walk
before attempting to run a race with our stalwart brethren 'Of Kentucky. The committee gather some facts of interest from the report before them, which they present
as follows :. During the ten years since this Home was established it has received two hundred
and eighty-eight beneftoiaries. Some had been taken back by the Lodges which had
sent them; some had been placed in good homes; only nine had dfod, showing an
almost wonderful exemption from mortality. There remained in the home one bun·
dred and twenty-four. 'fhe expenses for the past year were $9,3i5 12, of which the
item for salaries was only $1,912 89, although the persons employed were superln·
tendent, matron, teacher, nurse, washerwoman, cook, and engineer. .As salaries are,

With thiij preliminary notice of the Home in Kentucky, the committee proceed

amendments as they may deem proper.
The laws and customs of this btate being somewhat different from those of Kentucky, we cannot adopt in full the charter under which that Home exists. In sub·
s~n~e•. however,. the committee follow what ha~ been found so successful in that Ju·
nsdiction, changing the same as they believe will bo more acceptable to their Oalifomia
~rethr~n. They propose an .Act of Incorporation·, under our general laws, sub~tan­
tially hke that which will be found hereinafter. It will be seen that they recommend
a Board of fifteen Directors, six of whom shall be the elective Grand Officers of the
Grand Lodge, and nine of whom shall be chosen by that body and so classified that
three shall go out of office in each year; all subsequent terms to be for three years.
They would make the Home in all reirpects an appendage of the Grand Lodge, and
at all times ·subject to its control. The Directors are to be officers of the Grand
Lodge, or to be chosen by it. The Grand ~faster is to be the President, al'ld th~
Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary are to hold those offices re~peotively in the
corporation. Reports are to be made to the Grand Lodge at each Annual Oommunication. While they believe that th& Grand Officers and the other Directors
will cheerfully give th&tr time and services to this institution, they think that the
necessary traveling expenses of those who attend the meetings of the Board should
be paid, and they have so provided. It may be a question whether these should be
paid ont of the Widows' and Orphans' Fund, or from the General Fund of the
Grand Lodge. The former is recommended, but the brethren can change that if so
desired.
The question of funds for the dUpport of the i11stltution js one of paramount
importance. The committee do not recommend the creation of any debt, unless,

To the M.·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of Oatifornia:In his Address to the Grand Lodge in 1877, Grand Master BROWNE reported his own
action in respect to the Incorporation of subordinate Lodges, and advised that the
Grand Lodge should take further and definite action upon the subject.
The matter having been again referred to your committee, they have· given the
subject careful consideration and are of the opinion that 11 Lodge can, through trustees, buy, hold, manage, aud sell property 11s eft'ectually and quite as conveniently
as It could If inoorporated, and that nothing won Id be gained by incorporation.
Now, the Lodge may appoint its trustees and give them such powers, and such
powers only, over it! property as it desires to give. They are at all times under
its control and direction. They can sell or mortgage, by direction of the Lodge, and
the proceedings are all simple, well understood, and Inexpensive.
On the other hand, if' 11 Lodge, incorporated under the provisions of the Civil
Code of the State, should desire to sell its real property, it could not move in the
matter without the authorization of the Superior Court of the counly in which the
property is· sitaate. To obtain that authorization, there would be necessarylst. A petitien to the Court for authority to sell. 2d. A notice by publication
that the Lodge desired such authorization. 3d. Proof that the notice had been given
and that the sale would be for the best interests of the Lodge. 4th. An order of the
Court authorizing the sale. That procedure would be neither simple nor speedy.
Your committee are unable to see that any useful purpose .could be attained by
incorporation, and they think that the tendency would be in many ways detrimental
to, if not subversive of, the good government and the best interests of the Fraternity.
They therefore recommend that the Grand Lodge do not authorize or permit the In·
corporation of its subordinate Lodges.
Your committee, to whom was referred a petition from Pleasanton Lodge, No.
218, formorly located at Pleasanton, but now at Livermore, in Alameda County,
praying that its name be changed and that it may hereafter be know11 and designated
as" Mosaic Lodge, No. 218," thus report:.As it appears from the petition that, owing to the name of the Ledge, numerous
mistakes have occurred, such as letters for the Lodge being sent to Pleasanton, its
former location, instead of Livermore, and as there appears no reason for d~nying
the request, your committee oft'er the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:Resolved, That Pleasanton Lodge, No. 218, now located at Livermore, In Alameda county, be known and designated hereafter as" Mosaic Lodge, No. 218."
Your committee have examined the fourteen special dispensations IBBued by the
Grand Master during the year, and find that the requirements of our laws have been
observed by the Lodges presenting petitions therefor, and that the dispensations
have been iBBued in accordance with our regulations. They therefore recommend
that the action of the Grand Master therein be approved.

no authority to thus dispense charities to Individual Masons or their widows and orphans living within the jurisdiction of the subordinate Lodges. It Is not org~nlzed
for that purpose, nor has it the necessary machinery therefor. That duty la devolved
upon the several Lodges, and the most that the Grand Lodge can do is to donate money
to Lodges an~ Boards of Relief in proper cases. It may further be said that it ia not
p~o~er for this Grand Lodge to take charge of or dispense aid and assistance to
d1m1tted Masons or their families.
Yonr committee therefore recommend that the petition be denle• but they further
recommend that a contribution, for the purpose named, be taken ~p in the Grand
Lodge, and that Abell and North Butte Lodges be advised to do the same

Bro. LEONIDAS E. PBA'l'T, from the specie.I committee to whom was
referred that portion of the Address of the Grand Master relative to
the death of Bro. JAMES A. GABFIELJ?, President of the United States,
p1·esented the following report :To the M. '. W." Grand Lodge of California :When a great man falls, the nation formally puts on the habiliments of woe.
When a good man dies, the people weep. One who was both great and good-as good
as he was great, and as great 118 he was good-a leader and a master among menhllB fallen ; fallen at the post of duty; fallen as heroically 118 mortal ever fell;
fallen at the moment when his grand and exquisite character was impressing itself
most effectually upon the nation which he represented.
Our people for a season stood appalled in the presence of their great calamity;
and now the mingled tones of sorrow, like the voices of a thousand waters, hi.ve
come unto us from all our sister States. More than this: they come from every land
where the light of civilization has penetrated. Not Amerioa alone, but all the world
mourns· for the loss whioh humanity has suffered, as if the affliction w«l.re too great
for only one people to endure.
The benefactors of mankind should ever be remembered. It is a goodly thing to
honor the illustrious dead; and, sorrowing end oppressed, we join the countless
throng of mourners. We make ourselves .a part of the fifty m1llions of people who,
without distinction of party, or raoe, or sect, or creed, with bated breath and quivering lips, have gone out in grand and solemn procession to lay their gratitude, their
benedictions, end their prayers upon the grave 'of

Few men have achieved so much in so little time. Soholar, ~tatesman, soldier,
and philanthropist, he was perhaps the best produotion of his age-the true11t type
of American character that the century has produced. From the humblest walk in
life, by his own inherent strength and force of character, he rose-worthily, grandly,
and deservedly rose-'to the most exalted position on the earth. The example alone
of such a life and character is worth more to posterity than are the lives and
achievements of thousands of ordinary men.
He sleeps, but his influence will live forever, The world will still move on ; and
men will still be born, live, die, and be forgotten. But, as the sun will still rise and
set, as the restless ocean will still beat and chll.fe against its shores, as the planets
will still move on in their appointed orbits, so will the moral effects of this man's
life be transmitted from generation to generation through all time to come.
When our Grand Master said that "he was one with whom a nation was satisfied
and of wl\om a nation was proud," he paid the grandest possible tribute to the worth
and greatness of the dead President. We would add something to these words if we
could, but to elabcrate would only weaken the force of the Grand Master's
expression.
To the aged and desolate mother, to the bereaved and devoted wife, and to the
fatherless children, we tender our profound though unavailing sympathies.
Noble citizen, heroic soldier, and honored statesman; kind and f11ithful husband,
son, and father; good friend, true man, and worthy Mason; he needs no eulogy
from us. He has builded his own monument in the hearts of his countrymen. His
deeds alone-his worthy deeds-have rendered him im)llortal.

And they recommend that these sums be paid from the general fnnd, as required

Your committee to whom was referre'd the petitions of .Aztlan Lodge, No. 177, and
.Arizona Looge, No. 257, by their representative, Bro. Tno111As J. BUTLER, asking for
the correction of that certain clause in the report qf the Committee on Finances 111St
year, reported on page 568 of the printed proceedings thereof, wherein it is stated
that those Lodges asked for a remission of their dues on the ground of poverty, etc.,
cheerfully admit the error and are happy to be able to report that then, and
now, as they are Informed, these Lodges are prosperous and the brethren generally
in good oircumstancea. The petitions also ask that the Grand Lodge dues for the
year ending July 31, 1881, amounting to $90 for the Lodge No. 177, and $42 for the
Lodge No. 257, be refunded.
These separate prayers in the same petitions do not seem entirely consistent. If
those Lodges are not poor, they should not ask for charity. They pay no represen·
tative dues, and of course rec.eive no representative pay ; bui in all other respects
they enjoy every right, privilege, and advantage in this Grand Lodge and elsewhere
that belongs to any other Lodge in this jurisdiction.
There is no analogy between the case presented by theae•J,odgea and Hawaiian
Lodge, No. 21, the dues of which are annually remitted. The last named Lodge is in a
foreign country, located at a busy port in mid-ocean where there are constant calls
for aid to Masons from all parts of the world, and separated frem the Grnnd Lodge by a
long and tedious sea voyage; while the petitioners are on or near the line of a great rail·
road, bringing them into close and quick communication with San Francisco. In fact
there appears to be no real difference between the Arizona Lodges and 'those of Cal·
ifornia, some of which, though not in miles so far away, yet, if the means of communi·
cation be considered, are equally distant. In view of these considerations your
committee recommend that the prayer of the petitioners for a return of dues be de·
nled.
All which is respectfully submitted by
GEORGHi 0. PERUNS,
JONATHAN D. HINES,

Bro. FRANOIS E. BAKER, from a minprity of the same committee,
presented the following report :To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lo<lge of Oalifornia :~
The minority of your committee, to whom was referred the appeal mentioned In
the foregoing report, do not, after a careful examination of the evidence In the case
share in the conclusions reached by a majority of the committee.
'
The commissioners· who tried this case, by a unanimous vote, declared the accused
brother "not gu.Uty." The record shows that the trial was fairly conducted, both
accuser and accused having equal facilities for being heard. The evidence was al! in
conformity with masonic law and usa1P9. There fa but little conflict in the testimony
given, the evidence on behalf of the accused being mostly explanatory of the facts
established by the prosecution; and, if all the testimony in the case be true, the
commissioners were fulfy justified in their conclusion a~ to the innocence of the accuse~. That they did accept the testimony given on behalf of the accused as true,
Is evidenced by the unanimity of their ver4iot.
The trial-commissioners oonstituteii the ttlhunal provided by masonlo law and
usage to hear and weigh the testimony tending to show the guilt or innocence of the
accused, and to determine from such evidence thefaota involved in the controversy.
They have heard the testimony, with full opportunity to observe the manner and

202

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 15,

bearing of the witnesses, to consider what testimony was given under the lnfloenoe
of prejudice or partisanship, and to determine the weight and credibility (of which
they are the exclusive judges,} to which such evidence is entitled. After they, as
impartial men, have determined the facts , with all these advantages before them, it
would, in the opinion of the minority of your committee, be a dangerous innovation •
for the Grand Lodge or any of its committees to attempt to determine what portion
of the testimony is true or what is false, or to disturb the finding of each a com·
mission. The adoption of the following resolution is therefore recommended :--'
Reaolved, That the action of Fi4elity Lodge , No. 120, in acquitting Bro. MosEs
BLUH, Jr., or a charge of uumasonlc conduct, be and is hereby affirmed.
All which is respectfully submitted by
FRANCIS B. BAKER, of the Committee.

Bro. ALVAH R. CONKLIN, from a majority of the Committee on
Grievances, presented the following report :7b the M.·. W. ·• (Jrancl Lodge of California :A majority of yonr committee, to whom was referred the app,e al of Bro. HENBY
A. Ross, Master of 8fltJ'l!tJf.lle Lodge, No, Wl, from the action of Cal.ifornia Lodge,
No. 1, in acquitting B11110N BLUH from a charge of unmasonlc conduct on the
first day of August, 1881, have carefully examined the voluminous evidence contained In the transcript of the trlal·record and report as follows:This is one of a series of cases growing out of business transactions Involved in
the failure of the firm of BLUH, So11s & Co., and the evidence is of the same purport,
substantially, as that adduced in· the cases of MosEs BLUM, Jr.1 and AMEIL HocnHEIMER. The charges were preferred by the J noior Warden of Bifoeyville 'Lodge,
No. 201, by its order, and the appeal was taken by the Master of that Lodge, both
acts being the action of the Lodge through its proper representatives, and the appeal
being thus properly taken.
·
The commissioners who tried this case, being of Oalifomia Lodge, No. 1,-that
being the Lodge within whose jurisdiction the accused resided-upon their findings
stood four for" not guilty" and four for "guilty,'' and the Master decided that this
sort of finding was a judgment of acquittal, inasmuch as it was not
a judgment of conviction.
In this your committee are of the opioiou.
that the Master was in error. The Constitution (see Sec. 8, Article IV, Part VI,}
provides for a judgment of a majority to render a decision, and, whether the judgment be a conviction or an acquittal, the rule for the concurrence of a majority of
the whole appears to be mandatory. Without such concurrence there is no finding, and the commission &re in the position, as one might say, of a "hung jury,"
there being no verdict or judgment-a majority of the commission not having concurred in any judgment.
The facts, however, as addnced before the commission, yet remain; and they
stare yo11r committee in the face wlth a conclusion which is irresistible-that of the
guilt of t.he accused.
A vast amount of time and expense In the trial or this case has been ioc'u rred,
which your committee do not feel that they could, with justice, again inflict npon
California Lodge, especially when so emphatic a case Is made out against the accused. They therefore offer the following resolution aud recommend its adoption:Reaolved, That the action of California Lodge, No. 1, in acqnitting S1HON BLUH,
formerly of Buck6ye Lodge, No. 195, of unmasonic conduct, be reversed and set

Bro. FRANCIS E. BAKER, from a minority of the same committee,
presented the following report :To the M. •. W." Grand Lodge of CCllifornia :The minority of your oommittee respectfully dissent from the views expressed
by & majority thereof, as set forth in the foregoing report. The testimony given at
the trial of this case was conflicting. Upon one charge there appears to be no finding
by the commlssioners, as they were evenly divided lo their opinions in regard to the
guilt or innocence of the accused, and I therefore think that the Master erred in de·
clariog him to be not guilty of that specification ; and, if any appeal had been properly taken, I should recommend that the matter be remanded to California Lodge
with instructions to retry the accused upon that charge, for the reason that he is
entitled to be tried by a commission elected from among bis peers, and that they
should first determine his guHt or Innocence before that question oao be considered
by the Grand Lodge or its committee.
Upon an Inspection of the record, however, it Is the opinion of the minority of
your committee that the Grand Lodge has no jorlsdlotlon to review the action of
California Lodge, for the reason th11t the appellant is not one of the persons authorized by the Constitution to appeal. The charges were preferred by Bro. WrLLIAK
KILLEBREW, Jnnlor Warden of 811veyville Lodge, No. 201, (by order of the Master of
that Lodge,) who Is the accuser In this case. The appellant, Bro. HENRY A. Rose,
Master of BiltJ'l!tJille Lodge, is therefore neither the accuser nor the accused, and
the Grand Lodge has already decided that the provision of our Constitution permitting either party to appeal Is a prohibition to all others, and that only the accuser
and the accused have the right to appeal. To reverse that decision now will nnsettle
the rules and regulations already established, and relegate the practloe lo these
cases, which Is now very generally understood, to the vague domain of doubt and
uncertainty, Wherefore I recommend the adoption of the following resolution : Re1olved, That the appeal of Bro. HENRY A. Ross from the action of California
Lodge, No.1, lo acquitting Bro. SIMON BLUM of'a charge of unmasooic conduct, be
and is hereby dismissed.
All whlc,11 is respectfully submitted by
FRANCIS E. BAKEB, Of the OommiUee.

its esoteric work. Every action of the Lodge relating hits business matters should
be clearly and concisely set forth therein, and in every case where, by our Const!·
tation and regnlatlons, a )llrticuln.r mode of procedure is prescribed, the minutes
should show that the prescribed course has been pursued-not by stating 11 mere
conclusion, but by a plain st11tement of the facts wheuce the conclusion followed.
In enry matte1· upon which the Lodge is required to act, the minntes should show
that it had so acted; as for instance :-No moneys (except such as may be dis·
bursed by the charity committee,) can legally be dr11wn from the treasury of a
Lodge without its express consent and under its instructions ; such consent should
always appear in the minutes, and every warrant drawn upon and"pald by the treas·
urer ebould be shown by the minutes to have been thus expreHly authorized to issue.
These are instances of some of the more essential rules to be observed by the
Secretary of a Lodge in keeping its minutes, and they are.especially referred to here
because all of them have been infringed upon and violated by some one or the Lodges
applying for charters. Our careful and efficient Grand Secretary, by the compilation
and distribution long ago of bis pamphlet entitled " Example Lodge," has furnished
to the· various Secretaries a guide containing complete formulas for the recording of
almost every matter likely to arise in a Masonic Lodge, from the time of the first
preliminary meeting of brethren having in view the formation of a new Lodge, up
to the time when such Lodge may elect to surrender its charter and close its Masonic
existence; and, In the opinion of your committee, for new LodgeR to come here year
after year with their records kept in such a manner as to provoke and merit just
criticism for the infringement of, or non·.compliance with, the rules thus plainly far· ·
nished them, exhibits an amount of culpable neglect, not only on the part of the·
Secretaries of such Lodges, but al~o on the part of the Masters and of the bre!bren
who may have been appointed to examine and report upon the records, etc. before
their transmission here, which seems inexplicable.
As to Lompoc Lodge, your committee are pleased to report that its records are
not subject to the more severe criticism above mentioned. While somewhat defec·
tive, they aro so only in minor matterP, such as the following : In two cases the
records fail to show that the Lodge was opened on any degree of Masonry; the ·
statement of bills presented to and acted upon by the Lodge in several instances is in
so ch obscure language as to leave the action thereon in doubt; and there are other
defects of this character, all which were pointed out to its 1·epresentative and will
doubtless be corrected and obviated in tbe fntnre.
The records are also defective in this-that tbe final report of the Secretary rails
to show the complete financial condition of the Lodge. Otherwise the records are
correctly kept, and from them, supplemented by the testimony of its repreaent~ti~e,
your commi'ttee find that the Lodge is out of debt, has a small balance of.cash ID its
treasury, has twenty-one members upon its roll, is situated in a fionr1shing and
growing neighborhood, and has a seemingly promising future. They .therefore offer
the following resolntion and recommend its ad option:.Resolved, That a charter be granted to Lompoc Lodge, at Lompoc, Santa Barbara
County, and that it be numbered in accordance with the date of its dispensation.

Like the Roman consul, centuries ago, defiant and erect in his superb manhood-.

It is true that yon ha.u already honored him as you had never honored another;

But he deserved it all, and in honoring him you had only reflected honor upon
yourselves. He had returned honor for honor, measure for measure, filled, shaken
down and overflowing. Wherever Freemasonry was known his name had become
a hou~ehold word-respected, honored, and almost revered. His life had been absorbed in your service, and you were still debtor to him, and not he to you. J,et. us

The Masonic Board of Relief of this city, perhaps the most efficient and most

him.

The Constitution and Regulations of this Grand Lodge, embracmg In their com·
prehensive sweep not only the genera.I prinoiples but all the details of Masonic juris·

The reputation of your Grand Lodge abroad is second to none. It stands almost

nnrlvalled and yon are jnstly proud of it. Some of ns, who have also long been toilers In this body, have claimed some credit for ourselves In this regard and have felt

And how have your domestic affairs been administered? You have now two

And, over and against all this, what can be charged to his account·? It would be
strange, strange indeed, if in all this experience we had not had some animated contests! The man who was fit to be your Grand Secretary-the man who had the force
the purpose, and the decision of character to .fill that place, and the independenc~
to execute his purposes, must inevitably no"l'I" and then offend some sensitive brother.
Ther~ is a point where amiability becomes simple weakness, and we should have

. If. a cl.oud has so~eti~es flitte~ over us-if there has been occasionally a passing

If' for a moment I could absolve myself from your committee and from this Grand
B.ody, and speak for myself alone, I Hhonld tell you how much I happen to know of
him. In fifteen years of personQ.l and official intimacy I have come to know him

it. But, I am speaking for the committee and for yon, and personal matters must be
left for another and more appropriate occasion.
And here this committee ends its labors. The portrait of your Grand Secretary,
as you already know, we have placed in the position of honor in the gallery of your
Past Grand Masters; and here before you is the testimonial which we have prepared. The refined and solid silver of which Its pieces are composed is 11 fitting
symbol of the charar.ter of the brother to whom we now present it, and the beautiful
designs which ornament each piece are illustrative of his labors for this Grand
Body.
Brother ABELL, receive this testimonial from your brethren, and with it take also
the assurance of their profound gratitude, their continued confidence and fraternal
love, and their earnest and repeated prayers that you may long live to remember
with the deepest satisfaction the occurrences of this day.

A TRIBUTE FROM CALIFORNIA.

~his ~,0urniug ~agt,
BY THE GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS
OF THE

STATE OF CALIFORNIA,

IS RESPECTFULLY AND AFFECTIONATELY DEDICATED

To the Memory of
OUR BELOVED AND LAMENTED BROTHER

Jamts Q\bram ~artitlb1
L.A.':t'E

PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES.

"Tlte ft1'st among hfs equtds!'

When a great man falls, the nation formally puts on the habiliments of
woe. When a good man dies, the people weep. One who was both great
and good-as good as be was great, and as great as he was good-a leader
and a master among men-has fallen ; fallen at the post of duty; fallen as
heroically as mortal ever tell; fallen at the moment when bis grand and
ex<J.uisite character was impressing itself most effectually upon the nation
winch he represent.ed.
Our people for a season stood appalled in the presence of their great
calamity; and now the mingled tones of sorrow, like the voices of a thousand waters, hi.ve come unto us from all our sister States. More than this:
they come from every land where the light of civilization bas penetrated.
Not America alone. but all the world mourns for the loss which humanity
has suffered, as if the affiiction were too great for only one people to
·
endure.
The benefactorR of mankind should ever be remembered. It is a goodly
thing to honor the illustrious dead; and, sorrowing ~nd oppressed, we join
the countless throng of mourne1·s. We make ourselves a part of the fifty
millions of people who, without distinction of party, or race, or sect, or
creed , with bated breath and guivering lips, have gone out in grand and
solemn procession to lay then gratitude, their benedictions, and their
prayers upon the grave of

~amts ~. @arfidd.
Few men have achieved so much in so little time. Scholar, statesman,
soldier, and philanthropist, he was perhaps the best production of his agethe truest type of American character that the century has produced.
From the humblest walk in life, by his own inhernnt strength and force of
character, he rose-worthily, grandly, und deservedly rose-to the most
exalted position on the earth. The example alone of such a life and char·
acter is worth more to posterity than are the lives and achievements of
thousands of ordinary men.
He sleeps, but his influence will live forever. The world will still move
on; and men will still be born, live, die, an<l be forgotten. But, as the sun
will still rise and set, as the restless ocean will still beat and chafe a~ainst
its shores, as the planets will still move on in their appointed orbits, so
will the moral effects of this man's life be transmitted from generation to
generation through all time to come.
When our Grand Master said that "he was one with whom a nation was
satisfied and of whom a nation was proud," he paid the grandest possible
tribute to the worth and greatness of the dead President. We would add
something to these words if we could, but to elaborate would only weaken
the force of the Grand Master's expression.
To the aged and desolate mother, to the bereaved and devoted wife, and
to the fatherless children, we tender our profound though unavai:ing sympathies.
Noble citizen, heroic soldier, and honored statesman ; kind and .faithful
husband, son, and father; good friend, true man, and worthy Mason; he
needs no eulogy from us. He has builded his own monument in the hearts
of his countrymen. His deeds alone-his worthy deeds-havo rendered
him immortal.
Revered and honored brother I rest in peace. Thy works shall follow
thee, and thy fame shall be imperishable I

My theme will be PROGRESS, and in approaching a subject so vast and comprehensive, one is compelled to panse in utter astonishment at the magnitude of the
task which he has undertaken. So rapid, in the past hundred years, haR been the
p~ogress of the world in art, in science, in knowledge, In government, that it is akin
to an impossibility for one man to do jnstice to such a glorious theme. Even to
keep track of the unlimited nnmber of improved innovations made in every branch '
of lndnstry and advancement, would require the herculean investigating power of a
BACON, the innate comprehensiveness of a NEWTON, the prodlgions memory of a

appertaining to the powerful lmHgination of a J ULES VERNE. Hence, you cannot
but be silent if you perceive that I tremble even on the threshold of my adventure.
No one more than myself is more fully aware of the importance of this great and
happy occasion, and no one more fully realizes the dangers which beset me on the
road to progress.
To speak separately of all the branches of the many things which go to make up
the sum of human life would require a very large volume and many ye·a rs of close
and carefal study; so it is not to be expected that, in a short and hurriedly prepared
address, ample justice can be given to the subject. Let us, however, select a few
that most directly absorb the attention of mankind, and, by a sensible condensing
process, pay a passing tribute to the developments of the ages gone by.
As the first and most natural calling of man was agriculture, it Is but reasonable
that we shonld give some time to a consideration ·of it. The ancients devoted

so little, prior to the light which advanced and progressive s<>ience has thrown over

historians have ever been in the dark concerning them. But, thanks to the progress of
scientific investigation in this nineteenth century, many relics of the practices of the
ancients in agricultural matters are now being exhumed from their long burial places
under the ruins of the most famous cities of antiquity.

only knowledge of a reliable character transmitted to us of the Egyptians is found in

The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the qrand
Lodge, as follows :BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA:The hour which marks the close of another Masonic year is at hand; again the
gavel has sounded in the East; and once more we are called from refreshment to
labor in the Grand Lodge of Calirornia.
As we are about to enter upon that great and important .undertaking of reviewing
the record of the past, and marking ont the pathway.for the future Masonic year,
with becoming reverencp we should invoke the blessing of the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe, and return thanks for His goodness iu watching over us, in preserving and strengthening our faith in lb.e principles of Freemasonry, and for permitting us to return in health, strengtli and vigor to our annual labors.
Having laid aside for a time the working tools of our usual vocations, and left
behind daily enjoymeniii, cares and vexations, and divested our minds and consciences of the vices and superfluities of life, we come to greet each other as coworkers and brethren in the grandest benevolent fraternity on earth, and to renew
our devotion to the teachings of Freemasonry.
With joy and pride we extend to you a fraternal greeting, and welcome you as
members of the Grand Lodge, and as representatives 0£, Masonry, which in the lo.ng
and distant ages of the past, and down to the present, has successfully resisted the
anathemas of Church aud State, religious bigotry and political persecution, and
constantly spread and promulgated its moral and civilizing influences; and now, with
full confidence and becoming pride, looks forward to still greater successes and more
glorious victories.
In accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, it becomes mv duty to
present for your consideration a review of my ofll.cial acts during the brief period of
my soowardship.
The press of official and professional business during the year has occupied my
time and 11ttention to such an extent that I have not been permitted to make as many
and ·such fraternal visits to and among the subordinate Lodges as it was my desire
and intention to do wheo I entered apon the discharge of the duties of this office. I

. tl

Grand Lodge of .Oalifornia.

have, however, been enabled to visit some of the Lodges, and many 11leasant memories occasioned thereby are treasures never to be forgotten.
Immediately after the last session of the Grand Lodge I made my first official
visit to Mission Lodgli, No.169. A large number of brethren were present and a
few hour• were spent with much Masonic .profit and pleasure.
On the ninth of December, accompanied by Bro. THos. H. B. ANDERSON, Grand
Or tor of· the Grand Lodge, a fraternal and official visit was made to Sacramento
Lodge, No. iO, on which occasion the Lodge conferred the third degree in a manner
which is seldom equalled, and perhaps never excelled, and which reflected great
credit apon the officers of the Lodge a·nd elicited the admiration and commendation
of all present. 'Past Grand Masters N. GBEENI! 0URTIB, WILLIAM A. DAVIES and
GEORGI! C. PERRINS were preYent, as we~e also a llirge number of Visiting brethren.
On being called to refreshment we found a bounteous repast in waiting, to which
ample and substantial justice was done with prudence and temperance.
On December thirty-first I visited Stanislaus Lodge, No. 206, at Modesto,' and
publicly installed its officers elect for the ensuing Masonfo year. The bodge has
recently moved into a new and commodious hall in a brick building, and the Lodgeroorn is handsomely and ,substantially furnished, and of it the brethren may very
justly be prond. Many visiting brethren and members were present with their wives
snd daughters, and the occasion was one which reflected credit upon tho Craft.
After the ceremonies of installation were completed the usual festivities were enjoyed, by a banquet, music and d,ancing.
For a time the very ftee and indiscriminate use of the blackball prevented this
Lodge from prospering, but I am happy to report that good counsel and example
have since prevailed, and it is now one of ou~ tnost prosperous Lodges.
On the evening of January twelfth I paid a fraternal visit to Reading Lodge, No.
254, and publicly inst~lled its officers. The Lodge-room was crowded to overflowing
with the members and visiting brethren, accompanied by their wives, daughters and
sweethearts, all Qf whom manifested much interest and ple11sare In witnessing the
ceremonies of the occasion. The usual festivities of the banquet, music and dancing
f•lllowed, to which was added the presentation of a beautiful Past Master's jewel
to Bro. CHAUNOE\" CARROLL BUSH, the first Master of the Lodge.
On the twenty-ninth of Jannary last I convoked Suisun Lodge, No. 55, at Suisun,
Solano County,' for the purpose of inquiting into certain irregularities which had
theretofore occurred in that Lodge, In balloting upon applications for the degrees.
The acts and irregularities complained of, and which all conceded had been committed, interfered with the regularity and inviolability of the ballot, and were well
calculated to disturb and break the peace and harmony of the Lodge and to create
discord and confusion; Ample evidence was at hand to show that the irregularity
occurred by the action of a member whose identity was unknown to the Lodge, and
all elforts to diacover the offender proved unavailing. Upon such a state of facts no
recourse was left except to reprimand the unidentified member over the shoulders of
the Lodge, and to reserve the matter for future consideration and possible development. From the report of the Inspector I learn .that harmony has been restored,
·and that the Lodge is about to resume its former prosperous condition.
On April twenty-ninth I viaited A.din Lodge, No. 250, on which occasion, the
Mas1er being unavo,idably absent, I occupied his chair and conferred the third
degree. The work of the Lodge being completed, we were called to refreshment,
which was bounteous and heartily enjoyed. The occasion was line long to bo remembered.

On the twenty-fourth of .A.pril I convoked the Grand Lodge at Red Blo!f, Tehama

With much regret it becomes my duty to report the arrest of the charter of Union
Lodge, No. 58, a.t Sacramento. In March last, I met the Master of that Lodge, who
informed me that he had convened bis Lodge on Sunday and conferred the first degree, and inquired if he had committed an error in so doing; and, if so, what would
be the consequence? I informed him that it was a violation of the law, but that
if no complaints were ..made a.bout it, and if it was not repeated, I wonld take no
further notice of the miW;ter. A short time after, I met several brethren who at
once complained of the . matter; and on my return home I found a report from the
Inspector of the District, concerning the same, accompanying which was enclosed
a copy of a notice that had been published in a. aally pa.per, notifying mell!-bers of
the Lodge to meet on Sunday, March twelfLh, at the Lodge-room.
The Inspedor informed me that, having seen the published notice of the meeting,
he at once sought the Master of the Lodge and informed him of the decision or this
Grand Body, forbidding a Masonic Lodge to work npon the Sabbath day; called
his attention to the volume and pages of the proceedings where the ea.me might be
found; and advised a.nd requested him not to open his Lodge for work on Snnday.
In addition to the report of the District Inspector, my attention wa.s called to the
matter by the Master of %hama Lodge, No. 3-which meets in the same ba.11-an~
who informed me that he had also advised the Master, as early as the precedmg Friday, not to open his Lodge, and that work. on the Sabbath was prohibited by the
Grand Lodge.
l
With snch facts before rue, on March thirty-first I addreBSed a letter to the Master,
Wardens and brethren of Union Lodge, in which I informed them that the matter had
been reported to me, and inquired if the facts as reported were correct; and if so,
whether they were at the time aware of the decision of the Grand Lodge, forbidding
· a Lodge to work on Sonday, and ca.lied their attmtion to the volume and pages of
the proceedings where such decision could be found.
I also expressed my regret that the occasion had arisen, which ·reqnired of me as
an dtllcia.l duty, thus to question a.ny subordinate Lodge concerning its proceedings, and assured them that I did so with a desire to obtain a full and c~mplete
knowledge of all the facts and circumstances, that the welfare of the craft might be
carefully guarded.
To this letter it was confidently expected that a courteous reply would. be made,
acknowledging and regretting the error, and expressing assurances that it should not
again occur; and, had each been the result, no report of this natnre would have been
necessary.

From the foregoing it will be seen that, of the collective number of five hundred
and eighty-one widows and orphans reported, but seventy-six in all are named as
indigent or probablJ so; and an examination of the reports will show that not
all tbese would desire, or would be desired by the Lodges under the jurisdiction
of which they reside, to go to the Widows' and Orphans' Home proposed, should
·
such an institution be established.
The undersigned deems it proper to say that new jewels and new clothing (collars and apron@,) for th~ Grand Lodge ongbt to be provided. In 18.13, as appears
from our records, its first clothing and jewels were procnred from New York. 1'hat
clothing had become somewhat soiled and· worn, and, upon the recommendation of
Grand Master PRATT in 1870, a new outfit wa~ procur11d. ·since then, to save that new
clothing for use only at annual or important communications of the Grand Lodge ,
the old clothing has been seut out to be used when cotner-stones were to be laid or
Lodge Balls to be dedicated, until it has ceased to be at all respectable in its appearance. It is therefore suggested that ag11in new clothing be provided for the use of
the. Grand Lodge.at its important communications, in order that that last named, now
much soiled, may, in its torn, be used for the purposes just above mentioned; and
that the old clothing be relegated to the ragman. No jewels have been procured
since those received from New York in 18a3, as 11bove stated. They are worn, old• fashioned , and not sufficient in number for the offi9ers now borne upon our register;
and it is to be hoped that new ones may be provided which will correspond with the
emblems embroidered upon the new clothing. The old ones will be sufficient for the
secondary clothing and the uses for which it is now so often required.

Inspector BENJAMIN W. BABNES, of the seventh district, reports that the fonr
Lodges under his charge are not in as flourishing a condition as he could wish.
Being located iu partially deserted mining districts, their opportunities for increasing
their membership are not favorable. He writes that two of them, St. Louis, No.
86, and Gibsonville, No. 158, have wisely decided to consolidate, and that, although
few in members and doing but little work, that which the Lodges do perform is well
done and in accordance with the ritual prescribed by the Grand Lodge.
Inspector JosIAH P. BBOWN, of the eighth diRtrict, reports tlie continued prosper·
ity of the four Lodges committed to his charge. Although but little work has been
done: he finds the officers proficient and thoroughly qualified, the books well kept,
and the financial condition quite satisfactory.
Inspector !ANTHIS J. ROLFE, of the ninth district, repo!ts in detail the condition of
the four Lodges therein, and it is gratifying to know that in two instances a manifest
improvement has been made. In Madison Lodge, No. 23, he reports a better state
of feeling existing, which he attributes to the influence of the new Master, Bro.
THEODORE H. WILHELM, who. he says, "is young, zealous· and conrteons_ to his
brethren. Two candidates have been elected, being the first in several yee.rs, and
the Master, and, in fact, all the officers are doing excellent work." Bro. RoLFE also
reports that this Lodge has, since the first day of J1mnary, 1871, expended in charity
the sum of $17,207.25, and had still in its treasnry, on the first day of January, 1882,
the sum of $1,354.27. He also.reports Quitman Lodge, No. 88, to be in a much more
flourishing condition than at the date of his last report. The debt of $1°,200, with ·
which it was then burthened, has been reduced to $600, and the members look
forward with confidence to its final extinguishment. Several candidates have
received the degrees, and the prospect looks brighter for the future of this Lodge.
Inspector JOHN G. BrsBE:lli, of the tenth district, reports that he had visited
seven of the eleven Lodges tborein, but was prevented by sickness in bis family from
visiting the remaining four. He promises to do so at the earliest.possible moment.
The Lodges visited were generally in good condition, but some of the officers re·
quired instruction in the work, which he had given so far as was possiblll.
Inspector GARRETT W. WALRAVEN, of the eleventh district, has succeeded in em·
bodying in his report the " soul of wit," if". brevity" iB to be so·considered. It con·
sists of t'lree lines upon a half sheet of note paper, and conveys the gratifying intel·
ligence that the Lodges in his district, four iu number, were in good condition. and
proficient in the work. While iL is pleasant to know this, a little · more of detail
would have given agreater degree of satisfaction.
· Insp.ector JosEPH A. FLINT, of the twelfth district, reports a very satisfactory
condition of the five Lodges under his supervision. He thinks that the twelfth will

proficient iu the work and perform their ~uties with fidelity and zeal.
Inspector JosEPH B. COOKE, of the thirteenth district, reporti all the Lodges

Lodges and the removal of Meridian Lodge, No. 182, from Meridian to Oollege City,
