Inspector EDWARD W. KING, of the fourteenth district. reports the four Lodges
under his charge to be in good condition and doing their work in a creditable manner,
InspectoT ALBERT WRIGHT, of the fifteenth district, report<! that all the Lodges
therein, eleven iu number, are in good working condition, that peace and harmony
prevai~ and that" each vies with the other in the effort to perform the work agreeably to the instructions and mandates of the Grand Lodge." He gives expression to
some rather radical ideas with reference to measures which should be taken to insure uniformity of work and phraseology; bnt, with judicious modification, much
practical benefit would result from their adoption. He says:-

1882.]

Grand Lodge fl/ California.

467

From the experience I have had as Inspector I am fully of the opinion that a determi11ed effort should be made on the part of the Grand Lodge, and enforced by the
Grand Lecturer, to compel all officers of Lodges-at least for a number of years-to
pass an actual examination before the Inspectors of their respective districts, previous to their installation. I believe that the Grand Lecturer and Inspectors of Ualifornia will bear me out in saying thai, although the tenor of the work is the same,
there is a lack of uniformity in details, and a decided difterence in phraseology
ill performing and rendering it among the various Lodges of the jurisdiction. It is
now some seventeen years since the W••rk of revision was accomplished in this State,
and du~iug the last twelve y~ars, the work, ~s adopt.ed by the Gr11nd Lodge, has been
transmitted to each succeeding officer by his predecessor with little or no reference
to the fountain head. Passing, as it has, from one generation of officers to another,
without revision, and not infrequently without care, it is not surprising that discrepancies and innovations have crept In, thereby marring the purity of our revised
ritual and changing or perverting its language.
It is the duty of the Inspector to inspect the work and correct irregnlarities when
time and opportunity will permit, but lie is seldom ca.lied upon to lecture the Lodges
systematically, as most of'them believe they need no lecturing, relying solely upon
local lecturers or Past Officers, whom they believe to be correct. I trust that some
provision will he adopted by the Grand Lodge whereby the evil herein pointed out
may be remedied, and a systematic course of lectures given to each Lodge in order
that the ceremonial and phraseology of our beautiful ritual may once more be made
uniform, in accordance with the principles which caused its adoption and the discipline which made its performance by the Lodges a Masonic law.
It is undoubtedly the fact that discrepancies in the minor details of the work do
exist, arising trom the causes pointed out by Bro. WBIGHT, and, if such discrepancies in minor details are tolerat.ed for any great length of time, they are almost certain to extend to essentials and thus destroy the harmony of the system. Not being
prepared at this time to present any definite plan by which the evil may be remedied,
I recommend the matter to the careful consideration of the Grand Lo<lge.

The office of Inspector is a position of honor and not '[WOjU. He is, for the pnr·
poses of his position, the representative of the Grand Mastei· ; and, alt hough he has
no executive power, it is certainly his duty to visit and Inspect each L odge in ·his
district at least once dnriog hie term of office, and to report, severally, to the Grand
Master and the Grand Lectnrer, in the manner required in hie commission and in onr
General Regnlation, No. 15. Bro. CLARK says that two of the Lodges in hie district
gave him no opportnnity to visit them, and did not even commnnicate with him. I
wish to call the attention ol Inspectors to the fact that it is not necessarily t be duty
of Masters of Lodges to communicate with them, nnless their services are required ;
bnt that It is their duty to commnnlcate with the Masters and inform them of the
time when they propose to visit their Lodges, in order that they may be prepared for
inHpectlon. The proceedings of the Grand (,odge, if lnspect?rs would only read
them, afford all the information neceBBary as to names of officers, times of meeting,
etc., and no Inspector who nnderetands his duty will wait for ao Invitation from a
Lodge. Lodges which are proficient in the work, and fully and carefully obey the
edicts and mandates of the Grand Lodge, are always ready aod willing to receive
the visits of the Inspector, and these are the ones which generally Issue invitations
to that officer. On the contrary, those Lodges which most need inspection are the
last to Invite the attention of the Inspector , and to these his attention should be
especially directed. The expenses incurred by the Inspector are aii especial charge
upon the Lodge which he may consider it necessary to visit, and each Lodge thus
visited is compelled by the law to pay them; so that oo Inspector should hesitate
one moment In the discharge of his duty for any pecuniary reason affecting either
himself nr the l.odge. As t here appears to be (uuacconntably to me) a doubt in
the minds of some Inspectors as to their powers a nd duties, I desire to say that the
law upon that subject is as plain as the Eugli•h language can make it, and l can only
account for this doubt by the suppo~ition that their fi1·st duty, as officers of the Grand
Lodge, has been neglectad, viz: that of reading their own commlBBione and the law
applicable tQ their positions.

Yet we are confronted with the fact that, notwithstanding that the law upon the
subject is thos explicit and plain, fifteen oi;it of the thirty-three Inspectors have
neglected to make a report to the Grand Master; and, having thus failed to discharge a. duty so plainly enjoined upon them, your committee a.re asked to present
a plan by which the discharge of snob duty may in future be secured!
Io the opinion of your committe~, tho brother who, being appointed to an
Inspectorship and accepting the trust., fails to discharge the duties thereof, and more
especially who fails to make the reports required of him in the absence nf an excuse .
considered as sufficient by the officer to whom such report should have been made,
deserves and should receive tbe censure of this Grand Lodge, his appointment should
be revoked, and thereafter he should not be re-appointed; and, holding these views,
they think that the remedy for the existing evil Is not to be found in a change of the
la.w bnt in the enforcement of it as it already exists. These officers are to be
app~inted by tbe Grand M~ter, under and in pursuance of General Regulation N~.
ta. No term of office being prescribed, their tenure is necessarily subject td the will
and pleaFure of the appointing power; and hence, for any dereliction of duty on the
part of the Inspector, his certitlcate may at any time be revoked and somebody
appointed in his place who will discharge the duties of the office.
Adverting again tn the report of th" committee of last year, a resolution thereby
reported (see page 181, Proceedings of 1879,) ao<l adopted by this Grand Lodge,
was as follows:" R··soltied, That no Inspector, who has failed to make the report required by law,
should be re-appointed to such position unless satisfactory explanation be given for
·
such failure."
Which resolution, in the opinion of your cotnmittee, covers the entire ground and
renders any additional action in the premises- by the Grand Lodge on necessary.
It appears to me that any Inspector who reads the foregoing can scarcely be in
doubt as to his powers and duties.

The Grand Master, in his able and well written Address, said he was happy in being
able to repeat the congratulations of the previous year on the favorable temporal
auspices under which they met. In some sections of the State the seasons might not
have been as propitious as men could wish, but still all had many things for which to
be thankful. Nearly unbroken were the ranks of the Grand Lodge; but Death had
removed one who was as highly respected and as sincerely beloved as any one who
had ever occupied a seat therein. He alluded to thew:-. Bro. JAMES HI<RVEY JOINER,
who had been called away in the midst of a still vigorous manhood. The Grand
Master paid a glowing ·eulogy upon the worthy brother:He was an honest, true and sincere man, aad the feelings of esteem and aJfectioo
towards himself .that be excited in the brel\j!ts of those who knew him well, were as

The Address of the Grand Master is very long, filling nearly twenty-five pages of

Grand Master bas no taste in that direction, but the humblest Masonic reader' will
have no difficulty in ascertaining what the Grand Master is driving at. If he comes
across a certain agricnltnral instrument used in stirring np the soil, he just calls it a

another figure from the agricnltural world, we would say that there is no skim milk

of the Arkansas strawberries. We will help oar readers to a few spoonsfull of tpis
cream, only regretting for their sakes that we cannot give it to them by the cnp·fnll.

The Committee on the " Masonic Charity Foundation Fund" reported at length
on that subject, reviewing the action heretofore bad. and urging more energetic
measures in ~1e future, looking to the esta_blishment of a" Masonic Home." Two
Lodges had contributed, respectively, five hundred and two hundred and fifty dollars.
The whole amount given thus far was a little over four thousand dollars. The committee further said that, in their opinion, "no attempt should be made toward the
practical operation of a Ma.sonic Home until the funds for such purpose shall have
reached an amount guaranteeing from its income a successful maintenance of the
project. They are firmly of the opinion that at least $100,000 is needed to accomplish
the desired end. They are further of the opinion that this amount, with a properly
organized effort, can be raised in five years." A permanent commission of three was
appointed to takP. the whole matter in hand.
The sum of twelve hundred dollars was contributed by the Lodges for the relief
of the Michigan sufferers.

Then comes the Masonic historical statement to which we alluded:In later ages, in England as upon the Continent, LodgeR became attached to the
Convents, and were more or less governed by Monks, .according a.s the leading
architects were Monks or lay brethren. Hence arose the custom of holdinl!' Lodge
sessions In Convents. When an Abbot became Master or Wardeo ,' he was addressed
as Worshipful Master or Worshipful Brother, a mode of address which has been
handed down to our time in connection with the first office of the Lodge. As years
rolled on, it was deemed advisable that intlueotial individu.als who loved and pro- ·
tected the arts, shonld be receive~ into the Order, although they were not practical
architects arid builders; and they were desi1_ruated as a~ed Ma.sous. The Lodge
at York, which became t.he most important in the country, received none as companions who were not free men, establishing the characteristic of the Institution,
that no person once admitted into it could in any manner be impeached in his possession of Masonic privileges.
Whatever we may think of this and like statements, as Ma.sonic history, none
can find fa•1lt with the following excellent advice given to the brethren at the close
of the Address :Make your Masonry no mere n1tme nor formality. Gather the spirit of its
teachingR. Exemplify that spirit in your Intercourse with each other aud with the
world at large. IL will make you better, and you will make the world better. Masons' lip• . outside the lodge-room, shonld be silent ln regard to Masonry's mysteries.
Masons' lives should be vocal for it. May your lives give no uncertain utterance.

The Grand Master gives a resume of the history 11nd work of the "Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home;" and urge~ a liberal support of the institution by the Fraternity. It waso1iommenced in 18671 The first building was completed in 1870 at a

on the lottery 11cheme, thus antborlzed, for a number of years, but the G~and Lodge
came out minu& $20,000. In 1836 the Legislature anthorized the sale or lease of t his
privilege uutil the Grand Lodge could at least make its losses good. In 18~2 tl1e
commissioners made such sale to Walter F. Gregory & Co., on their agreeing to pay
$500 annnally, In semi-annnal installments, until $30,000 should be received by the
Grand Lodge. The assignees have paid the sum ol $30,276 66, hu1-it is claimed that
the deficit of $20,0l>O should also be made good, which would leave $19.723 34 still
due. A resolution was therefore offered and adopted, authorizing t.he Grand Treasurer to receive semi-annnally ench sums, in liquidation of the debt, ns a majority or
the commissioners should deeide the Grand Lodge was entitled to receive. This
seems, in this anti-lottery day, a curious way to raise revenue; bat in olden times it
was not considered wrong even to bnild churches from the proceeds of lotteries.

NEW YORK.
The one hundred and first Annua.1. Communication of the Grand Lodge of New

sixth day of June, 1882,--'-the M. •• W.-. HoBAOE 8. TAYLOR, Grand Master, P.residing,
and the R.-. w.-. EDWARD M. L. EHLERS being the acting Grand Secretary. Six

The Address of Grand Master TAYLOR is 11 model document of its kind, ably
written in the best of English, and so well and j udicionsly worded that no one can
mistake as to what its author intends to say, nor is he ~fraid to speak his mind
freely when occasion calls, in censure as well as in approval. Upon their meeting for
the first time in the second century of the existence of the Grand Lodge, the Grand
Master congr11t11!11ted the Fraternity upon the favorable auspices attendant upon
their assembling. He then alluded to the honnrable dead of the year, first mentioning the .M.'. w.·. STEPHEN H. JOHNSON, II Past Grand Master and an eminent
Mason and civilian, who had held responsible offices in the legislative and jndicia.l
departments of the State Government. He died at his home in Schenectady soon
after the Centennia.1 Meeting of the Grand Lodge.
Fnll and appropriate mention is then made of the death of Grand Secretary
J.ums M. AusTIN, M. D., who had filled that important office for nearly twenty-eight
consecutive years. So well and favorably was this eminent Mason known, not only in
that jurisdiction, but also throughout the Masonic world, that we make no apology
for copying at length the remarks of· the Grand Master :R. ·• W.'. JAMES M. Al7STIN died December 3, 1881. He was at the tiine of his
death. and had been for twenty-seven consecutive years, Grand Secretary of this
Grand Lodge. Although for some months his health had been somewhat impaired,
bis death was sudden, and its announcement caused 11 feeling of deep sadness
throughout the State. On Friday. November 25th, Dr. AUSTIN, while in bis office
engaged in the discharge of his dntieB", had an attack of apoplexy, and was conveyed
to his home. On tha Sunday following, in respon~e to 11 note received from his
family, I visited him. I found him sitting in an easy chair, dressed, and apparently
in the full possession of his facultie.s. I had a long interview with him, in which he
indicated what he would wish to have done, in the event of his illness proving fatal,
and I gave him such comforting assurances as I could. He seemed to be impressed
with the idea that he would not recover, but I could not believe that his apprehensions were well-founded. I left him fully believing that I should see him a.gain, but
after that day until his death he was unable to see me.
. Thus passed away, full of years and of honors, one to whom we had looked up
for more than 11 guarter of 11 century for counsel and guidance. To him, more
than to a.lmost any otber man, does the Masonic fraternity in the State of New York
owe its prosperity and its influence In other jurisdictions. His name, more than
a.lmost any other, was 11 respected, 11 familiar name, wherever Mason~y exists. To
us bis loss is well-nigh irreparable; and it will be many, many years, before the
void which his death has caused can be filled. He has left us the example of 11 wise
and good man and Mason. Let us profit by this, and let us cherish his memory in
our inmost affections.

services, for the family and friends, being held at his residence, and the Masonic
services immediately afterwards in this room, which was filled with those who

We have taken occasion in some of our previous reports to refer to the unusual and,
as it &eemed to us, unseemly political electioneering that had invaded, if not captured,
this Grand Lodge. A.ii one result, and a very natural one too, the Grand-Master refers
at some length to a difficulty which had arisen between him and two of the Long
Island Lodges, and which culminated in the arrest of thfl warrants of both those
Lodges. To show how far such nnmas'onio, party-politics action c1m be carried, we
give a brief resume of the whole matter, as presented by the Grand Master •• The
" one-term" principle in the election of Grand Master has so long prevailed in
New York that it has come to be considered as the settled ~w of the jurisdiction.
Strenuous opposition thereto has been manifested for several years pa.st, and the two
parties seem to be drs wn up in battle array as. fiercely as if they were the ' ' Demo- ·
crate" and "Republicans" of the political arena. Now for this particiµar illustration :.
The Grand Master was informed that the District Deputy of the Firot Masonic
District, (that of the Long Island Lodges,) appointed by him, was circulating a petition addressed to theDeputy Grand Master, who would be the Grand Master in regular succession, a.sking for the appointment of a certain brother as the future Deputy. A number of the Masters of Lodges had signed it. The Deputy had also "made
statements in regard to the Grand Mlll!ter which were not true, and which were prejudicial to his influence and authority as Grand Master." These charges relat.ed to
his alleged opinions and a.eta on the "one-term " hobby. At an interview, the Deputy admitted his action in relation to the petition, but emphatically denied making
the statements alleged. Receiving definite and positive information to the contrary,
the GrandMaster, without assigning any reason, removed the Deputy and appointed
another brother in his stead. Subsequently, the Lodge of which .the late ·Depnty
was a member "passed a series of.resolution8 which were printed and Widely circulated, with the seal of the Lodge attached." These resolutions, and those subseqnently adopted by another Long Island Lodge/to whi~h the to-be-appointed Deputy belonged; are characterized by the Grand Master as "slanderous in their character and false in their statements," and he Bpecifies wherein; notably that "the
Grand Master sought and obtained the e.lection of Deputy Grand Master on the oneyear principle." So far from this, he had always been opposed to that as a pernicious
rule, and had urged his predecessor, in t~e strongest term3, to assent to a re-election.

The Grand ¥aster ·arrested the warrants of both Lodges-the Master of the flrstnam~, however, contemptuously refusing to obey the edict of surrender, but the

Senior Warden subsequently complied, and deposited the charter with the Grand
Secretary. Buch ·were the reported fa.eta, and we give, in connection therewith, some
of the very pointed comments of the Grand Master:I believe that this state of things is the natural outcome of the intense anxiety
of individuals to be elected to the highest offices in our Grand Lodge-an anxiety
'11'.hich will not permit them to wait, until by long service, their t!tness shall oo
d91Ponstrl!.ted and recognized-but who, regardless of the best interests of the fraternity, endeavor to accomplish their object by practices until recently unknown in
:Masonic elections, and whwh if continued, will degrade us in the estimation of our
brethren in other jurisdictions, in none of which would such practices be tolerated.
Bo notorious is this evil, and so disastrous threaten to be its consequences, that
no personal considerations should prevent it from being brought sguare1y before the
Grand Lodge. No considerations of delicacy shonld prevent tlie Grand Master
from bringing the Grand Lodge face to face with an evil which threat.ens its pros. perity, and which, if not checked, will endanger its continued existence. It ts a fact
known to all, that persons, past and present members of the Grand Lodge, make
organized and systematic efforts for the election of themselves or their friends to
· high office, bringing to their aid all the questionable arts of the professional politician, and striving by artificial and unmasonic means, to creat.e ench a sentiment
for or against a particular person as will insure his success or defeat,· before the
Grand Lodge as a body shall have come together. The Grand Lodge is in fact
deprived of it.a right to the free choice bf its officers. Members a.re persistently
eolicited to vote for or against particular individuals, a.nd their att.ention is diverted
from the discharge of the serious duties which they are selected to perform. The
all-absorbing question has grown to be, not, '\'i hat measures shall the Grand
Lod~ take for the good of the fraternity? but,
Who shall be elected to office?
The aggrandizement of individuals is not the purpose for which this G~d Lodge
was created.• Its officers are its servants, called to occupy high pjaces, not for their
own exaltation; but solely because the necessities of the Grand Lodge require their
services. No person has the right to demand elevation to office. It is forthe Grand
Lodge itself to select its officers from amon~ those it deems deserving.
This unmasonic political epil'it has become intensified in consequence of the
more frequent changes in Grand Lodge Officers which has taken .place within the
last few years. Formerly, when changes were Iese frequent, time was.given for any
excitement which existed during or previous to an election in the Grand Lodge to
subside. Bnt now, no sooner is one election over than combinations are formed for
the next, and thus the fraternity is kept in perpetual turmoil. I commend this subject, in all its bearings and in all its possible consequences, to the serious consideration of the Grand Lodge.

The following paragraphs we copy from the Annual Report of Bro. MILLS, the

well as of successes :·
. When the Trojan Prince had escaped from Asia, and was storm-driven awa:I'

Carthage requested the story of his trials. The way-worn hero was reluctant to revive the memory of the sorrows through which he had passed. And our teachers

In like manner, a report on the Orphan Asylum for 1881 is a story of successes,
struggles with mud, rain, ice, snow and hail, followed by drought, dust and sickness.
For nearly three months the roads werll impassable. We could not even send to
mill. Empty wagons stuck fast, and were abandoned in front of the Orphan Asy"
!um·. Dirt roads were even dangerous, and we had no railroad. We were compelled
to drive our teams, or see our children suffer. Our best mule fell a victim to mud
and stormy weather, aud others were so injured as to diminish their value. At last
the spring came, and rains ceased entirely, and for five months the earth was parched
with drought. 'Vegetables could not be raised, and the mills could not grind the
wheat and corn. We lived on Irish potatoes and onions in the spring, and turnips
in the fall. Other vegetables had to be brought from other parts .of the State.
Just then the Superintendent was sick, and for several weeks had to sit up in bed·
and· transact busmess. And yet more children than we ever had before have been
comfortably fed, clothed, and faithfully instructed.
The Superintendent then gives the statistics of the Asylum, which show that the
total number of orphans admitted up to December, 1881, was six hundred and
twenty-eight. One hundred and forty were now on the roll and being cared for,
forty-three having been dismissed during the year. Of these the Superintend~nt
says:-

Grani Lodge of California.

1882.J

567

Of the total number dismissed, about ninety per cent. are doing well, prospering
in their labors, and useful to the State. Those who fail to do well are generally
those who ran away, or whose parents interfered with their progress. The general
health of the children has been remarkably good. The children adopted are among
the happiest in the State, and remunerative employment was ready for all who were
dismissed.
During the year the Grand Master, officers and members of
the Grand Lodge, and Committees of the Subordinate Lodges, have comforted and
relieved the Superintendent by their cordial co operation. Churches, benevolent
societies, and liberal individuals have so freely forwarded their contributions in cash
and kind that we have not suffered anypecumary distress. It is safe to·say that our
noble and generous people do not intend to let their orl!hans suffer for food, clothing
or instruction. During the nine years through which our work has extended,
our faith has ended in fruition, our hopes have been lost in the sight of a pleasing
reality, and our never-failing charity has reacted on this life and extended its
blessed influences beyond the gi·ave.

dearest little girl in this institution. I owe much to the benevolent Order which
founded this institution, and which has clothed me with its highest honors. And I
owe still more to this whole community for the extraordinary encouragement and
patronage which they afforded me in an honorable profession for more than a quarter of a century. *
* * This stone which we set up to-clay under these
oaks, in this house is a live stone. lt can hear; inquire of it, and lt can answer.
Ask it now, or let your children aak a thousand years to come:-" What meaneth
this stone? Who built this house? Who founded this institution?" And it will
answer :-'"l'he Masons." "For what purpo.se?" "To nurse its orphans." "By
what means?" "By voluntary contributions." "Who were its officers and teach. ers?" They will all be named. " Who were its pupils?" The roll will be called.
"Who laid the corner-stone? Who were the orators? What were the circumst¥Jces?" All will be answered; not a syllable omitted.
A word to the pupils of this institution :-Twenty miles west of this, on a large
rock on the side of a mountain, some fifty years ago, two poor boys were caating the
probabilities of their future lives, which seemed gloomy enough, when one of them
sprang up and clenched his hands and stamped the rock, and said:-" There is a :P,ep,
in the Senat;e of the United States for me to hang my hat on, and I mean to do it. '
Some thirty years thereafter, when he who had been that boy entered the Senate of the Confederated States as 11 member thereof, the first thing thathe saw was a
large hat-rack with pegs on it. And he hung his hat on it, and instantly the incident
on the mountain rock flashed across his memory. And if he were on the mountain
rock to-clay, it would speak to him as J>lainly as .he speaks to you. So let every inmate of this institution vow a life of usefulness and honor, and call this stone to
hear him, and it will hear him, and be a witness for him lest he forget his vow.
The same boy who stamped the rock on the mountain, when he came to. get his
license to practice his profession, had not a dollar to pay for his license, and had to
borrow a srt'all sum from a generous friend, and he returned the money out of his
first earnings. Well, the money being returned, did that make them even? Not
so, thought the boy. He felt a debt of gratitude which dollars and cents coµld not
pay, and therefore he waa glad to do the large professional business of his friend,
without charge, for a quarter of a century. Now, this institution has selected you
out of thousands just as dependent as you, and will qualify you to go out and act a
profitable, useful and honorable part in the world. The institution will have loaned
you the money to procure your license. Will xou pay it back again? Uf course
you will. Will that make you even with the institution? Not so, thought the boy.
JS'o, no; you will still owe it a debt of gratitude which a life of affectionate serviaes
only must pay. What the institution has done for you, yon must help it do for
others. And then, in old age, if you shall visit this stone, it will have treasured up
for you and will speak to you of all the incidents of your pupilage, and all the history of a well-spent life, as plainly as I speak to you to-clay.
Strike the stone hard, Grand Master, and set it firm, and let it hold this building
sure for ages and ages to come. And let it be a witness for us that we will never
forget the covenant which we have this day made,-" To TAKE CABE OF THE
ORPHAN."

The "Committee on Landmarks" submitted a report on a somewha.t curious
~tale of ~hingd, Ma.sonically, which had been referred to them. It appears that the
by-laws of a certa'n Lodge provided that " t he trustees of the hall should take
charge of the regalfa and other furniture of the Lodge. a~d keep the same in repair,
purchase new furniture and regalia when directed, and make a written report to
the Lodge," etc. Upon inquiry, the committee ascertained that these trustees were
neither elected by the Lodge nor appointed by the Master, but were c1·eated under
the provisions of a deed, which granted to nine persons a certain lot and a twostory brick hall thereon, to hold in trust for the Lodge in question. The deed further required that in case of vacancy, by death or otherwise, the Lodge should
nominate some of its members to till the same. Originally, this nomination must
be confirmed by the Court of Common Plea• of Philadelphia, but subsequently that
mode of approval was ohanged from the Court to the Grand M1111ter. Thus the
committee found a body of trustees named who were neither officers nor a commit- '
tee of the Lodge, and yet were chargGd by the by-laws with a duty which the
"Ahim6n Rezon,"-tbe supreme law in that jnrisdiction,-expreesly d eclared
should devolve upon the Master . By this by-law, then , the property which he is
qharged with the management of ia placed iu the entirfl care of those over whom he
has no con,trol. The committee was decidedly of the opinion, and so reported, that
the by-law was clearly in derogation of Masonic regulations, and should be annulled. Their report was unanimously adopted.

The only decision reported by the Grand Master states a case and gives some ad·
vice, which may be of use even in this jurisdiction, as follows:·
A candidate had been elected to receive the three degrees. Snbseqnently a
Master Mason in good standing, but not a member of that Lodge, informed the W.·.
M.-. that he objected to the candidate bein~ made a Mason. At this stage of the case
my advice was asked. I directed the W. ·. M. •. to investigate the matter in a quiet
but thorough manner, and, If be became satisfied that the objection was well founded,
to refuse to initiate ; and, should this action be taken, to report tb.e fact to the Lodge,
that a record might be made of it; that in that event the candidate would be rejected
material and should be so treated. I am informed that the W.·. M.·. found npon investigation that the objection was well founded and refused to proceed with the initiation.
From the :ibove circumstance, one thing is evident, and it is the lesson to be drawn
from it-that the committee appointed upon the application failed and neglect~d to
do their dut:v. This is too frequently tqe ca•e In all Lodges. Buch committees
should ever bear in mind that they are io truth and io fact investigating committees.
They shoold never be contented ~o report favorably becans~ no one has voh~nt~r!IY
come forward to accuse the apphcant of crime, or of practices and moral obhqu1tieo
that render him an unfit otone for that spiritual temple which all Masons are required
to build. The good of Masonry demands that they should make an effort to find out.,
nay, that they should search ont, the character and habits of the applicant : an~,
should they come to the conclusion that he is not a man of good moral character, is
.not " under the tongue of good report," or is of so low a grade of intellect that if
admitted he could neither understand nor properly appreciate the lessons of. o~r
ritual, they should have the courage to so state. Take as yonr motto : "That it 1s
better not to grow at all than to grow by the accretion of bad material."

will not directly approached, for the simJ>le reason that it was supposed then, as now,
that each individual brother was familiar enough with the teac1iings and practices
of the Mormon Church to know that a person believing in its doctrines could not be
made a Mason. The experience of the pa•t decade has proved sufficiently that the
Grand Lodge acted wisely in leaving the qu :stion au open one, and in depending entirely on the good judgment of its membt:cs.
While the fraternity in Utah believes in and upholds the universality of the Masonic institution, and recognizes the riitht of everycrafte)'.llan to join any charch and
embrace any creed he chooses, and demands of him only that ho 11hall admit tbe
theological belief taught on the threshold of our sacred Temple ; and further. that he
must be loyal to the <lovernm•nt under which he live~, rmrl yield a wUling obedience
to aJJ. its laws. the Masone in Utah contend tht.t the latter important prerequisite is
wanting in the Mormons, because one of the chief tenets of their church in Utah is
polr.gamy, which a Unitec;l States Statute has declared to be a crime, and which all
civilized nations consider a relic of barbarism. It has been said that not all Mormons in Utah. practice polygamy, and this is even so; but it is nevertheless true that
all believe it to be a revel11.tion of God, and consequently all of them, by retaining
membership in the church, uphold the tenet and thereby teach and encourage others
to enter into polygamous relations that mako them abettors of the crime, and they
are therefore, by the laws of our country, the decisions of our courts and the moral
sense of an enlightened world, amenable and guilty. It is their application of the
dogma to J>ractical life. and their enjoining it UJ.>On all as a duty commanded by God,
that Gonstuute• their criminality, and not the simple ht-lief in it. Hence every disciple of and adherent to the Mormon doctrine as taught by BmGBAM You1m, is barred
out of ~ur Lodges, beci\use we cannot comprehend tbat a deed committed in the jurisdiction of a sis tar Grand Lodge and there considered to be a crime in the·eyes of
.Freemasonry as well a.sin the eyes of the law of the land, should be upheld and.considered to be a reli11:ione tenet. in Utah.
In view of the foregoing facts, every thinking' Mason must admit that the course
heretofore pursued by our Lodges is the onl,v correct one, and that to be true to themselves and to the craft at large, they can pursue none other. The craftsmen of Utah
have seen so much of the evil doinga of Mormonism that they have a perfect abhorrence of it, and will do all in tbeir power to keep the noble and pure instrtution of
Freemasonry free from its evil influences. The Grand Lodge of Utah is wall awa.re
of it.s sin~ular and anomalous situation, but the craft throughout the globe may be
assured that, as a link in the Masonic cha.in, it has in the past and will in the future
perform its sacred duty to the satisfaction of every sister Grand Lodge. For futther
information concerning thi• subject, I refer to our proceedingB' or 1879, p. 29, and
1882, pp. 28 and 78, copies of which were mailed to you at the- time, and which.AVill
more fully elucidate our past actions. Our future mtentions in the premises may
be judged thereby.

Ours is a language of symbols. We teach morality. and enforce duty, not merely
in didactic prose, but in the poetry of allegory and parable. All our forms and
rites have attached to them a deep signifk11nce, and are designed for wi;;e and,usetul
purposes. The ceremonies in which we have just participated carry with th1;1m to
every intelligent mind the reiteration of the great truth proclaimed from the lrlount
overlooking \jennesa.ret. that to build wisely or securely-either for the individual or
the community, for time or eternity- we must lay &foundation upon the solid .rock.
This proposed monument is a great symbol, a.nd is designed by its projectors in the
poetry of art to inculcate to generations in the distant future great moral lessons of
public duty, and to stimulate the cultivation and nractice of public virtue by the force
of honorable and honored example. How beautifully cons;stent is that obj!lCt with
our history and traditions, and with the sublime morality we teach.
Ours is in no just sense a seoret society. It is a confidential society. The times
and places of our meetings, our purposes and objects, our rolls of membership, our
code of morals-are all publicly known and avowed. Our membership embraces
m en of every grade ~f re.pec~?le society, every sect of religion, eve~ shade of po~jt­
ical opinion; and it 18 the pnvilege of every member of one Lodge m good standing
with his own Lodge to 'a ttend any of the meetings of sister Lodges.
Our code of morals is known and understood to be the same which is proclaimed
from every Christian pulpit and Hebrew s~agogue whenever the pe<>ple are assembled for the worship of the living God. Every M11.11on is especially enjoined to be a
peaceable subject or citizen, and never to allow himself to be involved in r.ots or

ENGLAND.

Proceedings were r eceived from the Quarterly Communica.tions of the United
Grand Lodge, held in March, June, and September, 1881. At the March Communication an interesting case involving the secrecy of the ballot was brought forward.
A certain Bro. TunoB ~BEVon was a member of a Lodge which met in Hornsea, in
Yorkshire. Some members of the Lodge resided in Hull, and others in Hornsea.
On one occasion two gentlemen proposed for initiation were blackballed. The ballot-box when opened disclosed only four balls, three being black. One brother immediat.ely stated that he had voted favorably, and, as the other three were known, it
was at once evident that they had cost the blackballs-the secrecy of the ballot-box
thus being violated. Some of the members of the Lodge, to make a bad thing worse,
determined that these brethren, if poBBible, should be excluded from the Lodge. A
summons was prtipared, printed, and circulated among the brethren of the Lodge,
the papers also containing a resolution by Bro. TREvon for auch exclusion. The
summons affirmed that the brethren who had cast the bfa.ckbo.lle were actuated by
unworthy motives; and further, that knowing that three blackballs were necessary
to exclude the candidates (such being the rule in this Grand Jurisdiction), had combined for that purpose. One of the summonses fell into the hands of a non-Mason,
whereupon, Bro. VoIGT, one of the three accused brethren , sued Bro. TREVOR at law,
for libel, and won hie case. Bro. TREVOR then went before tho Grand· Lodge and•
affirmed that the suit had cost him over one hundred and sixty pounds ; that he was
acting in defense of the Masonic Fraternity; that the suit had impoverished him;
and he prayed the Grand Lodge to donate to him the sum of one hundred and fifty
pounds, in part payment of his expenses. He further affirmed that the Lodge knew
that the offending brethren voted a.go.inst the candidates merely for spite, because
they had openly declared that the " majority" in the Lodge should not be increased,
and that they would blackball every one whom the" majority" might propose. It
eeeme that it was arranged among the" majority " (whatever or whoever that might
be,) that only one of their number-the Junior Warden-should vote, and thus the
blackballers were entrapped. Bro. TBEVOB so eloquently advocated his cose that h e
was almost sure of encoese-a motion to proceed to other bueine;s haying been voted
down by a decided majority. But finally a motion to refer the whole matter to the
"General Board," a sort of Standing Committ.ee, prevailed. The Board were instructed to report at the June Quarterly Communication. They did so, and against
the application, on the .ground that such an appropriation of Grand Lodge funds
would be an innovation and constitute a very inconvenient precedent. The Grand
Lodge unallimouely concurred, notwithstanding the vigorous protest of Bro. TREVOR.
The " sober second thought," in this case, was a wise one. We can only o.dd that, in
California, short work would be made of such a case and of the brethren who thus
so openly violated one of the fundamental Landmarks of F reemasonry.
Charity means something with our English bre\hren. In tho months of January,
February, and March of 1881, the various Lodges contributed to the Grand Lodge
Fund of .Benevolence the sum of four thousand one hundred and thirty-one pounds,
or over twenty thousand dolle.re.
His Royal Highness, the PBINOE of WA.LES, was re-elected Grand Master, and Col.
SHADWELL H. CLERKE, Grand Secretary; the EARL OF MABOII is Senior Grand warden; and the Hon. Mr. Justice CAVE, Junior Grand Wa rden . ·

IRELAND.
We have received from our Grand Secretary quite a number of circulars aud
pamphlets relating to the status and work of the Grand Lodge of Ireland. We ~so

v11nerable Body of Ma.i;ons.
The PRINCE OF wALES is Patron of .Masonry in Ireland, and the DUKE OF ABEBCORN is Grand Master, having held that import&nt position since 1874. His predecessor was the DUKE OF LEINBTER, who was Grand Master from 1813 to 1874; and
his predecessor, the EARL oF DoNOUGHMORE, was 'first elected in 1789. Among
the Grand Masters since the first one in 1174, we find the names of the father of the
DUKE oF WELLINGTON, n.nd of his father, when the latter was Lord Lieutenant of
Ireland.
There are Masonic provinces or districts iu Ireland and elsewhere, holding charters under the Grand Lodge; some of these comprising only one county. Each
province bas a Provincial Grand Master and subordinate officers, .and when the
Grand Lodge m eets in Dublin, which it does every month, each province sends up
its three principal officers. In this way an unwieldy body lS avoided. The provinces,
with the number of Lodges in each, are as follows: Antrim, 77; Armagh, 23; North
Connaught, 5; South Connaugbt, 5; Down, 48; L ondonderry, 2; Donegal, 23 ;
Meath, 11; Midland Counties, 11; Munster, 17; North Munster, 9 ; South E!istern,
7; Tyrone and Fermanagh, 19; Wicklow and Wexford, 7; Victoria (Melbourne) , 8;
New South Wales, 8; New Zealand, 13; South Australia, 10; Queensland, 8; Ceylon,
4. There are thirty-five Lodges in the City and County of Dublin, not included in
any of these provinces. The whole number of. Lodges on the register of the Grand
Lodge is one thousand and fifteen. There are no statistics as to the number of
Masons, but it is supposed to be about thirty thousand. The oldest charter that can
be found is that of J>uhlin, No. 2, bearing date 1727.
Of the higher branches of Musons in Ireland, Bro. BABRows says, there are
twenty-six Royal Arch Chapters in Dublin, and one hundred and twenty-nine in Ireland. The Grand Commandery or Priory is presided over by the DUKE OF CoNNAUGB.T, third son of the QUEEN. There are thirteen Commanderies in Dublin, and
forty~igbt in all Ireland. We now quote directly from Bro. BABBows :-

COLON AND THE ISLAND OF CUBA.
Masonry in Spain and its dependencies has been subject to many vicissitudes and
to the most bitter persecution by the Government and Clergy. l:lo severe and unyielding has been this persecution, that the brethren have heretofore been obliged to
preserve the strictest secrecy with reference to their meetings, and, in the event of
the publication of any document addressed to the Craft, the officers have been compelled to use fictitious signatures in order to conceal their identity and escape the
malice of their enemies.
Under such circumstances it is scarcely to be ·expected that the organizations
would make much material progress. Within the last three years, however, the vigi-

lance, or rather the vir•1lence, of the oppression has apparently been somewhat relaxed, as we find in ·the proceedings of the United Grand Lodge of Colon and the
Island of Cuba that the proper signatures of the Grand Officers have been attached.
In our last report we alluded to the union of the heretofore antagonistic Grand
Lodges of the Island of Cuba and of Colon, and we here renew our congratul..tion·s
to our insular brethren upon the unanimity, harmony, and zeal which characterized
the second Annual Communication of the United Gra11.d Body.
The Grand Lodge assembled in the City of Habana, on the twenty-seventh day of
March. 1881. In the absence ot' the Grand Master and Deputy Grand Master, the
R. ·. W. '. Bro. ANTONIO MESA y DOMINGUES, Senior Grand Warden, presided. The
Grand Secretary presented his Annual Report, in which he states that, although
during the past year the material progress of the Grand Lodge has not been great,
"very much has been gained in moral tone by the establishment of a uniformity of ·
work, by strengthening the orga11ization, and, above all, by the fraternal congratulations and recognitions with which we have been greeted by foreign Grand Lodges."
The United Grand Lodge has been recognized by thirty-four Grand Lodges, without counting fourteen which had previously recognized the former Grand Lodge of
the "Island of Cuba," and two of that of Colon, all which will doubtless give speedy
recognition to the new organization. The returns from forty-seven subordinate
Lodges show an aggregate membership of 2,793. The Gi•and Treasurer reported a
balance in the treasury of $3,880. 71. The Grand Master delivered an Address, in
which he c.ongratu!ates his brethren upon the progress made during the year and
upon the present prosperous condition of the Grand Lodge. He says:We have great reason to congratulate ourselves upon the complete success of the
union·; we have gained in strength, in extension, and prestige; we have unequivocally proved what may be done upon the principle of association, based upon the
ideas of mutual respect and consideration. We are already strong; we have no fear
that disorganization will undermine our existence, or that the aggressions of those
who, having parted from us, still term themselves brothers, nor of those who look
frowningly upon us and distrust Uij because we are Masons, will interrupt our progress or retard our development. Numerous are the Lodges which obey your authority; perfect the order which within them reigns; laudable the spint which
animates them; and great the zeal which they have shown in the realization of the
work confided to them. Our laws are good, and we have received great consideration
and encouragement from our brethren abroad.
.
The Grand Master expresses his regret that one of the subordinate Lodges hns
refused its allegiance to the United Grand Lodge, and, upon various false pretexts, has
united itself with one of the bodies connected with a faction termed "Spanish Masonry." A temperate, dignified and exhaustive reply was made by the Grand Master
to its arguments and assertions, and it is h<iped that this recalcitrant Lodge will yet
see the error of its ways and accept its proper allegiance. Six dispensations for the
formation of new Lodges ha.d been issued during the year. In closing his address,
the Grand Master makes a~ eloquent appeal to his brethren to continue faithfully in
their march onward upon the path of progress which they have entered, despite the
malevolent acts and insinuations of their enemies. He says: "With us, Masonry is
not a vain superficiality, a mere form; its foundations are broad and deep; its
principles, and nothing but its principles, inspire, sustain, and direct us."
A lengthy, and exceptionally well-prepared Report on Correspondence was presented by Bro. ENRIQUE A. LECERFF, in which the proceedings of eighty-five ·Grand
Bodies are reviewed. Many of the reviews comprise the proceedings of three years,
and are written in a courteous and fraternal spirit. California, for 1879 and 1880,
receives a good share of his attention. Of the Address of Grand Master BnoWNE, in
1879, he says: "It is lengthy, written in elevated style, full of philosophical thoughts
and practical suggestions." The reports of Bro. ABELL he characterizes as "magnificent," and he is pleased to say some kind words of our own humble effortJ1, for which
we tender our thanks. 'rhe report is one of the most interesting of those which have
come before us, as notice is taken of several Grand Bodies whose proceedings seldom,
if ever, find their way to our table.

The Administrative Council of this Grand Lodge met at Lausanne, Oct. 2, 1880.
A question· was discussed on that occasion which has since attracted the attention of
the Grand Lodges and prominent masons of Germany. It is a.< follows:
"Can Freemasonry do anything to induce the na1i.· ns to settle their disputes by
an. Internationa.l Court of Arbitration, instead of going to war."
After a discussion in which all present participated, it was determined to submit
the question to the daughter Lodges for examination. It was also decided that as
soon as the Lodges had made their reports, the Grand Lodge would apply to other
Grand Orient.a for support.
. The Grand Lodge thereupon issued a circular .to its Lodges, dated Oct. 25, 1880,
which asked these questions:
"1. Can Freemasonry do anything to indnce the nations to settle their disputes
by the establishment of International Courts of Arbitration, and thereby blot out the
scourge of war?
" 2. If' answered in the affirmative, what course should l!'reemasonry pursue to
accomplish that purpose?
Of the twenty-three opinions furnished, twenty-one were from the Lodges and two
from individua.l brethren.
Two of the Lodges answered the first question in the negative; one expresses
doubts that Masonry could contribute anythmg to accomplish the wished-for result,
unlePs it had an army at command to enforce its determination. Another oonl!lders
it iIJ!.possible to remove the necessity for war as long as differences exist in race,
rehg10n, etc.
On the other hand, a number of the Lodges demonstrate'that it is the sacred duty
of Masonry to l!'b<!r for the abolition of w!l'r; that for that purpose it was necessary
to make our principles known to the profane world through the ;press, conferences,
et.c., etc. A number propose to accomplish the objoot by improvmg and reforming
,the instrnctions in history in school, and by instilling in the minds of youth a deep
abhorrence against war,

Ancl here we again end our yearly walk through the green fields 11nd by the pleasant brooks of Masonic Literature. We have given under each Grand Lodge heading
the statistics of the Jurisdiction. Bumming these up at the close, we find the result
to be : Grand Lodges in North America, 55; number of subordinate Lodges, 70,094;
number of affiliated M~ons, 562,193. For other statistics we are indebted to the
able and accurate re}>t)rt of Bro. DnuMMOliD of .Maine, viz : re.ised, 21,885; affiliated,
17,362 ; dimitted, 17,36-.l; (?) expelled, 801!; suspended for unmasonic conduct, 257;

The three largest Juriadictions are, New York, n, 811; Illinois, 88,168; P ennsylvanir., 84,342. Five other JuriRdictions have over twenty thousand members, viz ;
Ohio, 29,100; Michigan, 25,831; Massachusetts, 25,205; Indiana., 23, 700; Missouri,

In submitting this, our thirteenth Report, to the Grand Lodge, we are, as ever,
sensible of ita me.ny imperfections, With an interregnum of only two years, we
have occupied the position of Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, since
the year 1868. Necessarily, the entire labor of reviewing and writing falls upon the
Ohairman, and the writer bas endeavored to meet the responsibilities of the position
as best he could, When first accepting the appointmem, it was with fear and trembling. We were following Bro,_ABELL and_other Maeouio w:iters in our own•state,
and were to be judged by our scholarly c<rlaborers in other jurisdictions, who }Jed already attained high fame in their reports. The plan we marked out for personal g11id

ance we have uniformly followed. We shrank f~om. usurping the province of Grand
Masters and Oommitte& on Jurisprudence, and left to others the discussion of questions of Masonic law, abstract and particnla.r. We wished rather to ~'ive onr readers a
full synopsis of what our brethren were saying and doing in other jurisdictions, with
such oomments and suggestions a.a seemed just and pt"oper at the time. We are not
vain enough to think or say that others have eince followed onr example, but the fact
is that a large majority of our brethren, upon simila.r committees, now do the same,
and have thrown the discussion of law questions to the winds. Nor has tha.t fact at
all detracted from the merits and excellence of their reports.
To oiir brethren in Q.alifornia we again return thanks for the kindly consideration
with which they have always received our niporte. We have tried to ple¥6 them,
and shall only be too glad to know that we have succeeded. Again we submit our
work for their inspection, trusting that experience has not been loe_t in its lessons,
and that ae we grow older we are the better able to do" good work and aqua.re work."
Many a white hair has appeared on bead and Qj)p.rd since we made our first P.ppearance as Reporter for the Grand Lodge. But if there has been any diminution in
sight or nature.I force, there has been none in our love and veneration for onr noble •
institution, and in onr desire to add to its attractiveness at;)d usefulness, as one of

To our brother Reporters we have · mp.ny fup.nks to offer. From these we

their words of kindness have been fully P.ppreciated. We trust that we have not
written a word that could offend one of them. If we have, such was surely the
farthest from our intent. If the G. A. 0. T. U. spares our life, and Grand Masters

The cleare•t and best thinkers were ignorant of the troe ncoooot of the creation

'!;'hey were ignorant of the origin of evil and the cause of depravity among man·

The marriage relation was abolished; o. man was no longer to have his own wife,

Concerning the -human soul and its destiny after death, various and contradictory

What your committee said in regard t.o a somewhat similar amendment proposed.
last year is applicable to this.' As the law now stands, suspension for non-payment
of dues is a summary proceeding without even the form of a trial. If a member of a
Lodge is more than six months in arrears for dues, the Secretary sends him a notice
of that fact, and if, at the next stated meeting, the dues be not paid, or sickness or
inability be shown as the cause for such non-payment, he must be declared to be
suspended, nnless the dues be paid or remitted, or the ·time of payment be by the
Lodge extended. This summary proceeding was adopted more than twenty yeara
ago, and it seems to have met the very general approbation of the fraternity. Your
committee would not advise any change, and they think that it wonld be great injustice to place any impediment in the way of a brother's restoration other than that
now provided for-the payment of his arrearages and such further dues, as would
have accrued had he continued in good standing.
If any change is to be made it should be radical, and should provide that, in case
of delinquency in payment of does, the delinquent should be tried upon charges of
wilful neglect of duty, as for other Masonic ott'ences. Then if the verdict were that
he was guilty, the judgment of suspension would be final and conclusive. Bot, so
long as the proceeding for suspension is in such cases summary, the means of restoration should be equally summary. Your committee return the amendment with the
recommendation that it be not adopted.

In the United States the rule is well settled that a Grand Lodge may be formed in
every State and in every Territory organized by the general government, whenever
three or more chartered Lodges established there nnite in its formation; and that,
when established, its jurisdiction Is exclusive and all L<fges previously estab·
lished, though not participating in its formation, must forthwith snrrender their old
charters and rec~ive new ones from the new Grand Lodge. Here, we recognize the
Grand Lodge of a State or Territory as having alisolute control, within its territorial
jorisdictiou, of the first three degrees of Masonry by whatever rite ·they may be conferred. But we do not understand that this rule has been settled or recognized
eisewbere, or that it has become a general law or Masonry. In Germany there are
several Grand Lodges exercising concurrent jurisdiction. In France there is a Grand
Orient practicing what is known as the French Rite, and a Supreme Council practicing the Scottish Rite, and these exercise concurrent jurisdiction in the republic and
its dependencies. In Hnngary there is a Supreme Council and a Grand Lodge exerciMing concurrent jurisdiction.
The Grand Lodges or England, Scotland, and Jreland, have steadily refnsed t o
recognize the rule, and, whenever a Grand Lodge has been establi.shed io any Province
in the British Empire where these Grand Lodges or either of them had previously established Lodges, they have refused to acknowledge the newly establishecl Grand
Lodge except upon condition that their subordinate Lodges should be allowed to
maintain their allegiance and continue their work under their old charters without
interference so long as they eboold desire so to do. Jt was so in the case of the
Grand Lodge of CanBda and in the cases of the other Grand Lodges of the Provinces
of the Dominion of Canada. the Grand Lodge of England still maintnins Lodges in
the Pl'Ovince of Ontario and in the Province of Quebec. The Grand Lodge of Canada

•In 1857 the Provincial Grand Lodge of Upper Canada renonnoed its allegiance to
the Grand Lodge of England and formed the "Antient Grand Lodge of Canada."
The next year, 18.58, the" Antient Grand Lodge of Canada" united with the Grand
Lodge of Canada. In 1859 a compromise was effected between the Grand Lodge of
England and the Grand Lodge of Canada hy which it was agreed that the Lodges
at that time holding charters from the Grand Lodges of England and Scotland should
be allowed to continue their work and their allegiance so long as they should desire
to do so. Upon the consummation of that agreement the Grand Lodge of Canada.
was recognized by the Grand Lodge of England.
This Grand Lodge declined to recognize the Grand Lodge of Canada until it had
been recognized by the mother Grand Lodge, and it was not till 1858 that recognl·

trouble-had snrrendere<J their old charters and been enrolled upon iti registry, and
that the Grand Lodge of Scotland had recalled and cancelled the patent of its Provincial Grand Master at Montreal.
Following the conquest ol Canada in 1760 and its occupatien by the English, the
Grand Lodge of England established Lodges there, and, prior to 1847, liad established
in the lower Provincll two Provincial Grand Lodges, one at Montreal, the other at
Quebec, and all the Lodges within the two Provinces worked under English charters.
In 1847 the Lodge Elg·i n, No. 348, was instituted at Montreal nuder a warrant from
the Grand Lodge of Scotland, and was the first Scotch Lodge there established. In
1855 the Grand Lodge of Canada was formed, claiming and exercising jurisdiction
over Upper and Lower Canada. In 1869 the Grand Lodge of Quebec was formed,
claiming jurisdiction over the Province of Qnebec.
The Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland refused to recognize the
claim or the Grand Lodge of Canada to exclusive jurisdiction, and would recognize
it only upon the condition that the Lodges holding charters from them should he
allowed to continue their allegiance so long as those Lodges should so desire. So
the matter was adjusted with the Grand Lodge of Canada. The Grand Lodge of
Quebec also 888erted exclusive jurisdiction, ~nt the Grand Lodges of England, Scot-

maintain such Lodges. At the time of the formation of the Grand Lodge of Quebec,
in 1869, there. were only two Scotoh Lodges in the Province. One of these took part
jn the formation of the Grand Lodge, the other, the Lodge Elgin insisted on maintaining its allegiance to its mother Grand Lodge.
ln February, 1877, the Grand Lodge of Scotland resolved to open fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge of Quebec and appointed and commissioned Bro. DUN·

unanimous vote of its members refosed to transfer its allegiance, demand was made
that the Gre.nd Lodge of Scotland should direct the Lodge to place itself under the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Quebec. This the Grand Lodge of Scotland refused to do; and afterwards rescinded the resolntion opening fraternal relations,
recalied the commission to Bro. DuNB.lR, granted two new charters for Lodges in
Montreal, and appointed and commissioned Bro. GEOR(}E A. BAYNES as Provincial
Grand Master at Montreal. These two Lodges were to be and were constituted on
the twenty-fourth day of Jone, 1878. The edict of non-intercourse was issued Jnne
21st.

The second qoestion, whether in the case presented there was any verdict or de·
cision on which a jodgment coold be based, seems to os to be determined by Section
'
·
8, Article IV, Part VI, of the Constitution.
That section reads as follows:SEOTION 8. After all the testimony shall have been received, the CommiBBionere
shall proceed to deliberate npon their verdict and sentence, with none present save
themselves, the Master.and the Secretary, which lastsha.ll have no voice in the proceed·
lngs. ':lhe fudgmem of a majority of all the oommi.lisioners shall be taken as the dec.ision of the whole; and, when the trial is ~oncluded, the Secretary shall make a fair
copy of the record and finding, nuder their supervision, which shall be signed by the
Commissioners, attested by the Secretary, and presented to the Master, who, et the
next meeting of his Lodge, shall, in the presence of its members only, announce the
result, and direct the Secretary to record the same as the judgment of the Lodge
and file the record for safe keeping among its archives."
For the trial of that case there were nine commissioners, and there conld be no verdict or decision in the case, unless five of the nine were agreed. Four voting" guilty"
and four" not gnilty," there was no verdict and the Master shonld not have received
the stat.ement as a verdict, hut should have returned it to the commissionel'I! with instructions to deliberate further and to call in the other commissioner. If one of the commiBBioners had died pending the trial, or his attendance conld not, for any reason, be securllji, and a majority of the whole nomber elected were not agreed and coold not agree
upon a verdict, then it would have been proper for the Master to discharge the commissioners and to call his Lodge together again to elect other commissioners fdr the trial
of the case. There certainly can be no verdict or judgment of conviction or acquittal
until a majority of.ttll the commissioners elected to try the case have rendered averdict of conviction or acqnittal. 1.'he Master who presides at the trial has no discretion or aothority in the matter of the verdict or decision, except to receive the ver·
diet when properly signed by the commissioners and attested by the Secretary, to
announce the resolt at which the commiBSioners have arrived, and direct .th~ Secre·
1ary to enter it of record as the jodgment of the Lodge. In the case under consid·
eration there was no verdict and therefore no result to he annoonced or recorded,
and the annooncement and record which were in fact made were wholly without
authority and void. It follows that the charges preferred by the Jonior Warden of
8iloeyville Lodge are still pending and ondetermined in Oalifornia Lodge, No. 1.
v oder the circomstances of tbiij case what further proceedings sboold be bad and
before what tribunal? Upon this qoestion yoor committee &gree with Bro. BAKER,
that the trial shonld be had and verdict rendered by a commission eleeted from the
members of the Lodge to which the charges were presented; and that, nuder oar
Oonstitotion, the Grand Lodge has no jurisdiction to consider a case opon lt.s merits
until a trial-commission has rendered a verdict thereon. Article IV, Part VI, of the
Constitution, makes specific provision in regard to trials when charges are preferred
against liny member of the fraternity other than the Grand Master and M48ters of
Lodges, and it seems to be plain that both the accoser and the accosed have a right
to Insist opoo a trial and verdict by a commiBBion of the Lodge having jurisdiction of
the case. Yoor commi~e therefore propose and recommend the adoptlon of the
following resolotion :Resolued, That the judgment of acqolttal amtoonced and recorded in California
Lodge, No. 1, Aogost 1, 1881, in the matter of charges of onmasonic conduct pre·
ferred ugaiost SrnoN BLUM by the Jonior Warden of Bilueyville Lodge; Nu. 201, be
and the same is hereby reversed; and that Oalifornia Lodge, No. l, proceed again to
elect commissioners for the trial of the said SIMON BLUM upon the said charges so preferred and still pending in that Lodge, in accordance with the provisions of Article
IV, Pnrt VI, of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge.

not before enspooted, indulged·in an unbecoming indiscretion.
Harmony must prevail in all Masonic Lodges. To this end ea.ch memb"er must
contribute, and to it all oth&r considerations must yield. An acting Master may at
any time call to preside, and to assume the functions and discharge the do ties of his
office, any Past Master present, if, from any cause whatever, he sees flt to do so; and
this, hie a.ct, may not be questioned by any one, The Master ought to qualify himself, and, on all occa.sione when present and not indisposed, discharge the duties of
hie offiC() himself. He may not, however, call upon two or more Past Ma.eters present

to conjointly discharge the duties of Master. There can be but one Master at a time
"to rule and govern" a Lodge ; and when a Paet Master is invited to the station of the
Master, he alone must direct and control, and he alone is responsible for the condnct
of the Lodge while he holds the gavel. Thie responsibility cannot be cast upon two
to act jointly.
On the occa.sion, referred to in the transcript, which gave rise to the charges, iteeems
tliat the acting Master consented that the ceremonies illustrating the funeral of our
late distinguished Bro. JAMES A. GARFIELD might be participated in by two Paet
Masters present, acting conjointly with him1Jelf; whereupon there was manifested a
feeling against the accused participating, and he was informed of it by a Paet Master
and the acting Master, which had the very natural result to incense the accused, and,
on the impulse of the moment he did those things which are charged against him as
unroas.onlc conduct. There is no pretence of deliberation on the part of the accused.
If in a Lodge there exists a feeling e.ga.inst its humblest member or one who has
filled tho highest office in its gift, and there are grounds for that feeling amounting
to nnmasonic conduct, he should be charged with and tried for it, a.nd convicted or
acquitted, and thus restore harmony. If the feeling is not so founded, but is
groundless, the existence of this feeling against him should not be withheld from
him until some important occasion arises when be is about to participa.te in Masonic
ceremonies, and then surprise him by a revelation which induces a state of feeling
on his part which is uncontrollable.
All Paet Masters who have taken pride in their work are pleased to have commendation from their brethren. Is it surprising that condemnation should produce feelings of mortification, and, if unjust, of anger? It is a. commendable
emulation as to "who can beet work," but to "agree" is far more commendable.
No contention should have existed on this occasion, and for it the Master is not
without blame. Had he performed the service himself, or had he been prompt and
positive in naming one Pa.st Master to take hie gavel and yielded to him hia pla.ce,

conduct of the accused should be viewed with the eyes of brethren. In my judgment
there was no deliberate intention on the part of the accused to be disobedient to the

think that his conduct wa.s the resuh of s.n impulse uncontrollable at the time,-s.n
indiscretion which should be forgiven, in view of his long gc..od standing in the fraternity.

Bro. WILLIAM C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports : To the M. •• W. '• Grand. Lod.ge of California :Youl' committee, to whom was referred certain decisions and other matters reported
by Grand Master DENSON in his Address at the last Annual Communication, report
aM follows :I. Section 2, Article III., Part II(., of the Constitution, provides that "no Lodge
in this State shall receive an application for the degrees of Masonry unless tB.e ap.plicant shall have been a resident within the State during twelve months, and
within the jurisdiction of the Lodge during six months, next preceding the date of
his application," with certain specified exceptions.
·
The question was asked whether this inhibition would apply when the petitioner,
being a resident, had been temporarily absent from the State during some portion of
the last dix months. Grand Master DEssoN decided that it would not apply, and the
decision commends itself as right. That section, like all other sections of the Constitution, should receive a reasonable construction, and it would be very unreasonable
to construe it to mean· that, if a resident of Ban Francisco or any other portion of
the State should, during the last six months, or during the year next before the date
of his petition, go to Portland or Virginia City, on business or for amusement, and
be absent from the State for a few days or weeks, his petition could not be received,
The purpose of the section is that no petition should be received until the petitioner has been long enough an actual resident of the State and of the territorial jurisdiction of the Lodge to give its members an opportunity to know the man and to
determine whether they would choose to receive him as a memuer of their Masonic
family; and the requirement of the section is, as the Grand Master said, only that
he be in good faith a resident.
II. A case arose in Janesville Lodge, No. 232, in which the candidate, during the
progress of the work of the third degree and while he was being instructed in respect to the guard and sign, was taken with a sudden and serious illness, which not
only rendered it necessary that the work should be suspended, but that he should be
immediately carried to his home. As he continued to be dangerously ill for some
considerable time, the Lodge naturally desired to be informed as to his standing and
its duties under the circumstances. The Grand Master instructed the Lodge that
the party was a Master Mason and, a.s such, entitled to all the comideration and attention which should be be>towed by the Lodge upon its members, and that, in case
of his death, he should receive Masonic burial; but that, until further instructed, he
could not sit in a Masters' Lodge.
This seems to your commi.ttee to be a just interpretation of the law, and to express
fully and exactly the status and rights of the party and the duty of the Lodge and
its members.
III. In regard to the trial of a non-affiliate, the Grand Master decided, after consultation, that the expense attending such trial must be borne by the Lodge making
the charge, because ho found that to be the established custom; but, not being satisfied that the rule, so established and to which he adhered in the particular case, was
just, he <1.esired that the matter should be submitted to the Grand Lodge, so that a
certain rule might be adopted to govern such cases. He suggests that such trials are

1882.]

Grand Lodge of California.

659

frequently, if not generally, for the benefit of the fraternity at large rather than of
the complaining Lodge, and that it would be only just that the aecessary expense
should be borne by the fraternity at large.
This, at first view, seems just; but your committee think tbat no practicable rule
conld be adopted other than that now prevailing, and which was followed by the
Grand Master. It may be assumed that the non-affiliate against whom charges are
preferred is a resident within the jurisdiction of the particular Lodge preferring
the charges, and that that Lodge has a special interest in seeing that justice is meted
out to the offending party. In cities and large towns, where there are several Lodges
having concurrent jurisdiction, it seerris right that such Lodges should contribute
rateably to the expense in such cases, but they should make such contribution by
some rule to be adopted and out of some fund to be provided by themselves.
Your committee approve the decision of the Grand Master in the case before him,
but do not recommend any additional legislation upon the subject.
IV. The Grand Master decided, in answer to several inquiries by Lodges, that,
when a petitioner for the three degrees had been elected and, having received the first
degree, or the first and second degrees, had waited for several years before presenting himself for further advancement, a new ballot was neither necessary nor proper.
The sixth section of Article III., Part III., of the Constitution, reads as follows:SECTION 6. No Lodge, unless it be otherwise provided in its by-laws, shall have
more than one ballot for the three degrees; but, tbough an applicant may be elected
to receive them, it', at any time before his initiation, objection be made by any member, he shall not receive the degree until ~uch ob,iection shall have been withdrawn;
and such objection shall, unless withdrawn within sixty days, have the effect of a
rejection by ballot' and shall be BO reported to the Grand Secretary; ano if, after his
initiation, but before being passed, or after passin~, before being raised, objection to
his advancement be made by any member, such obJection shall be referred to a com·
mittee, with power to inquire into the cause thereot, who shall, at the next stated
meeLing (unless further time be given) repo1t thereon; and upon the reception of
such report, if no cause for the objection has been &•signed, or if the cause assigned
be, in the opinion of two-thirds of the members present, not a vahd and Masonic
one, the Lodge may confer the degree in tbe same manne1 as if no objection had
been made.
·
This is the law, and it Meelil6 to be so explicit that no Master of a Lodge otight to
mistake or misunderstand its meaning. One of the duties which ought to be impressed upon the officers of Lodges is that they should make themselves reasonably
familiar with the body of Masonic law as decla1ed in our Constitution and published·
for their special guidance. Some of the questions proposed to Grand Masters seem
to indicate an entire disregard of this duty.
V. In regard to non-affiliates the Grand Master decided that a non-affiliated Mason
living within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, whether that jurisdiction were exclusive or
concurrent, had the right to oiler to contribute to the funds of the Lodge a sum
equal to its µ10nthly due~, and that the Lodge could receive or refuse to receive the
contribution; that the tender thereof would place the maker of it in good standing
and give him the right to receive the courtesies and charities due to all Masons; but
that the receipt of the money, even when continued for a series of months or years,
did not impose any special care or duty upon the Lodge receiving it, and that in case
of the death of one of those contributing Masons in a city like San Francisco the
funeral ·expenses should be borne by the Board of Relief.
Section 1, Article II, Part V, of tqe ·Constitution, provides that if a non-affiliated
Mason, more than six months a resident within this State, "shall refi.tse or neglect
to make applici.tion for membership to some Lodge therein, or to pay to the Lodge
within the jurisdiction of which he resides, during the whole period of such resi·
dence, an amount equivalent to its ·regular dues, while able so to do, he shall be
deemed unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not be entitled to nor be the
recipient of any of the rights, privileges, or charities of the ol'der."
That section leaves no doubt as to what the non-affiliate must do; bot, suppose that
he, living in a city, does for a series of years contribute regularly to one Lodge, does

. root. 12, ·

that Lodge owe him no obligation r The Lodge can receive or refuse to receive bis
contribntions, as it can receive or refose to receive bis petition for membership· but
if a particular Lodge does receive from him for a Jong time bis contributions, i~ the
duty which it owes to him simply the duty which all Masons owe, or ls it a particular and a legal dnty ! It is true that our Constitntion bas net defined and declared
w~at is the duty ef the Lodge under such circumstances; still it seems to yonr committee that the Lodge does owe a reciprocal duty, and that its obligation to care for
that brother in distress is not alone the general obligation which we all recognize
bot is specific, particnlar and clear. It is indeed a strong moral obligation, and s~
strong that no Lodge, having the ability to care for ana relieve him, sbonld refuse or
be permitted to neglect to do so; and, in case of the death of a brother under socb
circumstances, be should be buried by and at the expense of the Lodge which bas

Your committee think that the decision should be approved, but that no legislation in regard to the matter proposed is desirable. The whole matter now rests in
the discretion of the Grand Master, who can and will act as the circumstanc~e of each
case demand; · and it would be much safer to leave the matter to rest In bis discre tion
than to attempt to regulate it .by a fixed rule.
