X. The Grand Master reported that, more than once during the year, interested
relatives of a Mason under suspension for non-payment of dues, who was sick and
about to die, had tendered to the Secretary of his Lodge the amonnt of money necessary for bis restoration "under each oircnmstances as to convince the officers of the
Lodge that the tender was made for the mercenary purposes of others, and not at
the Instance of the suspended brother;'' and in respect to such cases he adopts the
language of' Bro. GIDEON WING, Past Master of Columbia Lodge, No. 28, where he
says:In my jndgment when a brother is so inil iilnent to Masonry as to refuse to pay
the smali amount required for dues, having the ability to pay, and Is suspended, and
while under suspension is about to die, it looks like fraud and deception for nny Interested person-particularly one not a Mason-to volnnteer the payment of the small
amount reqnisite to restore the suspended brother, for the manifest purpose of imposing npon the Lodge the burden of burying him and taking care of bis family.
Masonry Is not an insurance society, and every Mason renounces selfish motives
prior to entering oar portals; bot there seems to be some tendency toward a deireneracy of motive, and many appear to think entirely too much of what can be gamed
out of MBllonry. No man is bound to submit to what be knows to be a fraud; why,
then, should a Lodge! I would not lightly impugn the motives of any one, but if I
know that the relative of a suspended Mason, in volunteering to pay up his dues, had
only selfish and pecuniary motives in view, I should certainly decline to receive the
payment, for the knowledge of the unworthy motive would rebnt all presumptions
of acquiescence on the part of the suspended brother.
The case stated by Bro. WING. is a strong, and we think, an nnusnal one. As
stated by him the brother is amply able to pay his dues bot becomes indifferent and
refuses to pay, and is for that cause suspended •. Be is taken sick and is a boot to die,
and then his friends, without bis knowledge or acquiescence, volunteer the payment
of the amount necessary for bis restoration. The pnrpose of this payment is to
impose upon the Lodge th 1 burden of burying him and caring for his family. If
· in any given case all this were manifest, and were known beyond any peradventure to
the Secretary, he might perhaps rightfully refuse to receive the tender, bot we can
hardly conceive a caae where a Secretary could have certain knowledge of all these
matters. Bis presumptions or conclusions would not answer the requirement.
The suspended brother had the absolute right, at any time, even upon his dying
bed and in articulo mortiB, to make the payment, and neither the Secretary nor his
Lodge could rigbtfnlly have refused to receive it. The tender of the amonut, whether
received or not, would have effected his Immediate restoration, and no inquiry would
have been allowed as to bis motive In making the payment or.tender.
The resnlt would have been the same if a third person bad, at bis reqnest, mRde
the paymeni or tender. The act would have been his as much as If made by his own
hand . The maxim, quifacitper alium facU per se, applies e.xactly, and it would make
no dilference whether the person employed were a Mason or not. A child could do
the act as elfectnally as a man. Nor would it make any difference whether the money

It is very true, e.s was said by Bro. WING, that our fraternity is not an insurance

charter shonld be recalled. We want no idle Masons in the Lodge, and- we want no
inefficient Lodges in the State. A Lodge must and will at some time be called upon
to relieve distress; and it ought to be prepared and ready therefor. It should always

The objections made to this amendment are, first, that it is not in the uniform

As to the first objectio~, it may be remarked that the uniform code is silent npon
the ~ubject, and that, whde that code Is a wise compilation and is beneficent in its
operation, it ought not to be considered _a s e·mbraclng all the wisdom, not only or

that any more wise or complete plan can be adopted.
'
It attacks a custom, which prevails in many, if not In all, the States and jurisdictions of Masonry, of commuting the payment of monthly dues by the payment of a
gross sum at a single time, that sum being graduated by the amount of monthly dues

twen~y·fi~e ye~rs dischar~ed the burdens of Masonry, from any l'nrther pecuniary
eontribnt1ons; ID fact saymg to him" Well done; enter into thy Masonic rest. We
"!'ill be the staff of thy declining years, as thou hast been our support hitherto."
The payment of a gross sum of one hundred dollars is equal to a Masonic lite
paying one dollar per month dues, of not less than twelve years. It has been calcu~
lated ~hat this is more than the aver~e duration of Masonic membership, so that,
financially, the Lodge would be no loser if every member should avail himself of the
proposed legislation. Bnt, practlcally, few will become life-members upon these
terms, as our Lodges are becoming forehanded, in owning their temples and deriving
rents therefrom, the tendency of which is to a reduction of dues. There are, how·
ever, ~ome who will provide against possible reverses, and others who will be willing
to reheve themselves and the Lodge of the care and labor of quarterly collections.
It is not perceived npon what principle of Masonic law or usage a commutation on
the terms propose~ can be objected to. If unjust to a brother, it is only offered as
a privilege to him which he may accept or not ; if unjust to the Lodge, it may repea
it at Rny time. It has been objeotod that the principle of li~e-memberships has oper-

Bro. EDMUND C. ATKINSON, from the special committee to \Vhom

•

Yonr committee have carefully examined the Report of the Grand Lecturer and
are pleased to report ihat they find it an able and interesting. paper, replete with
information respecting the Masonic work of the jurisdiction, and containing many
practical suggestions which, if adopted, would tend to Jessen the labors of the Grand
Lecturer and the Inspectors and enhance the welfare and prosperity of the various
Lodges. They commend the Grand Lecturer for the zeal and fidelity with which he
has discharged the important duties of his office, and congratulate the Grand Lo.dge
upon the excellent results in general of the system of inspectorship.
Your committee have given particular attention to that part of the Report which
refers to the duties of Inspectors, and in their opinion said duties have been so ·
plainly set forth in the reports of committees heretofore, and in resolutions adopted
at former Communications of this Grand Lodge, that aU who have a desire for
knowledge upon that subject have had ample facilities for obtaining it. Printed
copies of the proceedings, with reports and accompanying resolations carefally
indexed, have been furnished to each and every Lodge of the jurisdiction for the
purpose of supplying such information; yet your committee, realizing that some
Masters apparently do not read the proceedings, and that a few Inspectors are in
doubt, concur in the opinion of the Grand Lecturer that a surer means of supplying
the information where it is most needed would be found in issuing a circular or
pamphlet setting forth the reciprocal duties of Inspector and Lodges, and supplying
each Lodge and Inspector with a copy thereof. They therefore recommend that
such circular or pamphlet be issued and in such manner be distributed.
The suggestion of an Inspector that a blank be issued, wherein Lodges could
report to the Inspector their financial standing and general working condition by
answering questions therein to be propoancied, does not meet the approval of yoar
committee. They can readily see that in some instances it might be beneficial, especially in the economy of time and trouble, but they are of the opinioa that in gen·
erst it would be injnrions, as snch blank would, they apprehend; too often take the
place of the Inspector's visit.

668

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 13,

The recommendation of another Inspector that the Senior Warden be required to
become proficient in the work, equally with the Master, and be required to pass a
like examination and obtain from the Inspector a certificate of qualification, has
the unqualified endorsement of yonr committee, for the reason that, as the Senior
Warden usually succeeds the Master, when qualified to perform the duties of that
officer, the prosperity of the Lodge would be especially enhanced and, in the main,
the Inspector's labors would be materially lessened.
In relation to the qualifications of Inspectors, your committee fully concur In the
opinion expressed by the Grand Lecturer that it would be advisable for Inspector&,
when in attendance at the Grand Lodge, to hold meetings for the purpose of comparing and correcting their work. This, your committee believe, would be very
beneficial, provided that such exercises were under the immediate direction and
supervision of the Grand Lecturer ; and they would further suggest the propriety of
appointing no brother as Inspector whose interest in Masonry does not prompt him
pnnotnally to attend the Annual Communications of this Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfally submitted by
EDXUND 0. ATKINSON,
GEORGE HINDS,
JOSEPH B. Coou,

Bro. WILEY J. TINNIN, from the Committee on Finances, presented
the following reports :·
'.lb the M.-. W. ·• (}rand Lodge of ·California :-;-

Your committee, to whom were referred the reports of the Masonic Boards of
Relief of the cities of San Francisco, Sacramento, and Los Angeles, have examined
those papers and find that the Boards whence they come appear to have properly
extended the charities and guarded the Interest and standing of our Order in their
several locations. The necessity for these Boards In our large towns, for the intelligent dispensation of charity to those who are worthy of It, cannot he questioned; and
·the subject has been so sufficiently written of heretofore that nothing further regard·
ing it need now be said.
The financial statements of these Boards will be found in their several reports at
pages 474 to 477 of these Proceedings, and need not here be reproduced. Your committee are of the opinion that the assistance heretofore given them by the Grand
Lodge should he continued, and they therefore offer the following resolution and
recommend its adoption:Resoltled, That the sum of twenty-six hundred dollars be appropriated. from the
General Fund, to be distributed as follows: -to the .Masonic Board of Relief of San
Francisco, two thousand dollars; to the Masonic Board of Relief of Sacramento,
three hundred dollars; and to the Masonic Board of Relief of Loe Angeles, three
hundred dollars.
Your committee have considered the matter referred to them from the Committee
on Jurisprudence in regard to an appropriation from the Grand Lodge to pay the expenses of a re·trial npon a charge of unmasonic conduct preferred by Bil'lleyTJillB
Lodge, No. 201, against a Mason who is a non-affiliate and who resides without the
jurisdiction of that Lodge.
·
n appears that at a former trial, by Oalifornia Lodge, No. 1, the commissioners
were unable to agree upon a verdict in consequence of the absence of one of their
number, and that 8il:oey11iile Lodge bore the expenses of that trial. Our Committ.ee on
Jurisprudence appear to think that it would he a hardship on BillleyllfUB Lodge to pay
the expense of the re-trial of a case in which the fraternity at l&rge is as much interested as is that Lodge.
While your Oommittee on Finances agree with the Committee on Jurisprudence in
their opinion as to the justice of the matter, they greatly doubt the policy of making
this a precedent by which this Grand Lodge may in the future be required to pay
the expenses of trials by subordinate Lodged--believing that it is not the province or
duty of the Grand Lodge to pay the expense of trials by subordinates, unless they be
specially ordered by the Grand Lodge under extraordinary circumstances.
Your committee have concluded that in this special case there are circumstances
which may jll8tlfy the payment, and they therefore offer the folio.wing resolution and
recommend its adoption :.
Resol1JBd, That the sum of one hundred dollars, or such portion thereof as may be

Bro. WILLI4J!l C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following report :7b the M. ". W. •. Grand Lodge of California:Yonr committee have examined that portion of the Adr'ress of tbe Grand Master
relating to the arrest of the charter of Union Lodge, No. 58, in September last, with
the letters, reports and papers therein referred to, aud have heard the statements of
the Master of the Lodge, who, by request, appeared before the committee; and, after a careful consideration of all the facw, have arrived at the conclusion that the
action of the Grand Master should be approved.

The Master, after having been advised of the aotion of tbe Grand Lodge in respect to work on Sonday, nevertbeless opened his Lodge on tbat day and proceeded
to confer tbe degree of Entered Apprentice; and, in reply to tbe Grand Master's letter
of inqoiry, attempted, witb tbe approval of bis Lodge, not to excose tbe infraction
of tbe law by reason of inadvertence or the urgency of tbe particular case, nor
indeed to make or oft'~r any excose for what had been done, bot, In a manner indicating insobordlnation and independence of aothorlty,"to advise the Grand Master that be had wholly mistaken tbe meaning and purport of tbe law-that he,
tbe Master, had examined those portions of the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge to
which his attention bad been directed by the Grand Master, and that, while' they
expressed the sentiments of the Grand Lodge on the qnestlon of work by Lodges
on Sunday, they could not "bb totbred into a prohibition preventing a Lodge f'rom
conferring degrees on Sonday;" and, in cooclnsloo, he says that-" While the Lodge
is of the opinion expressed in the report of t he committee, (of the Grand Lodge) it
believes it bas committed no wrong, infringed no law, violated no Masonic principle,
in conferring this degree on the day In question."
This letter was conceived, as we bave said, in a spirit or insobordinatlon, and was
so arrogant and improper In its tone that, in the opinion of your committee, the Grand
Master might well have arrested the charter upon its receipt; bot he, thinking that
perhaps no disrespect was intended, and that a little farther reflection on the p11rt of
the Master, aided by the advice of his brethren, woold probably lead to a more senslble reply, delayed action. This letter was sobmitted to the Lodge, with that of the
Grand Master, and it must be. assumed therefore that its expreSBions were not hasty,
but were carefolly considered, and they are for that reason the more oft'e nsive and
reprehensible.
Indeed it is difficolt to conceive an excuse for soch a letter Crom the Masten of a
Lodge to the Grand Master. To ynur committee the Master excuses himself by
referring to the first snbdlvision of Section 1, Article II, Part IV, of the Constitotion,
which provides that the Master shall have power "to congregate his Lodge when·
ever he shall deem it proper ;" from which he conclodes that the decision of Grand
Master BHOWNE and of the Grand Lodge In 1879, as It did not porport to be an amendment of that section, did not declare a rule which he as Master was bonnd to respect.
Probably if he had, in a respectful manner, callell the attention of the· Grand
Master to this provision of the Constitotion and his Interpretation of it, he wo11ld
have been qoietly admonished as to bis observance of that decision, so approved as
the law of the Grand Lodge, and no further notice would have been taken of it.
That woold have shown a willlngneSB to surrender even his own interpretation of
the law to the opinion of the Grand Master, who, as he ooght to have known, has
anthorit.t daring the recess of the Grand Lodge to exercise all its execntive powers
and to interpret and construe its laws.
.
Yoor committee are satisfied that the action of the Grand Master shoold be fully
sostained, yet they think that the Lodge and it3 Master have been sofficiently punished for the oft'e nce committed, by the arrest of its charter and the temporary
suspension of those of its member~ who participated therein. They have known
the Lodge and many of its members for a long time, and are aware that it has been and
believe that it will continue to be one of the most efficient and prosperoos Lodges
In the State, and that It will not again knowingly infringe any law of the Grand
Lodge. They therefore recommend the adopUon of the following resolution :Resolved, That the charter of Union Lodge, No. 58, lately arrested by the Grand
Master, be and is hereby restored to said Lodge, and that all its members, sospended
by order or the Grand Master, be and are restored to their membership and standing
therein.
And your committee, for the porpose of directly bringing the law, ns stated in the
decision of Grand Master BROWNE and approved by the Grand Lodge, to the attention
of all Masters of Lodges, and so placing it In our proceedings that it shall receive

Yonr committee, to whom w11s referred the petition of AMIEL HocHHEillER for
restoration, have had the same under consideration, and, in addition to inspecting
such documentary evidence as was presented, have attentively listened to such witnesses as were introduced before them. The petitioner was suspended from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry by the judgment of Bilveyville Lodge, No. 201, of
which he was at the time a member; and this judgment was affirmed by the Grand
Lodge at its Annual Communication in 1880.
Upon the twenty-ninth day of July, 1882, at a stated meeting or Sil11eyviUe Lodge,
No. 201, Mr. Hocnn1111111s petitioned said Lodge to restore him to all the rights and
privileges of Masonry. At a stated meeting of that Lodge held on the twenty-sixth
day of Angust, 1882, the said petition was acted upon by the Lodge, (there being
thirty members present,) and the application for restoration was rejected by an
almost unanimous vote. Upon this the petitioner applies to this Grand Lodge for
restoration. During the investigation it lias been nrged npon yonr commltt.a that,
since his suspension, the petitioner has sustained a good character both in business
and private life, having removed from the jurisdiction of the Lodge which suspended
him, and living in another part of the State. Residing now in the vicinity of Laurel
Lodge, No. 245, and doing business in the town in which it is situated, he bRs not
seen tit to seek the recommendation of that Lodge that he be restored. In view of
the fact that bis brethren who suspended him are unwilling that he should return to
the Order, and the reasons .1dven your committee why he should be restored being
insufficient to justify them in arraying themselves as judges against those whose residence and knowledge of the case entitfe their judgment and action to weight in the
absence of clear proof that they are governed by uncharitable motives, your cemmlttee feel unwilling at this time to recommend the restoration of the petitioner.
They therefore submit the following resolution and recommend its adoption _: Resolved, That the petition of AMIEL Hocnn11:1.11EB, for restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry, be and is hereby denied.
All which is respectfully submitted by

Bro.'W1LLIAM C. BELOH£B, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports :To the M. •• W. •• Grand Lodge of California :Sincerity Lodge, No. 132, asks the Grand Lodge to reconsider the case of Bro.
BENJAMIN W. SHEPHERD, which was decided in 1879. That Lodge, in 1878, had declared Bro. SHEPHERD to be sospeoded for non-payment of dnes. A memorial from Bro.
8HEPBE:ao to the Grand Lodge in 1879, asking that this snspensioo be set asida, was
referred to the Committee on Jnrisprndence, and that committee, from the memorial
and a letter written by Bro. GEORGE W. BoYDRN, then Master of the Lodge, which
gave a very full detail of thii. facts, fonnd that Bro. BHEPHRllD was a life-member of
the Lodge and exempt from dnes from the date of lhe removal of the Lodge to Taylorville. The following _la the conolnding sentence of its report:Your committee are of the opinion that the declaration of the snspeosion of
Bro. B. W, SHKPHERD was witnont authority of law and void, and that he is still a
life-member of that Lodge in good standing and must be so returned by the Lodge.
That report was concurred in by the Grand Lodge, and the direction in the sentence above qnoted became a mandate to Sincerity Lodge. That mandate the Lodge
has wholly disregarded, and has not at any time since, in its annnal reports to the
Grand Lodge, reported the name of Bro. BBRPHERD as one of its members.
In 1880 Bro. BOYDEN, who was still Master, filed a statement with the Grand Secretary which, in effect, stated that his former statement was incorrect and that he
had been misled by what he had heard and supposed to be trne, and asked that
the Grand Lodge rescind its former order. The Grand Lodge refused to consider his
request and advised that, if any further action was desired, it could be had only npon
the formal application of the Lodge and after notice given to Bro. SHEPHERD.
The papers now placed in the hands, of your committee are presumed to have
been intended as snch formal application. They consist only of two letters addressed
to ttie Grand Secretary, dated on the 6th and 7th of Angnst, 1881, stating, in eftect,
that Sincerf.ly Lodge gives notice that it will, at the next Annual Communication of
the Grand Lodge, show by its records that B. W. SHEPHERD was never a life-member
of that Lodge; that it" had a perfect right to suspend him for non-payment of dnes;"
that it desired "a rehearing after these facts have been established;" and that it
would "take an appeal from the decision of the Grand Lodge in the case, etc."
No copy from the records of the Lodge nor any evidence of any kind accompanied
those letters, or has since been forwarded or presented. Tho,ie papers are all that
have been placed in the hands of yonr committee, and, as it appears that the Lodge
therein proposes to ask a rehearing only after establishing the fact "that Bro. SHEPHE.BD never was a lire member of Sincerity Lodge," It is concl:oded that the Lodge
does not desire, at least at this time, to nrge its application for a rehearing •. Your
committee therefore recommend that the present application, if i1 can so be called,
be denied.
Bnt, before closing their report, they desire to call the attention of the Grand
Lodge again to the fact that Sincerity Lodge has thns far wholly disregarded the or·
der and· direction of the Grand Lodge, made In 1879, in respect to retnrniog Bro.
SHEPHRllD as a m~mber in good standing of that Lodge. The doty of the Lodge to
place his name upon its roll of members in good standing, and to return him as ench,
is plain, and is one that the Lodge cannot safely negl~ct.
Relative to decisions npon questions of Masonic law and other matters reported
in the Address of Grand Master TAYLOR at the present Oommnnlcation :-

LOct. 14,

During the year the Grand Master, in response to questions proposed to him, h!ls
decided:!. That a sob ordinate Lodge conld not, by a vote thereof, give any porijon of the
fonds of the Lodge In aid of the Garfield :M.onnment Association·.
Your committee agree with the Grand Master. The funds of a Masonic Lodge
are set apart for its necessary expenses and for the special calls of charity for
which the Lodge was instituted, and no Lodge should expend such fonds for any
other purpose, however worthy or patriotic it may be. For oil purposes, other
than those recognized as purely Masonic, the members of the. Lodge, desiring to
make contribntions, should make them from their private fnnds.
II. That the Master of a Lodge is justified· in refusing to entertain a oharge of nn·
masonio conduct against a Mason when the only specification is that the accused had
refused to renew a promissory note which the accuser had allowed to become barred
by the statute or limitations.
In a report made in 1871, and concnrred in by the Grand Lodge, the Committee on
Grievances said: "It Is not the province of the tribunals of Masonry to adjust
mere legal rights, whether pecnniary or otherwise, as the conrts of law alford all the
necessary facilities for the adjustment of eocb questions." Statutes of limitations
are jnetifled by legislators and approved by courts in every civilized eonntry, as the
expression of a wise pnblio policy; and certainly we shonld not make the Lodge the
plaoe where a negligent creditor should be allowed to attempt an enforcement of bis ·
stale claim.
III. That the reversal by the Grand Lodge of a judgment of expnlslon by R
subor1inate Lodge restores the party to all bis rights and privileges in hie Lodge.
Tb.is Is simply the law, and it is somewhat Sn'rprlslng that any Me.sonic officer in
the jurisdiction was so ignorant as to have asked for a decision thereupon.
IV. That when a Mason, who is a member of a Lodge but resides within the
jurisdiction of some other Lodge in this State, is guilty of an offense, charges may be
preferred against him either in bis own Lodge or in the Lodge within whos.e jurls·
diction be resides-both having jurisdiction, the one by reason of hie membership,
the other by reason of hie residence.
This is a just interpretation of the third subdivision of Section 1, Article U., Part
Ill., of the Constitntion, wbiob defines the judicial powers of the Lodge to embrace
"the exercise of discipline over its own members (except the Master,) arid all other
Masons wUhin its jul"iAdiution, and the settlement of contro'l'ersies between them ;
subject always to a revision by the Grand Lodge on appeal."
V. That it Is the dnty of an Inspector to refuse to give a certificate of qnallftcation to any Master elect who fails to qnalify.
To this yoor committee would add only that the Inspector should report to the
Grand Master the case of every Master elect who fails to qualify within a reasonable
time, that he may order a new election in the Lodge, or take sncb other steps as he
may deem necessary.
.
VI. That contribution by a non-affiliate of a sum equal to the regular dnes, and
the signing of the by-law of the Lodge to which be oontribntes, does not make him
a member of that Lodge; that be "bas no business to sign the by-laws;!' and that
membership in a Lodge can be acquired only in the manner prescribed in the Con·
etltution.
Your committee have only to express their sympathy for the Grand Master who
was reqnired to answer a question e.s:blbitlng such profound ignorance of the law,
Vil. That it Is neither right nor proper for a Master frequently to debate ques·
tions while ocoupying the Ohair.
The Master ought never to participate in the debate of questions before his Lodge,
unless be first calls one of bis Wardens or a Past Master to the Chair and takes the
floor.
VIII. That, nnder Article IX or the uniform code of by-laws, the Master may

enjoin seorecy upon all present in bis Lodge in regard to so oh matters as may trans·
plre therein which, in his judgment, should not be known elsewhere.
Undoubtedly, and, for any violation of such injunction, a charge of nnme.sonlo

IX. That there is no Masonic statute of limitation which will bar the proseon·
tion of a brother for on masonic conduct:
That an application for affiliation, accompanied by the necessary amount of
dues and the fee therefor, (if a fee be required,) plaoes the applicant in good stand·

application every six months or oftener if be choose; but that the particular appli·

That, if a non-affiliate who had thus maintained hie good standing should die, it
is the duty of the Lodge or Lodges having jnrisdictlon to bury him with Me.sonic
honors:
That, In case of a vaoancy In the office of Treasurer of a J,odge, the Master
should fill the 'l"&Cancy by appointment, and that no election can be held for that
purpose till the next annual election oconrs, except by dispensation from the Grand

That it is the duty of the Master ~fa Lodge to install bis sncceesor, and that it
is not the privilege of a Master elect to select the installing officer or in any way in·
terfere with the duties or privileges of the office nntil be bas been installed; bot that
a Master elect who bas been installed by a Pe.st Master, though selected by him·
self, is duly installed:
And that the Master bas discretion to admit or exclude visitors; and that, when
objectiou ls made, be may reqnire that the reasons therefor be stated to him and that
he must be the judge of their sufficiency.
All these last decisions, included under No. IX, are in acl)ord with our Constitution
and former decisions of onr Grand Lodge, and should be approved.
The Grand Master also decided that, when a judgment of conviction for an alle11ed
Me.sonic ofiense bas been reversed ancl set aside by the Grand Lodge, charges for
the same olfense may again be preferred and the accused be again put upon trial
therefor, a.nd that the testimony oftered ii\ the former trial, with other testimony,
·
.
may again be olfered.
Your committee do no~ agree with the Grand Master in this decision, although
they are aware that it is sustained by some Me.sonic. authorities of good repute.
There is a maxim which has come down to us from the old Roman judges, and which
has b~n adopted in every modern syst.em of jurisprudence, that it is for the
public weal that there should be an end to a litigation ; and, following this maxim,
that a defendant shall not be twice vexed with the same contention, whether that be
In its nature civil or criminal. Your committee think that the maxim should have
the same application in Me.sonic as in civil tribunals. On appeal from the judgment
of a subordinate Lodge the accuser may introduce in Grand Lodge any additional
or new evldenoe which be may have discovered; but, when the Grand Lodge bas determined that th~ accneed ought not to have been convicted, and bas vacated and set
aside a judgment of conviotion, witbont ordering a new trial, they think that its judg·
ment ought to be final and conclnsive. It is for the interest of our fraternity that there
1honld be some end to litigation.
In three instances the Grand Master was asked to interfere when objections were
made to the advancement of candidates-in one, by a Mason who was not a member
of t.b e Lodge in which the candidate bad been initiated, and in two others by other
Lodges. In all these cases he advised and, as your committee think, very properly,
that the Junior Warden or some member of the Lodge should make objection in
order that the canses of objection might be investigated. It is a matter of wonder
to ns that any Lodge or Master should have been found so derelict in Its or bis duty
to the fraternity as not to give immediate att.ention to objections made or stated by

688

Proceedings of tlie

[Oct. 14,

another Lodge, or even by any worthy Mason, to any candidate knocking a.t its doors
for advancement. The fraternity have a. right to assume that the iuvestiga.tion will
be fairly conducted and that all proper evidence will be gladly received and honestly
considered in the Lodge having jurisdiction, and your committee think therefore
that its determination should be final, and would not now propose any amendment
to or change of the law in that respect.
·10 the matter of the complaint by Wilmington Lodge, No. 198, against Los
Angeles Lodge, No. 42, reported by the Grand Master, it seems to your committee
that the first, and really the only qnestion for determination ·is which, if either of
the two Lodges, had jurisdiction at the date of the petition over the person of the
~nd that is a qnestion of residence at the date of the petition and for the
last six and the last twelve months next preceding that date. If Los Angeles Lodge
had jnrisdiction·of the petitioner, then its determination as to the validity of objections was final; but if it had not, under Section 2, Artfole III, Pa.rt III, of the Constitution, then a.II it had done with respect to him was unlawfully done and it ought not
to be permitted to do any other act in the matter of his petition or advancement.
Your committee have heard the statement~ of officere of the two LOdges and of
several brethren, but have been unable to arrive at any definite conclusion as to the
fact of the residence of the party. They therefore recommend that the whole matter be referred to the Grand Master, who can, in such form and ma.oner as in his
judgment shall seem most advisable nnder the circumstances, make inqniry as to the
facts, and, npon a determination of those facts, can make such order and give such
direction a.s the exigencies of the case shall demand; and they fnrther recommeQ.d
that, until the Grand Master she.II announce his decision to Los Angeles Lodge,
that Lodge be directed to take no further step or proceeding in the matter of the
advancement of the party in respect to whom the controversy has arisen.
Yonr committee are sorry to see that some ill feeling has been engendered on ac·
count of this controversy. There ought to have been no ill feeling heretofore, and there
should be none now. As soon as notice was given to Los Angeles Lodge that its
jurisdiction was qnestioned in the matter, it should have immediately stopped all further proceedings and, with the complaining Lodge, have taken the necessary steps
for a. determination of the vexed question; and all this should have been; doue in a
kindly spirit, with the purpose only of arriving at the facts. No Lodge should encroach upon the jurisdiction of another, or confer the degrees upon any one unworthy to receive them; and it is ouly fair to presume that it would not knowingly do so.
Hence there should be the utmost readiness and willingness to correct any errors in
that regard, and, in case of error, to endeavor as far as possible to correct it.
Whenever we see any considerable a.mount of feeling exhibited in such cases, we are
always led to suspect that there is something wrong somewhere.
All which is respectfully submitted by

The foregoing catalogne comprises one thousand four hnndred and forty-nine
bonnd volumes of Masonic books f of which there are·
7 volnmes, folio, containing 2,476 pages;
46 volnmes, 4to., containing 13,837 pages;
1161 volnmes, 8vo., containing 620, 224 pages ;
158 volumes, 12mo., containing 46,005 pages ;
21 volnmes, 16mo., containing 4,214 pages;
38 volumes, 24mo., containing 19,460 pages;
18 volumes, 32mo., containing 3,84.0 pages;
being in all 1,44.9 volumes, and aggregating 710,056 pages, thns showing an
average of nearly five hundred pages per volume.
In addition to the Transactions of Grand Bodies no.med in the foregoing, there are
a large number of pamphlets on hand, which, if a comparatively few oi the earlier
years could be procured, would, when bonnd, considerably increase the number and
antiquity of the books of that cle.88.
